Trades Numeracy
Textbook

Whole numbers to trigonometry, with key-by-key calculator steps for the TI-30Xa and the Sharp EL-531XT. For fabrication, pipe trades, millwright and carpentry pre-apprentices.
Skills for Success: Numeracy
Metric and imperial

About this book

This textbook covers the mathematics a pre-apprentice uses every day in the shop: whole numbers, fractions and decimals, percent and ratio, measurement and unit conversion, formulas and how to rearrange them, perimeter, area, volume, right triangles and trigonometry.

Each chapter opens with what you will learn and the key words to watch for. The ideas are explained in plain language, then shown in worked examples. Short Try it sets let you practise straight away. Each chapter ends with Shape Canvas worksheets that use the same drawings and practice ideas as the ACCESS Shape Canvas app.

Two calculators are used throughout: the Texas Instruments TI-30Xa and the Sharp EL-531XT. Every calculator box shows the keys for both, side by side, and what each display reads after the last key.

Sizes are given in metric first and imperial second. Answers to every Try it set and worksheet are in the separate Answer Key. The companion Exercise Book has more practice for each chapter.

The book serves four trades: fabrication, pipe trades, millwright and carpentry. Carpentry sits alongside the other three. Its examples and worksheets cover framing, stairs, sheet goods and concrete, and its code values are quoted from the BC Building Code. The page Using the BC Building Code explains how those quotes work.

Appendix A, Kitchen Math, follows Chapter 13. It covers recipe scaling, cooking measures and food yield percent.

How to read a size

In this book 1,250 mm means one thousand two hundred fifty millimetres. 5′ 312″ means five feet three and one half inches. The symbol ≈ means “about equal to” and is used when an answer is rounded.

How to use this book

Worked examples

Examples are numbered by chapter. Read the question, try it yourself, then check each step.

Example 1.8Counting bolts
A job needs 24 brackets. Each bracket is held by 4 bolts. How many bolts are needed?
Solution
  1. 24 groups of 4: 24 × 4.
  2. 20 × 4 = 80 and 4 × 4 = 16. 80 + 16 = 96.
96 bolts

Using the BC Building Code

The carpentry pages of this book quote the British Columbia Building Code 2024, Book I: General, written BCBC 2024 in this book. The code is set out in three Divisions. Division A covers compliance, objectives and functional statements. Division B holds the acceptable solutions, which are the technical requirements. Division C holds the administrative provisions.

Part 9 of Division B is titled Housing and Small Buildings. It applies to buildings of 3 storeys or less in building height, with a building area of not more than 600 m², used for residential occupancies, business and personal services occupancies, mercantile occupancies, or medium- and low-hazard industrial occupancies (Division A, Sentence 1.3.3.3.(1), page 1-12). The framing, stair, footing and floor values in this book all come from Part 9.

How a code number is built

LevelNumberFor example
Part9Housing and Small Buildings
Section9.8.Stairs, Ramps, Landings, Handrails and Guards
Subsection9.8.4.Step Dimensions
Article9.8.4.1.Dimensions for Risers
Sentence9.8.4.1.(1)The numbered sentence (1) inside the Article
Clause9.8.4.1.(1)(a)A lettered part of a Sentence, where the code uses one
Subclause9.8.4.1.(1)(a)(i)A part of a Clause, where the code uses one

The first number is the Part, the second the Section, the third the Subsection and the fourth the Article. The requirements themselves are in the Sentences, the numbers in brackets. A Sentence can be broken into Clauses and Subclauses.

How this book quotes the code

Every code value in this book names the Article and Sentence it comes from and the page of the code it is printed on, like this: BCBC 2024, Division B, Article 9.8.4.1. (page 9-30). Page 9-30 is the page number printed in the code itself, not a page of this book.

Values are quoted at the level the code states them. The stair rise limits are given in millimetres, so the book quotes millimetres. When the book shows the same value in inches, that is a conversion for the shop, not a code value.

A quote, read from the code text

Except for stairs serving areas only used as service rooms or service spaces, the rise, measured as the vertical nosing-to-nosing distance, must comply with Table 9.8.4.1. For a private stair the table gives a maximum rise of 200 mm and a minimum rise of 125 mm. Source: BCBC 2024, Division B, Sentence 9.8.4.1.(1) and Table 9.8.4.1. (page 9-30).

The plates are teaching drawings

The side view panel of the ACCESS teaching plate for Article 9.8.4.1. The plate shows the idea. The code text sets the values.

The drawings with a BCBC source line under them are ACCESS teaching plates. Each one shows a Part 9 Article. They were drawn from the code text to help you see the math, but a plate is not the code. The book prints the drawing part of a plate and writes the requirement under it, with each value quoted from the code text. The code text governs. If a plate and the code ever seem to disagree, follow the code text.

The full set of 922 plates is in the bcbc folder of the ACCESS Indigenous Skills4Success Numeracy site, the same site as the Numeracy Hub. There is one folder for each Section of Part 9 and one file for each Article, named with the Article number and title, for example “9.8.4.1 Dimensions for Risers”.

Check the code that applies to your job

BCBC 2024 took effect on March 8, 2024. The order that set it up lets some work carry on under the 2018 code, for example work under a building permit applied for before that date. Before you rely on a value on the job, check which code applies to your project.

Chapter
1

Whole Numbers

Every job in the shop starts with whole numbers. You count bolts and brackets, read sizes off a drawing, add up a cut list and work out how many pieces you can get from one length of stock.

This chapter reviews place value, rounding and estimating, and the four operations: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing. Each method is shown by hand first and then on the TI-30Xa and the Sharp EL-531XT, so you can check your work two ways.

In this chapter you will

  • Read and write whole numbers using place value
  • Round whole numbers and use rounding to estimate
  • Add and subtract lengths on a cut list
  • Multiply and divide to find totals, pieces and spacing
  • Work out averages and multi-step shop problems
  • Check answers with an estimate and with your calculator

Key words

  • whole number
  • digit
  • place value
  • rounding
  • estimate
  • sum and difference
  • factors and product
  • quotient and remainder
  • kerf
  • average

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.1 Whole numbers and place value1.1 Whole numbers and place value

A whole number is a number with no fraction or decimal part: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. Whole numbers are written with ten digits, 0 to 9.

The value of a digit depends on where it sits in the number. This is called place value. Each place is worth ten times the place to its right.

NumberTen thousandsThousandsHundredsTensOnes
6,0966096
12,45012450
305305
Table 1.1Place value of three numbers.

A zero holds a place. In 305 the zero shows there are no tens. Without it the number would read 35, which is a very different length.

Example 1.1Reading a size off a drawing
A drawing gives the length of a beam as 12,450 mm. Write the number in words and say what the 2 is worth.
Solution
  1. Split the number at the comma: 12 thousand and 450.
  2. Read each part: twelve thousand, four hundred fifty.
  3. The 2 is in the thousands place, so it is worth 2 × 1,000 = 2,000.
Twelve thousand four hundred fifty millimetres. The 2 is worth 2,000.
Commas and spaces

This book puts a comma between each group of three digits in numbers with four or more digits, for example 12,450. You may also see a small space used instead, as in 12 450. Both mean the same number. The conversion table at the back of this book groups long decimals with spaces, as in 0.453 592 37.

Try it 1.1
  1. Write 3,048 in words.
  2. Write in digits: seven thousand six hundred two.
  3. What is the 5 worth in 25,410?
  4. What is the 9 worth in 6,096?
  5. Which is longer, 2,450 mm or 2,405 mm?
  6. Write in digits: twenty thousand fifty.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.2 Rounding1.2 Rounding

Rounding replaces a number with a nearby number that is easier to work with. You round to a place: the nearest ten, the nearest hundred or the nearest thousand.

  1. Find the digit in the place you are rounding to.
  2. Look at the digit just to its right.
  3. If that digit is 5 or more, add one to the rounding digit. If it is 4 or less, leave the rounding digit as it is.
  4. Change every digit to the right of the rounding place to zero.
Example 1.2Rounding a length
Round 2,847 mm to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred.
Solution
  1. Nearest ten: the tens digit is 4. The digit to its right is 7, which is 5 or more, so the 4 becomes 5: 2,850 mm.
  2. Nearest hundred: the hundreds digit is 8. The digit to its right is 4, which is 4 or less, so the 8 stays: 2,800 mm.
2,850 mm to the nearest ten, 2,800 mm to the nearest hundred.
Example 1.3Rounding up past a nine
Round 6,960 to the nearest hundred.
Solution
  1. The hundreds digit is 9. The digit to its right is 6, so the 9 goes up by one.
  2. Nine plus one is ten, so write 0 in the hundreds place and carry 1 into the thousands: 6 thousands become 7 thousands.
7,000
Round at the end

Do the whole calculation with the exact numbers and round only the final answer. Rounding each step adds small errors together and the result can be a cut that is too short.

Try it 1.2
  1. Round 1,374 to the nearest ten.
  2. Round 1,375 to the nearest ten.
  3. Round 6,096 to the nearest hundred.
  4. Round 6,096 to the nearest thousand.
  5. Round 49,950 to the nearest hundred.
  6. Round 845 to the nearest hundred.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.3 Estimating1.3 Estimating

An estimate is a quick answer made with rounded numbers. It tells you roughly what the exact answer should be. If your calculator gives an answer far from your estimate, a key was probably missed or pressed twice.

Example 1.4Estimating a cut list
A cut list has four pieces: 1,250 mm, 875 mm, 640 mm, 1,480 mm. Estimate the total length.
Solution
  1. Round each length to the nearest hundred: 1,300, 900, 600, 1,500.
  2. Add the rounded numbers: 1,300 + 900 + 600 + 1,500 = 4,300.
About 4,300 mm. The exact total, found in Example 1.5, is 4,245 mm, which is close to the estimate.
Key idea

Estimate first, calculate second, compare third. An estimate does not replace the exact answer. It catches mistakes before they reach the saw.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.4 Adding1.4 Adding

Adding puts amounts together. The answer to an addition is the sum. To add by hand, line the numbers up by place value, ones under ones and tens under tens, and add each column from the right. When a column adds to 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry the tens digit to the next column.

Example 1.5Total length of a cut list
Find the exact total length of the four pieces: 1,250 mm, 875 mm, 640 mm, 1,480 mm.
Solution
  1. Ones: 0 + 5 + 0 + 0 = 5.
  2. Tens: 5 + 7 + 4 + 8 = 24. Write 4, carry 2.
  3. Hundreds: 2 + 8 + 6 + 4 + 2 (carried) = 22. Write 2, carry 2.
  4. Thousands: 1 + 1 + 2 (carried) = 4.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
1250+875+640+1480=
Display 4245.
Sharp EL-531XT
1250+875+640+1480=
Display 4’245.
The TI-30Xa shows 4245. The Sharp EL-531XT shows 4’245, with a small mark between the thousands and the hundreds. The total is 4,245 mm.
4,245 mm, close to the estimate of 4,300 mm.

The TI-30Xa shows no separator between groups of digits. Read its display from the right in groups of three to put the commas back: 4245 is 4,245. The Sharp EL-531XT marks each group of three with a small raised mark, as in 4’245.

Try it 1.4

  2. 608 + 1,295 + 47

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.5 Subtracting1.5 Subtracting

Subtracting takes one amount away from another. The answer is the difference. Line the numbers up by place value with the larger number on top. When the top digit in a column is smaller than the bottom digit, borrow 1 from the next column to the left. That 1 is worth 10 in the column you are working on.

Example 1.6What is left of the bar?
The four pieces from Example 1.5 (4,245 mm in total) are cut from a 6,000 mm bar. Ignore the width of the saw cuts. How long is the offcut?
Solution
  1. Write 6,000 on top and 4,245 below it.
  2. Ones: 0 − 5 needs a borrow. The tens and hundreds are 0, so borrow through them: 6,000 becomes 5 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones.
  3. 10 − 5 = 5, 9 − 4 = 5, 9 − 2 = 7, 5 − 4 = 1.
Calculator

6000−4245=
Display 1755.
Sharp EL-531XT

Display 1’755.
1,755 mm
Example 1.7Finding a hidden dimension
A drawing gives the overall length of a part as 2,400 mm and two of its three sections as 750 mm and 900 mm. Find the middle section.
Solution
  1. The three sections add up to the overall length.
  2. Add the sections you know: 750 + 900 = 1,650.
  3. Subtract from the overall length: 2,400 − 1,650 = 750.

Display 750.

The middle section is 750 mm.
Check a subtraction by adding

Add the answer back to the number you took away. You should get the number you started with: 1,755 + 4,245 = 6,000.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.6 Multiplying1.6 Multiplying

Multiplying is a fast way to add the same number many times. 24 × 4 means 24 groups of 4. The numbers you multiply are factors, and the answer is the product.

Example 1.8Counting bolts
A job needs 24 brackets. Each bracket is held by 4 bolts. How many bolts are needed?
Solution
  1. 24 groups of 4: 24 × 4.
  2. 20 × 4 = 80 and 4 × 4 = 16.
  3. 80 + 16 = 96.
Calculator

96 bolts
Example 1.9Multiplying by a two-digit number
You need 36 pieces, each 125 mm long. What total length of stock do the pieces use? Ignore the saw cuts.
Solution
  1. Split 36 into 30 + 6.
  2. 125 × 6 = 750.
  3. 125 × 30 = 3,750.
  4. Add the two parts: 750 + 3,750 = 4,500.

Splitting a number into parts works well in your head. On paper, most people multiply in columns, one digit of the bottom number at a time. Section 1.10 shows the column method step by step, for numbers up to three digits by three digits, with a times table.

Saw cuts take material

A saw blade turns a strip of metal into chips. The width of that strip is the kerf. When you cut many pieces, the kerf adds up. With a kerf of 3 mm, 12 cuts remove 12 × 3 = 36 mm of stock. The problems in this book give the kerf whenever it counts.

Try it 1.6

  2. 48 × 25
  3. 125 × 64
  4. 18 pieces at 450 mm. Total length?
  5. 7 cuts with a 3 mm kerf. Stock lost?
  6. 6 rows of 14 bolts. How many bolts?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.7 Dividing1.7 Dividing

Dividing splits an amount into equal groups or equal parts. In 6,000 ÷ 450, the number being divided (6,000) is the dividend, the number you divide by (450) is the divisor, and the answer is the quotient. When the division does not come out even, the amount left over is the remainder.

Example 1.10Pieces from one bar
How many 450 mm pieces can you cut from a 6,000 mm bar? Ignore the saw cuts. How long is the offcut?
Solution
  1. Divide: 6,000 ÷ 450. The calculator shows 13.33333333.
  2. Only whole pieces count, so you get 13 pieces.
  3. The 13 pieces use 13 × 450 = 5,850 mm.
  4. The offcut is the remainder: 6,000 − 5,850 = 150 mm.

13 pieces, with a 150 mm offcut.
Whole pieces only

The calculator shows 13.33333333 pieces. Only whole pieces count, so the answer is 13. Even 13.9 would still be 13 pieces, because the 14th piece does not fit. Think about what the answer means before you round.

Example 1.11Long division by hand
Divide 4,500 by 36.
Solution
  1. 36 does not go into 4. It goes into 45 once: 1 × 36 = 36, and 45 − 36 = 9.
  2. Bring down the 0 to make 90. 36 goes into 90 twice: 2 × 36 = 72, and 90 − 72 = 18.
  3. Bring down the last 0 to make 180. 36 goes into 180 five times: 5 × 36 = 180, remainder 0.
  4. Read the answer from the top: 125.
Calculator

125. This undoes Example 1.9: 36 × 125 = 4,500.

Equal spacing is a division problem with one twist. When there is a hole at each end of a straight row, the number of spaces is one less than the number of holes.

Example 1.12Equal hole spacing
Six holes are drilled in a straight row along a 1,200 mm plate. The first and last holes are 100 mm from the ends. The holes are evenly spaced. How far apart are the holes, centre to centre?
Solution
  1. Distance from the first hole to the last hole: 1,200 − 100 − 100 = 1,000 mm.
  2. Six holes make 6 − 1 = 5 spaces.
  3. Spacing: 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 mm.
Calculator
TI-30Xa

Display 200.
Sharp EL-531XT
(1200−2×100)÷5=
Display 200.
200 mm centre to centre.
Key idea

In a straight row with a hole at each end, spaces = holes − 1. Draw a quick sketch and count the gaps if you are unsure.

Carpenters use the same idea the other way round: studs = spaces + 1. Section 1.12 counts studs and joists along a wall or floor.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.8 Averages and multi-step problems1.8 Averages and multi-step problems

The average of a set of numbers is one number that represents the whole set. Add the numbers, then divide by how many numbers there are.

Example 1.13Average welds per day
Over five days a welder completes 38, 42, 45, 40 and 35 joints. What is the average number of joints per day?
Solution
  1. Add: 38 + 42 + 45 + 40 + 35 = 200.
  2. There are 5 days, so divide by 5: 200 ÷ 5 = 40.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
(38+42+45+40+35)÷5=
Display 40.
Sharp EL-531XT
(38+42+45+40+35)÷5=
Display 40.
The brackets make the calculator add first and divide second. Chapter 3 explains why.
40 joints per day.

The average is one way to describe a set of numbers. Two more are the median and the mode. The median is the middle number once the set is put in order. For the welder, 35, 38, 40, 42, 45 has 40 in the middle, so the median is 40 joints. The mode is the number that comes up most often. Each number of joints comes up once, so this set has no mode.

Mean, median and mode

Mean (average): add them up and divide by how many. Median: put them in order and take the middle one. Mode: the one that comes up most often. Section 1.11 works through all three with shop tables and graphs.

Many shop problems take more than one step. Write down what you know, decide which operation each step needs, and check the final answer against an estimate.

Example 1.14Ordering brackets
A job has 3 units. Each unit needs 14 brackets, and you want 6 spares. Brackets come in boxes of 10. How many boxes do you order?
Solution
  1. Brackets for the units: 3 × 14 = 42.
  2. Add the spares: 42 + 6 = 48 brackets.
  3. Boxes: 48 ÷ 10 = 4.8.
  4. 4 boxes hold only 40 brackets, which is not enough. Round up to 5 boxes.

Rounding up or rounding down

When you are counting pieces you can cut, round down: a part piece is scrap. When you are counting boxes, lengths or sheets you need to buy, round up: a part box still has to be bought.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.9 Time on the job1.9 Time on the job

Shifts, breaks, timesheets and pay all run on the clock. The amount of time that passes between a start time and an end time is the elapsed time. Time does not count in tens: 60 minutes make an hour, so you cannot subtract clock times the way you subtract lengths.

Reading a clock

A clock face has two hands. The short hand points to the hour. The long hand points to the minutes. The numbers 1 to 12 mark the hours for the short hand. For the long hand, each number is 5 minutes more than the one before: the 1 means 5 minutes, the 2 means 10 minutes, and the 9 means 45 minutes. The small marks between the numbers are single minutes.

When the long hand is past the 12, the short hand has moved past the hour it just reached. At 7:15 it sits a quarter of the way from the 7 to the 8.

Example 1.15Reading three clocks
Read clocks A, B and C in Figure 1.4.
Solution
  1. A: the short hand is just past the 7, so the hour is 7. The long hand is on the 3: 3 × 5 = 15 minutes. A reads 7:15.
  2. B: the short hand is near the 12 but has not reached it, so the hour is still 11. The long hand is on the 10: 10 × 5 = 50 minutes. B reads 11:50.
  3. C: the short hand is past the 3. The long hand is on the 7: 7 × 5 = 35 minutes. C reads 3:35.
A is 7:15, B is 11:50 and C is 3:35.

Elapsed time

To find how long a job took, count up from the start time in three steps: up to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the minutes that are left. This works across noon too.

Example 1.16A job that runs past noon
A pour starts at 7:45 a.m. and finishes at 3:20 p.m. How long does it take?
Solution
  1. Up to the next whole hour: 7:45 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. is 15 minutes.
  2. Whole hours: 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. is 7 hours: 8:00 to 12:00 is 4 hours and 12:00 to 3:00 is 3 more.
  3. The minutes that are left: 3:00 p.m. to 3:20 p.m. is 20 minutes.
  4. Add: 7 h + 15 min + 20 min = 7 h 35 min.
7 h 35 min.

A clock face does not say morning or afternoon. Times from midnight to noon are a.m. and times from noon to midnight are p.m. Many sites, schedules and phones use the 24-hour clock instead, which counts the hours from 00 to 23 after midnight. For a p.m. time from 1:00 p.m. on, add 12 to the hour: 3:35 p.m. is 15:35.

Table 1.2The same times on the 12-hour and the 24-hour clock. 12:00 p.m. is noon.

Decimal hours and timesheets

Timesheets and pay use decimal hours. To change minutes to a decimal part of an hour, divide by 60: 45 minutes is 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 hours. To change a decimal part of an hour back to minutes, multiply by 60. Chapter 5 covers decimals in full.

Example 1.17A week on the timesheet
A pre-apprentice works the week below. Each day has a 30 minute unpaid lunch. Find the hours for each day, the total for the week in hours and minutes and in decimal hours, and the pay before deductions at $27.80 an hour.
Solution
  1. For each day, find the time on site by counting up from the start to the finish. Monday: 7:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. is 8 h 30 min.
  2. Take off the 30 minute lunch: 8 h 30 min − 30 min = 8 h.
  3. Add the paid time for the five days: 8 h + 8 h 45 min + 8 h 15 min + 7 h 30 min + 6 h 15 min = 38 h 45 min.
  4. In decimal hours: 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75, so 38 h 45 min = 38.75 hours.
  5. Pay: 38.75 × 27.80 = $1,077.25.

A job log shows 6.4 hours. How many hours and minutes is that?

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.10 Multiplying in columns1.10 Multiplying in columns

To multiply by a number with two or more digits on paper, work in columns. Write the larger number on top and line the digits up on the right. Multiply the top number by each digit of the bottom number in turn, starting with the ones. Each answer is a partial product. Then add the partial products.

The digits of the bottom number are worth different amounts. In 26, the 2 is worth 20. So when you multiply by the tens digit, the answer is ten times bigger, and you write a zero in the ones column first to hold the place. When you multiply by the hundreds digit, write two zeros. These zeros hold the places. They are shown in red below.

Example 1.19Three digits by two digits
A job needs 26 pieces of flat bar, each 347 mm long. Ignore the saw cuts. Find the total length by multiplying 347 × 26 in columns.
Solution
  1. Multiply 347 by the ones digit, 6: 347 × 6 = 2,082.
  2. Multiply by the tens digit, 2, which is worth 20. Write a zero to hold the place, then 347 × 2 = 694 goes in front: 6,940.
  3. Add the partial products: 2,082 + 6,940 = 9,022.
  4. Check with an estimate: 350 × 30 = 10,500. The answer is close.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
347×26=
Display 9022.
Sharp EL-531XT
347×26=
Display 9’022.
9,022 mm
Example 1.20Three digits by three digits
Multiply 408 × 235 in columns.
Solution
  1. Multiply 408 by the ones digit, 5: 408 × 5 = 2,040.
  2. Multiply by the tens digit, 3, which is worth 30. Write a zero to hold the place, then 408 × 3 = 1,224 goes in front: 12,240.
  3. Multiply by the hundreds digit, 2, which is worth 200. Write 2 zeros to hold the place, then 408 × 2 = 816 goes in front: 81,600.
  4. Add the partial products: 2,040 + 12,240 + 81,600 = 95,880.
  5. Estimate: 400 × 200 = 80,000 and 400 × 250 = 100,000. The answer sits between them.
Calculator
TI-30Xa

Display 95880.
Sharp EL-531XT
408×235=
Display 95’880.
95,880
Do not drop the zeros that hold the places

Without the zeros, the three rows of 408 × 235 would add to 2,040 + 1,224 + 816 = 4,080, far below the estimate of about 80,000. An estimate catches this mistake every time.

Column multiplication goes faster when you know the times table. Find a product where a row meets a column: 7 × 8 is in row 7 under column 8.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.11 Median, mode, tables and graphs1.11 Median, mode, tables and graphs

Section 1.8 found the average, also called the mean. The median and the mode describe a set of numbers in two other ways. Put the numbers in order first. That makes the median and the mode easy to find.

Example 1.21The median of an odd number of values
Find the median of the welder’s joints in Example 1.13: 38, 42, 45, 40, 35.
Solution
  1. Put them in order: 35, 38, 40, 42, 45.
  2. There are 5 values, so the middle one is the 3rd: 40.
The median is 40 joints. Here the mean is also 40.
Example 1.22The median and mode of an even number of values
A machine shop logs parts finished each shift: 12, 15, 9, 14, 15, 11. Find the mean, the median and the mode.
Solution
  1. Mean: 12 + 15 + 9 + 14 + 15 + 11 = 76, and 76 ÷ 6 = 12.67 to two decimal places.
  2. Order: 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 15. There are 6 values, so there are two middle ones, 12 and 14. The median is halfway between: (12 + 14) ÷ 2 = 13.
  3. Mode: 15 comes up twice. Every other value comes up once.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
(12+15+9+14+15+11)÷6=
Display 12.66666667
Sharp EL-531XT
(12+15+9+14+15+11)÷6=
Display 12.66666667
Mean 12.67 parts, median 13 parts, mode 15 parts.

Reading a table

Trade tables put numbers in rows and columns. Read across a row and down a column to find a value. The table below logs the bolts a crew used on each shift of a 7-shift week.

Table 1.6Bolts used on each shift.
Example 1.23Mean, median and mode from a table
Use Table 1.6. Find the mean, median and mode of the bolts used per shift.
Solution
  1. Mean: 46 + 52 + 48 + 52 + 55 + 41 + 49 = 343. 343 ÷ 7 = 49.
  2. Median: in order, 41, 46, 48, 49, 52, 52, 55. The 4th of 7 values is the middle: 49.
  3. Mode: 52 comes up twice.
Calculator

Mean 49, median 49, mode 52 bolts.

Bar graphs and line graphs

A bar graph shows each value as a bar. Read the value at the top of the bar against the scale on the left. A line graph joins the values with a line, so you can see a change from one point to the next.

Example 1.24Reading a bar graph
Use Figure 1.7. On which day were the most sheets hung? Find the mean, median and mode.
Solution
  1. The tallest bars are Tuesday and Thursday, 24 sheets each.
  2. Mean: 18 + 24 + 21 + 24 + 23 = 110, and 110 ÷ 5 = 22.
  3. Median: in order, 18, 21, 23, 24, 24. The middle value is 23.
  4. Mode: 24 comes up twice.
Tuesday and Thursday. Mean 22, median 23, mode 24 sheets.
Example 1.25Reading a line graph
Use Figure 1.8. How many rods were used from Monday night to Friday night? What is the mean number used per day over those 4 days, and what is the mode?
Solution
  1. Used each day: 240 − 205 = 35, 205 − 180 = 25, 180 − 150 = 30, 150 − 120 = 30.
  2. Total used: 240 − 120 = 120 rods.
  3. Mean: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 rods per day.
  4. Mode: 30 comes up twice in 35, 25, 30, 30.
120 rods. Mean 30 rods per day, mode 30.

  3. Find the mode of 5, 7, 5, 9, 7, 5.

  5. In Figure 1.7, how many more sheets were hung on Tuesday than on Monday?
  6. In Figure 1.8, on which day were the most rods used?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 1 Whole Numbers1.12 Carpentry: studs, joists and cut lists1.12 Carpentry: studs, joists and cut lists

In a wood-frame wall, the upright pieces are studs. They stand between a bottom plate and a top plate. In a floor, the joists lie side by side. Studs and joists are set out at an equal spacing measured from the centre of one to the centre of the next. Carpenters call this the spacing on centre, written o.c.

The BC Building Code sets the largest stud spacing allowed. Article 9.23.10.1, Sentence (1) says the size and spacing of studs shall conform to Table 9.23.10.1 (page 9-182). Part of the table for exterior walls is below. The spacings in the code are in millimetres.

Example 1.26Counting studs
A wall is 4,800 mm long. Studs go at 400 mm o.c., starting at one end, with a stud at each end. How many studs are there?
Solution
  1. Spaces: 4,800 ÷ 400 = 12.
  2. There is a stud at each end, so studs = spaces + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13.
  3. Count the studs in Figure 1.10 to check.

Example 1.27A length that does not divide evenly
A wall is 3,700 mm long. The studs may be no more than 400 mm o.c. Lay them out at 400 mm from one end, with a stud at each end. How many studs, and how wide is the last space?
Solution
  1. Spaces: 3,700 ÷ 400 = 9.25.
  2. A space wider than 400 mm is not allowed, so round the spaces up: 10 spaces.
  3. Studs: 10 + 1 = 11.
  4. The first 9 spaces are 400 mm: 9 × 400 = 3,600 mm. The last space is 3,700 − 3,600 = 100 mm.
Calculator

Display 9.25
11 studs. The last space is 100 mm.
Spacing is a maximum

When the spacing is the largest allowed, round the number of spaces up, never down. Rounding down would make every space wider than the limit.

Example 1.28A cut list for blocking
Blocking fits between studs that are 38 mm thick and set at 400 mm o.c. Each block is 400 − 38 = 362 mm long. You need 12 blocks, cut from boards 2,440 mm long. Each cut takes a 3 mm kerf. How many blocks come from one board, how many boards do you need, and how long is the offcut from each full board?
Solution
  1. Each block uses its length plus one saw cut: 362 + 3 = 365 mm.
  2. Blocks per board: 2,440 ÷ 365 = 6.68. Only whole blocks count: 6 blocks.
  3. Boards: 12 ÷ 6 = 2.00. Round up: 2 boards.
  4. Offcut from a board cut into 6 blocks: 2,440 − 6 × 365 = 250 mm.

6 blocks per board, 2 boards, and a 250 mm offcut from each full board.
Example 1.29Estimating sheathing
A shed has walls of 9,760 mm, 6,100 mm, 9,760 mm, 6,100 mm. The walls are sheathed with sheets 1,220 mm wide, standing on end, one row high. Ignore openings and corners. Estimate the number of sheets, then find it exactly.
Solution
  1. Estimate: round each wall to the nearest thousand: 10,000 + 6,000 + 10,000 + 6,000 = 32,000 mm. 32,000 ÷ 1,200 is a little under 27.
  2. Exact: the walls add to 9,760 + 6,100 + 9,760 + 6,100 = 31,720 mm.
  3. 31,720 ÷ 1,220 = 26.

  2. A wall is 3,000 mm long with studs at 600 mm o.c. and a stud at each end. How many studs?
  3. A floor is 5,500 mm long. Joists may be no more than 400 mm o.c., with a joist at each end. How many joists?
  4. In Table 1.7, what is the largest spacing for 38 × 89 studs in an exterior wall that supports a roof plus one floor?
  5. How many 600 mm blocks come from a 3,660 mm board with a 3 mm kerf on each cut?

Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT

A scientific calculator is a shop tool like a tape measure or a square. This book shows every calculator step on two calculators, the TI-30Xa and the Sharp EL-531XT. Both give the same answers, but they do not always take the keys in the same order. This chapter walks you around both faceplates: which keys do what, how each calculator wants its keys pressed, and how to read the display and check a result.

In this chapter you will

  • Find the main keys on both calculators
  • Turn on, clear and fix a mistyped number
  • Use the 2nd and 2ndF keys
  • Key in negatives, brackets, squares, roots, powers and π
  • Use the fraction, percent and memory keys
  • Set DEG and use the trig keys, then check the answer

Key words

  • key sequence
  • display
  • second function
  • D.A.L.
  • memory

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.1 Meet the two calculators2.1 Meet the two calculators

Both calculators have the same kinds of keys: number keys, the four operations (+ − × ÷), an equals key, and function keys for squares, roots, powers, π, fractions, memory and angles. The keys are in different places, so take a few minutes with the drawings below and your own calculator.

The display is the screen. The TI-30Xa display shows a number of up to 10 digits, with small indicators such as DEG and 2nd. The Sharp EL-531XT shows two lines: the calculation you keyed in on the top line and the answer on the bottom line.

A key sequence is the list of keys you press, in order, to do a calculation. Every calculator box in this book shows the key sequence for both calculators and the display each one shows at the end. Table 2.1 lists the keys that look or work differently on the two calculators.

JobTI-30XaSharp EL-531XT

Turn offOFF2ndF then ON/C (OFF is printed above it)
Second functions2nd2ndF
Change the sign of a number+⇄− after the digits+/− before the number
Square root√x after the number√ before the number, then =
Squarex² after the numberx² after the number, then =
Store in memorySTO then 1, 2 or 3STO then a letter key (A to F, X, Y, M)
Fix a mistyped digit←DEL
Table 2.1Keys that differ between the two calculators.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.2 Turning on, clearing and fixing mistakes2.2 Turning on, clearing and fixing mistakes

Press ON/C to turn either calculator on. To turn the TI-30Xa off, press OFF. To turn the Sharp off, press 2ndF and then ON/C, because OFF is the second function printed in orange above the ON/C key. These steps are for the battery TI-30Xa, the model drawn in this book. The TI-30Xa Solar works differently: its guidebook says to expose the solar panel to light to turn it on and to cover the panel with the slide case to turn it off.

Start every calculation with a clear calculator. The calculator boxes in this book all start that way: press ON/C twice before the keys shown, and check that DEG is on the display.

Example 2.1Fixing a wrong number
You meant to key 7 + 9 but pressed 8 instead of 9. Then you meant to key 125 × 4 but typed 1255. Fix each mistake without starting over.
Solution
  1. TI-30Xa: press ON/C once. One press clears only the number you were keying, so 7 + is still waiting. Key 9 and press =.
  2. TI-30Xa: press ← to delete the last digit typed. 1255 becomes 125. Carry on with × 4 =.
  3. Sharp: press DEL. When the cursor is at the right end of the line, DEL deletes the last character. Then key the right digit.

Display 16.
Delete the last digit

Display 500.
Sharp EL-531XT
ON/C once

Display 16.
Delete the last digit
125×4=
Display 500.
The Sharp column shows each line keyed without the mistake. On the Sharp, use DEL to make the fix. ON/C on the Sharp clears the entry.
7 + 9 = 16 and 125 × 4 = 500.
When in doubt, start again

On the TI-30Xa, pressing ON/C twice clears the display and every waiting operation. On the Sharp, ON/C clears the entry. If you are not sure what the calculator is holding, clear it and key the calculation again from the start.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.3 Second functions: the 2nd and 2ndF keys2.3 Second functions: the 2nd and 2ndF keys

There are more jobs than keys, so most keys do two jobs. The job printed on the key is its first function. The job printed above the key is its second function. To use a second function, press 2nd on the TI-30Xa or 2ndF on the Sharp, then press the key.

On the TI-30Xa, 2nd shows on the display while it waits for the next key. On the Sharp, the second functions are printed in orange, and 2ndF shows on the display after you press 2ndF. Some functions are a second function on one calculator and a key of their own on the other. The cube, x³, is an example.

Example 2.2Cube and cube root
Find 5³ (5 × 5 × 5) and the cube root of 27.
Solution
  1. On the TI-30Xa, x³ and ³√x are second functions, so press 2nd before each one.
  2. On the Sharp, x³ has its own key. ³√ is the second function printed above the x³ key, so press 2ndF first.

5³ = 125 and the cube root of 27 is 3.
Read the key before you press it

If the label you want is above the key, you need 2nd or 2ndF first.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.4 Two ways to take keys2.4 Two ways to take keys

The two calculators work out the same answer but want some keys in a different order.

On the TI-30Xa, a function key such as x², √x or SIN goes after the number, and it works at once. Key 144, press √x, and 12 shows straight away.

The Sharp has D.A.L. printed on its faceplate. For you, D.A.L. means this: press the keys in the same order the calculation is written. For √144 that is √ first, then 144, then =. The line is worked out when you press =. The top line of the display shows what you keyed, so you can read it back first.

Example 2.3Square and square root
Find 12² and √144.
Solution
  1. 12² means 12 × 12. Both calculators take x² after the number. The Sharp needs = to finish.
  2. √144 asks which number times itself makes 144. The TI-30Xa takes √x after the number. The Sharp takes √ first, as written.

12² = 144 and √144 = 12. Each answer checks the other.

  2. Write the Sharp keys for √81.

  6. Find the cube root of 64.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.5 Negative numbers2.5 Negative numbers

A negative number is less than zero, such as −5. Both calculators have a change-sign key that makes a number negative. It is not the minus key. The minus key subtracts one number from another.

On the TI-30Xa, key the digits first and then press +⇄−. On the Sharp, press +/− first and then the digits, the way the number is written.

Example 2.4A calculation with a negative number
Find 42 × (−5) + 120.
Solution
  1. The −5 is a negative number, so it needs the change-sign key, not the minus key.
  2. 42 × (−5) = −210, then −210 + 120 = −90. Both displays show the minus sign in front.
Calculator

Display -90.
Sharp EL-531XT

Display -90.
−90
Change sign or subtract?

Use the minus key between two numbers: 50 − 8. Use the change-sign key for a number that is negative on its own: 6 × (−4).

Section 3.8 in Chapter 3 covers positive and negative numbers in full: the number line, adding and subtracting with signs, and the sign rules for × and ÷.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.6 Brackets, powers and π2.6 Brackets, powers and π

Brackets tell the calculator which part to work out first. Both calculators have ( and ) keys and take them in the order written: for (12 + 8) × 3, key ( 12 + 8 ) × 3 = and both show 60. Chapter 3 explains when you need them.

An exponent says how many of that number are multiplied together. 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. Use the yˣ key: the number, then yˣ, then the exponent, then =. For 2⁵, key 2 yˣ 5 = on either calculator. Both show 32, and the Sharp shows 2^5= on its top line.

The π key enters the number π, about 3.14. Use it instead of typing 3.14, so the answer keeps all the digits.

Example 2.5Using the π key
The distance around a circle is π × D, where D is the diameter (across the circle through its centre). The area is π × r², where r is the radius (half the diameter). A round duct has D = 150 mm and r = 75 mm. Find both, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Distance around: π × 150 = 471.2388..., which rounds to 471.24 mm.
  2. Area: 75² = 5,625, then π × 5,625 = 17,671.458..., which rounds to 17,671.46 mm². Key 75 x² × π = on both calculators.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.7 The fraction key2.7 The fraction key

Both calculators have an a b/c key for fractions. To key a mixed number such as 3¼, key the whole number, a b/c, the top number, a b/c, the bottom number. The answer comes back as a fraction. Chapter 4 covers fractions in full.

Example 2.6Fractions of an inch
Add 3¼ in and 2⅝ in. Then change ⅜ in to a decimal.
Solution
  1. Key 3 a b/c 1 a b/c 4 for 3¼ and 2 a b/c 5 a b/c 8 for 2⅝.
  2. The TI-30Xa shows 5⌟7⌟8 and the Sharp shows 5┌7┌8. Both mean 5 and 7/8: the whole number, then the top number, then the bottom number.
  3. To change a fraction answer to a decimal, press 2nd F⇄D on the TI-30Xa. On the Sharp, press a b/c after the answer. The second row changes ⅜ to a decimal.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.8 Percent2.8 Percent

The percent key (%) is a second function on both calculators: 2nd % on the TI-30Xa and 2ndF % on the Sharp, where % is printed above the 1 key. On the TI-30Xa you finish with =. On the Sharp, 2ndF % works out the line itself, so you do not press = after it.

Example 2.7Percent of a number, and adding a percent
An order is for 250 bolts. Find 15% of 250. Then find 250 plus 15% more.
Solution
  1. 15% of 250: on the TI-30Xa key 250 × 15 2nd % =. On the Sharp key 250 × 15 2ndF %.
  2. 250 plus 15%: on the TI-30Xa key 250 + 15 2nd % =. On the Sharp key 250 + 15 2ndF %. The calculator adds 15% of 250 to 250.

15% of 250 is 37.5. Adding 15% gives 287.5, so order 288 bolts.
Percent without the % key

15% means 15 out of 100. You can always key it as × 15 ÷ 100: 250 × 15 ÷ 100 = 37.5. Chapter 6 covers percent in full.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.9 Memory: STO and RCL2.9 Memory: STO and RCL

A memory holds a number so you do not have to write it down and key it again. STO (store) puts a number in a memory. RCL (recall) brings it back.

The TI-30Xa has three memories, 1, 2 and 3. Press STO then 1 to store the display in memory 1. The Sharp names its memories with letters: A to F, X, Y and M. The letters are printed at the upper right above some keys. A is above yˣ, so STO then yˣ stores in A, and the box shows that key as A. On the Sharp, STO finishes the line you keyed and stores the answer.

Example 2.8Storing a cut list total
Two pieces, 1,250 mm and 375 mm, are cut from a 6,000 mm bar. Ignore the saw cuts. Store the total of the pieces, clear the display, then find the offcut.
Solution
  1. 1,250 + 375 = 1,625. Store it in memory 1 (A on the Sharp).
  2. Press ON/C. The memory keeps the number.
  3. 6,000 − RCL 1 = 6,000 − 1,625 = 4,375.
Calculator
TI-30Xa

Display 4375.
Sharp EL-531XT

Display 4’375.
The TI-30Xa shows 4375. and the Sharp shows 4’375. The memory kept 1,625 after ON/C on both calculators.
4,375 mm
Old numbers stay in memory

Clearing with ON/C does not empty the memories, so a memory can still hold a number from an earlier job. Store the number you need before you recall it.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.10 Angles: DEG and the trig keys2.10 Angles: DEG and the trig keys

The trig keys SIN, COS and TAN work with angles. Chapter 13 explains what they mean. Angles can be measured in degrees, radians or grads, and the calculator must be set to the unit you are using. This book uses degrees.

Each press of DRG changes the angle unit in the order DEG, RAD, GRAD. The unit shows at the top of the display. Before any trig calculation, check that DEG is showing. If RAD or GRAD shows, press DRG until DEG comes back.

The trig keys follow the same rule as the other functions. On the TI-30Xa, key the angle and then SIN. On the Sharp, press sin, the angle and =. The inverse keys, SIN⁻¹, COS⁻¹ and TAN⁻¹, are second functions. They take a number and give back an angle.

Example 2.9Trig keys and their inverses
Find sin 30°. Find the angle whose tangent is 0.75, to two decimal places. Then find 600 × tan 35°, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. sin 30° = 0.5.
  2. The angle whose tangent is 0.75 uses TAN⁻¹: 2nd TAN⁻¹ on the TI-30Xa, 2ndF tan⁻¹ on the Sharp. The display shows 36.86989765, which rounds to 36.87°.
  3. 600 × tan 35°: on the TI-30Xa, 35 TAN gives tan 35°, then × 600. On the Sharp, key tan 35 × 600 = as written. 420.1245229 rounds to 420.12.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.11 Checking a result2.11 Checking a result

A calculator does exactly what you key, including your mistakes. Before you cut or order, check the answer in at least one of these ways.

  1. Estimate first. Round the numbers and work it out in your head, as in Chapter 1. The calculator answer should be close.
  2. Work it backwards. If √144 = 12, then 12² should give 144. If 6,000 − 1,625 = 4,375, then 4,375 + 1,625 should give 6,000.
  3. Read the Sharp top line. It shows the calculation you keyed, so you can spot a wrong number before you press =.
  4. Key it again. If the second answer differs from the first, key it a third time slowly.

An answer with more than 10 digits does not fit on the display. The calculator then shows it with a small number at the right, called an exponent of 10. For 123,456,789 × 1,000, both calculators show 1.23456789 with a small 11, which means 1.23456789 × 10¹¹, or 123,456,789,000.

Write the answer with its unit

The display shows a number, not a size. Write the unit next to every answer you copy down: 4,375 mm, not 4375. A number without a unit is a guess on the shop floor.

Chapter 2 Your Calculator: TI-30Xa and Sharp EL-531XT2.12 Tape lengths in feet, inches and fractions2.12 Tape lengths in feet, inches and fractions

A carpenter’s tape reads feet, inches and fractions of an inch, such as 8′ 538″ (8 feet 538 inches). To work with a length like this on either calculator, change it to inches first. One foot is 12 inches, so the length in inches is feet × 12 + inches. The fraction key carries the fraction of an inch.

BEDMAS works the × 12 before the +, so no brackets are needed: key 8 × 12 + 5 a b/c 3 a b/c 8 =. Both calculators show the answer as a mixed number of inches, the same way they show any fraction answer (Section 2.7).

Example 2.10Keying a tape length
A stud is cut to 8′ 538″. Find its length in inches. Then find it in millimetres, to the nearest millimetre. One inch is exactly 25.4 mm.
Solution

  2. Millimetres: carry on from the answer with × 25.4 =. 10138 × 25.4 = 2,574.925, which rounds to 2,575 mm.
  3. On the Sharp, the second row puts the inches in brackets, because it keys the whole line in written order.

Example 2.11Adding tape lengths
Two pieces of trim, 7′ 458″ and 3′ 934″, are butted end to end. Find the total length in feet and inches.

  1. Change both to inches in one line: 7 × 12 + 458 + 3 × 12 + 934 = 13438 in. BEDMAS does both × 12 before the additions.

Chapter
3

Order of Operations

What is 3 + 4 × 5? Add first and you get 35. Multiply first and you get 23. Only one answer can be right, so everyone who works with numbers follows the same order, and so does your calculator. This chapter sets out that order, BEDMAS, and shows when the calculator needs brackets that are not written on the page.

In this chapter you will

  • Use BEDMAS to work a calculation step by step
  • Work out brackets, powers and roots in the right order
  • Work left to right for × and ÷, and for + and −
  • Treat a fraction bar as a grouping symbol
  • Key brackets so the calculator follows the same order

Key words

  • order of operations
  • BEDMAS
  • brackets
  • exponent
  • square
  • square root

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.1 Why order matters3.1 Why order matters

A calculation with more than one operation can be read in more than one way. The order of operations is the agreed order for working one out. When everyone uses the same order, a calculation written on a drawing or in a formula means the same thing to everyone who reads it.

Example 3.1Bolts in a crate
A crate holds 3 loose bolts and 4 bags of 5 bolts. The count is written 3 + 4 × 5. How many bolts are in the crate?
Solution
  1. The 4 bags of 5 bolts are 4 × 5 = 20 bolts. That multiplication has to happen first.
  2. Add the loose bolts: 3 + 20 = 23.
  3. Adding first, 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 × 5 = 35, counts the 3 loose bolts as if they were in bags. That is wrong.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
3+4×5=
Display 23.
Sharp EL-531XT
3+4×5=
Display 23.
Both calculators multiply before they add, so both show 23 even though the keys are pressed left to right.
23 bolts

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.2 BEDMAS3.2 BEDMAS

BEDMAS is a memory aid for the order of operations. Each letter stands for one kind of operation, from the first to be done to the last. The ladder on the first page of this chapter shows the four steps: start at the top step and work down.

LetterStands forExample
BBrackets ( ) and [ ](12 + 8) × 3: add 12 + 8 first
EExponents: squares, powers and roots100 − 5²: work out 5² first
D and MDivision and Multiplication, left to right24 ÷ 4 × 3: divide first, because ÷ comes first
A and SAddition and Subtraction, left to right20 − 8 + 2: subtract first, because − comes first
Table 3.1What each letter of BEDMAS means.
Key idea

D and M are one step, not two. Neither one goes first. Work them in the order they appear, left to right. The same goes for A and S.

Example 3.2Working through BEDMAS
Find 8 − 3 × 2 + 1.
Solution
  1. No brackets and no exponents.
  2. Multiply: 3 × 2 = 6. The calculation is now 8 − 6 + 1.
  3. Add and subtract left to right: 8 − 6 = 2, then 2 + 1 = 3.
Calculator

Display 3.
Sharp EL-531XT

Display 3.

  2. 20 − 12 ÷ 4

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.3 Brackets3.3 Brackets

Brackets group part of a calculation so it is worked out first. They come first in BEDMAS. Inside the brackets, use BEDMAS again.

Sometimes there are brackets inside brackets. Square brackets [ ] are often used for the outer pair so they are easy to tell apart. Work out the innermost brackets first, then work outward. On the calculator, every bracket is keyed with the ( and ) keys.

Example 3.3Brackets change the answer
Find 12 + 8 × 3 and (12 + 8) × 3.
Solution
  1. 12 + 8 × 3: multiply first, 8 × 3 = 24, then 12 + 24 = 36.
  2. (12 + 8) × 3: brackets first, 12 + 8 = 20, then 20 × 3 = 60.
Calculator

With brackets

Display 60.
Sharp EL-531XT
No brackets

Display 36.
With brackets

Display 60.
36 and 60. The same numbers give different answers.
Example 3.4A frame and brackets inside brackets
A rectangular frame is 450 mm by 300 mm. The distance around it is 2 × (450 + 300). Find it. Then find 2 × [15 − (4 + 6)].
Solution
  1. Frame: brackets first, 450 + 300 = 750. Then 2 × 750 = 1,500 mm.
  2. Inner brackets first: 4 + 6 = 10. The line is now 2 × [15 − 10].
  3. Outer brackets: 15 − 10 = 5. Then 2 × 5 = 10.

On the calculator, square brackets are keyed with the same ( and ) keys: 2 × ( 15 − ( 4 + 6 ) ) =. Close every bracket you open.

The frame is 1,500 mm around, and 2 × [15 − (4 + 6)] = 10.
Key the × before a bracket

On paper, 3(4 + 5) means 3 × (4 + 5). The × is often left out next to a bracket. On the calculator, always key the × yourself: 3 × ( 4 + 5 ) = 27.

Try it 3.3
  1. (6 + 4) × (3 − 2)
  2. (25 − 5) ÷ 4
  3. 3 × (7 + 8)
  4. 2 × (1,200 + 800)
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.4 Exponents, squares and square roots3.4 Exponents, squares and square roots

An exponent is the small raised number that says how many of that number are multiplied together. In 5³ the exponent is 3: 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.

The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself. The square of 5 is written 5² and read "5 squared": 5 × 5 = 25. The square root undoes a square. √25 = 5 because 5 × 5 = 25.

Exponents and roots come right after brackets in BEDMAS. An exponent belongs only to the number or bracket it touches.

Example 3.5What does the square belong to?
Find 100 − 5², (100 − 5)², 5 × 3² and (5 × 3)².
Solution
  1. 100 − 5²: the square belongs to the 5. 5² = 25, then 100 − 25 = 75.
  2. (100 − 5)²: brackets first, 95, then 95² = 9,025.
  3. 5 × 3²: the square belongs to the 3. 3² = 9, then 5 × 9 = 45.
  4. (5 × 3)²: brackets first, 15, then 15² = 225.

75, 9,025, 45 and 225.

A square root sign works like a bracket. The bar over the top covers everything under it, and all of that is worked out before the root is taken.

Example 3.6A root over a sum
Find √(9 + 16) and √9 + √16.
Solution
  1. √(9 + 16): the root covers the sum. 9 + 16 = 25, then √25 = 5.
  2. √9 + √16: two separate roots. √9 = 3 and √16 = 4, then 3 + 4 = 7.
  3. On the Sharp, key √ and then the sum in brackets. On the TI-30Xa, key the sum in brackets, then √x after the closing bracket.

Sharp EL-531XT

Display 5.
√(9 + 16) = 5 but √9 + √16 = 7. They are not the same.

A perfect square is a whole number that is the square of a whole number. The table below lists the squares of 1 to 20. Read it from left to right to square a number: 13² = 169. Read it from right to left to take a square root: 324 sits next to 18, so √324 = 18. A number that is not in a square column, such as 200, has a square root that is not a whole number. √200 is between 14 and 15, because 200 is between 196 and 225.

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.5 Left to right3.5 Left to right

Division and multiplication share one step of BEDMAS. Addition and subtraction share the last step. When a line has two operations from the same step, work them in the order you meet them, from left to right.

Multiplication does not always come first

The M comes after the D in BEDMAS, but that does not mean divide before multiply. They share a step. 24 ÷ 4 × 3 = 18, not 24 ÷ 12 = 2. In the same way, 50 − 20 + 5 = 35, not 50 − 25 = 25.

A bar is 6,000 mm long. You cut off 1,250 mm, then 875 mm, and then weld a 400 mm piece back on. Ignoring saw cuts, its length is 6,000 − 1,250 − 875 + 400. Left to right, that is 4,750, then 3,875, then 4,275 mm.

Example 3.7Left to right
Find 48 ÷ 6 ÷ 2, 24 ÷ 4 × 3 and 20 − 8 − 2.
Solution
  1. 48 ÷ 6 ÷ 2: left to right, 48 ÷ 6 = 8, then 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Working 6 ÷ 2 first would give 48 ÷ 3 = 16, which is wrong.
  2. 24 ÷ 4 × 3: ÷ comes first, 24 ÷ 4 = 6, then 6 × 3 = 18.
  3. 20 − 8 − 2: 20 − 8 = 12, then 12 − 2 = 10. Working 8 − 2 first would give 14, which is wrong.

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.6 The fraction bar groups3.6 The fraction bar groups

A fraction bar means divide. It also groups: everything above the bar is worked out as one number, everything below the bar is worked out as one number, and then the top is divided by the bottom. It acts like a pair of brackets around the top and another pair around the bottom.

On a calculator there is no fraction bar for a calculation like this, so you must key the brackets yourself: (top) ÷ (bottom).

Example 3.8Brackets for a fraction bar
Find 18 + 615 − 8 to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Top: 18 + 6 = 24. Bottom: 15 − 8 = 7.
  2. Divide: 24 ÷ 7 = 3.428571429..., which rounds to 3.43.
  3. Keyed without brackets, 18 + 6 ÷ 15 − 8 = gives 10.4, because the calculator divides 6 ÷ 15 first. That answer is wrong.

Example 3.9Hole spacing
Seven holes are evenly spaced along a 1,500 mm plate, with the end holes 150 mm from each end. Seven holes make 6 spaces. The spacing is 1,500 − 2 × 1506. Find it.
Solution
  1. Top first, using BEDMAS inside it: 2 × 150 = 300, then 1,500 − 300 = 1,200.
  2. Divide by the bottom: 1,200 ÷ 6 = 200.
  3. On either calculator, key ( 1500 − 2 × 150 ) ÷ 6 =.

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.7 Your calculator and BEDMAS3.7 Your calculator and BEDMAS

Both calculators follow BEDMAS. Key a calculation from left to right, as it is written, and the calculator holds back an addition until any multiplication after it is done. That is why 3 + 4 × 5 = gives 23 on both. The TI-30Xa guidebook and the Sharp manual both list this order, with anything in brackets worked out first.

The calculator only knows what you key. It cannot see a fraction bar, a root bar over a sum, or a square that belongs to a whole bracket. Before you key a formula from a drawing or a manual, find every grouping on paper, then key each one as brackets. On the Sharp, read the top line of the display before you press =.

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.8 Positive and negative numbers3.8 Positive and negative numbers

An integer is a whole number, zero, or a whole number below zero. Numbers above zero are positive. Numbers below zero are negative and carry a minus sign in front: −5 is read "negative five". A positive number can be written with a plus sign, +5, or with no sign at all.

Negative numbers show up wherever a job measures from a zero point: temperatures below 0 °C, elevations below a benchmark, and cuts that come out under the target length. Section 2.5 shows how to key a negative number with the change-sign key on both calculators.

A number line puts the integers in order. Zero is in the middle, positive numbers go to the right and negative numbers go to the left. A number is greater than every number to its left. So 4 is greater than −6, and −3 is greater than −8, because −3 is closer to zero. On a thermometer, −8 °C is colder than −3 °C.

Adding and subtracting with signs

Adding a positive number moves right on the number line. Adding a negative number moves left, so it is the same as subtracting: 6 + (−9) = 6 − 9 = −3. Subtracting a negative number moves right, so it is the same as adding: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8.

Example 3.10Temperature on a job site
At 6:00 the temperature on a job site is −7 °C. By noon it has risen 12 degrees. By evening it has fallen 9 degrees from the noon reading. Find the noon and evening temperatures.
Solution
  1. Noon: −7 + 12. Start at −7 and move 12 to the right. The answer is 5 °C.
  2. Evening: 5 − 9. Start at 5 and move 9 to the left. The answer is −4 °C.
  3. Key the −7 with the change-sign key, not the minus key.

On a building section, heights are often given as elevations from a benchmark, a level that is called 0. Levels above it are positive and levels below it are negative. The distance between two levels is always the higher elevation minus the lower one.

Example 3.11Floor and grade elevations
In the drawing, the second floor is at +2,745 mm, finished grade is at −610 mm and the basement floor is at −2,440 mm. Find the height from the basement floor to the second floor, and the height from the basement floor up to finished grade.
Solution
  1. Higher minus lower: 2,745 − (−2,440). Subtracting a negative is the same as adding, so this is 2,745 + 2,440 = 5,185 mm.
  2. Finished grade minus basement floor: −610 − (−2,440) = −610 + 2,440 = 1,830 mm.
  3. Key each negative elevation with the change-sign key.

Example 3.12Over and under the target length
Five blocks are cut to a target length of 368 mm. Each one is measured and written as over (+) or under (−) the target: +2, −3, +1, −4 and +1 mm. Find the total and the average difference from the target.
Solution
  1. Total: 2 + (−3) + 1 + (−4) + 1. Adding a negative is subtracting: 2 − 3 + 1 − 4 + 1 = −3 mm.
  2. Average: the total divided by the number of blocks. The fraction bar groups the top, so key brackets: (−3) ÷ 5 = −0.6 mm.
  3. The blocks run 0.6 mm under the target on average.

Sign rules

Same signs give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer. This holds for × and for ÷.

Example 3.13A cooler and a cold front
A walk-in cooler is at 3 °C when its door is propped open in winter. The air inside drops 4 degrees each hour for 5 hours. Find the temperature after 5 hours. On another day, the outside temperature falls from 4 °C to −14 °C over 6 hours. Find the average change per hour.
Solution
  1. Five drops of 4 degrees are 5 × (−4) = −20. BEDMAS multiplies before it adds: 3 + 5 × (−4) = 3 + (−20) = −17 °C.
  2. Change = new − old = −14 − 4 = −18 degrees. Per hour: (−18) ÷ 6 = −3. Different signs give a negative answer.
  3. The fraction bar of the average needs brackets on the calculator: ( −14 − 4 ) ÷ 6.

An exponent belongs only to what it touches. (−3)² = (−3) × (−3) = 9, because the bracket puts the minus sign under the square. In −3² the square belongs to the 3 only, so −3² = −(3 × 3) = −9. On the calculator, key (−3)² with brackets: TI-30Xa 3 +⇄− x², Sharp ( +/− 3 ) x² =.

  10. A rod should be 1,200 mm. Four rods measure +1, −2, −2 and +3 mm from the target. Find the total difference.

Chapter 3 Order of Operations3.9 Framing and stairs: BEDMAS on the job3.9 Framing and stairs: BEDMAS on the job

Carpenters write a few calculations again and again. Two of them, the stud count for a wall and the total rise and total run of a stair, are good BEDMAS practice.

Studs are set a fixed distance apart, measured from the centre of one stud to the centre of the next. This distance is the spacing on centre, written o.c. When a wall is laid out from one end, the number of spaces is the wall length divided by the spacing, and there is one more stud than there are spaces.

Studs in a wall
studs = length ÷ spacing + 1
Divide first, then add 1. If length ÷ spacing is not a whole number, round it up before you add 1, so no space is wider than the spacing. This counts the regular studs only. Studs at corners and beside openings are counted on their own.

The spacing comes from the plans, and it may not be more than the maximum in Table 9.23.10.1 of the BC Building Code, which Sentence 9.23.10.1.(1) points to (BCBC 2024, Division B, page 9-182). For an exterior wall of 38 × 89 studs that carries a roof, with or without attic storage, the table lists a maximum stud spacing of 600 mm. For the same studs carrying a roof plus one floor, it lists 400 mm.

Example 3.14Counting studs
A wall is 4,800 mm long, with studs at 400 mm o.c. How many studs does it need? Then find the studs for a 12 ft wall at 16 in o.c.
Solution
  1. BEDMAS divides before it adds: 4,800 ÷ 400 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13 studs. No brackets are needed.
  2. Brackets in the wrong place change the job: 4,800 ÷ (400 + 1) = 11.97, which is not a stud count.
  3. Feet to inches first: 12 × 12 = 144 in. Then 144 ÷ 16 + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10 studs. × and ÷ are worked left to right, then the + comes last.

A stair has risers, the vertical part of each step, and treads, the part you step on. The unit rise is the height of one step, nosing to nosing. The unit run is the depth of one step, nosing to nosing. In the stairs in this book the upper floor is the top step, so a flight has one tread fewer than it has risers.

Stair totals
total rise = number of risers × unit rise
total run = (number of risers − 1) × unit run
The brackets matter: the subtraction is worked out before the multiplication.

The BC Building Code limits the height of one flight. Article 9.8.3.3, Sentence (1), says: "The vertical height of any flight of stairs shall not exceed 3.7 m." (BCBC 2024, Division B, page 9-30). The flight in the figure is 3,610 mm, which is under 3.7 m (3,700 mm). For the unit rise of a private stair, Table 9.8.4.1 in Sentence 9.8.4.1.(1) gives a maximum of 200 mm and a minimum of 125 mm (page 9-30). For the unit run of rectangular treads in a private stair, Table 9.8.4.2 in Sentence 9.8.4.2.(1) gives a maximum of 355 mm and a minimum of 255 mm (page 9-31).

Example 3.15Total rise and total run
A private stair has 14 risers with a unit rise of 190 mm and treads with a unit run of 260 mm. Find the total rise and the total run. Is the total rise under the 3.7 m limit for one flight?
Solution
  1. Total rise: 14 × 190 = 2,660 mm. That is less than 3,700 mm, so one flight is within Article 9.8.3.3.
  2. Total run: brackets first, 14 − 1 = 13 treads. Then 13 × 260 = 3,380 mm.
  3. Without the brackets, 14 − 1 × 260 multiplies first and gives 14 − 260 = −246, which is not a length.

Chapter
4

Fractions

Many inch sizes are fractions. A tape reads 2516 in, a drawing calls for 38 in plate, and a cut list adds up lengths like 3638 in. To read, add and divide these sizes you need to work with fractions.

This chapter starts with what a fraction means and how to read an inch tape and a steel rule. It then covers equivalent fractions, lowest terms, mixed numbers and the four operations. Each method is shown by hand and then with the fraction key on the TI-30Xa and the Sharp EL-531XT.

In this chapter you will

  • Read an inch tape to the nearest 1/16 in and a rule to 1/32 and 1/64 in
  • Write equivalent fractions and put fractions in lowest terms
  • Change between improper fractions and mixed numbers
  • Compare fractions using a common denominator
  • Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and mixed numbers
  • Use the fraction key on both calculators

Key words

  • fraction
  • numerator and denominator
  • proper and improper fraction
  • mixed number
  • equivalent fractions
  • lowest terms
  • common denominator
  • reciprocal

Chapter 4 Fractions4.1 What a fraction is4.1 What a fraction is

A fraction names part of a whole. The whole is split into equal parts, and the fraction tells you how many of those parts you have.

In 38 the bottom number is the denominator. It tells how many equal parts the whole is split into: 8. The top number is the numerator. It tells how many of those parts you have: 3.

The line between the two numbers is the fraction bar. It means divide: 38 is the same as 3 ÷ 8. Chapter 5 uses this to change fractions into decimals.

A fraction whose numerator is smaller than its denominator is a proper fraction. It is worth less than one whole. 58, 34 and 1516 are proper fractions.

Example 4.1Parts of a bar
A flat bar is marked into 8 equal lengths. Three lengths are cut off. What fraction of the bar is cut off, and what fraction is left?
Solution
  1. The bar is split into 8 equal parts, so the denominator is 8.
  2. 3 parts are cut off, so 38 of the bar is cut off.
  3. 8 − 3 = 5 parts are left, so 58 of the bar is left.
38 is cut off and 58 is left. Together they make 88, the whole bar.
Try it 4.1
  1. A bar is split into 4 equal parts and 3 are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
  2. In 716, which number is the numerator?
  3. In 716, how many equal parts is the whole split into?
  4. A box holds 12 couplings and 5 are used. What fraction is used? What fraction is left?
  5. Which is smaller, 14 in or 18 in?
  6. Is 98 a proper fraction? Explain.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 4 Fractions4.2 Reading an inch tape and rule4.2 Reading an inch tape and rule

Inch tapes and rules split each inch into equal parts. On the rule below, the longest lines mark whole inches. The next longest line marks the half inch. Shorter lines mark quarters, then eighths, and the shortest lines mark sixteenths. This book reads tapes to the nearest 116 in, and steel rules to 132 in or 164 in.

  1. Find the last whole inch line before the mark. That gives the whole number.
  2. Count the sixteenth spaces from that inch line to the mark.
  3. Write the count over 16. That is the fraction part.
  4. Put the fraction in lowest terms (Section 4.3 shows how).
Example 4.2Reading marks A and B
Read marks A and B on the rule above.
Solution
  1. A: the last whole inch line before A is the 2. Count the spaces from the 2 line to A: 5 sixteenths. 5 is odd, so 516 is in lowest terms. A reads 2516 in.
  2. B: the last whole inch line before B is the 1. Count 12 sixteenths past it. Divide the top and bottom of 1216 by 4 to get 34. B reads 134 in.
  3. Check: B sits on a quarter line, the line for 34.
A is 2516 in and B is 134 in.
Count spaces, not lines

Start counting at the first space after the whole inch line. If you count the inch line itself as 1, every reading comes out 116 in too long.

A rule marked in 32nds splits each inch into 32 equal parts, and a rule marked in 64ths splits each inch into 64. The lines are close together, so read them in two steps. First find the last eighth line before the mark, then count the small spaces past it.

Example 4.3Reading 32nds and 64ths
Read mark C on the rule marked in 32nds and mark D on the rule marked in 64ths.
Solution
  1. C: the last eighth line before C is the 38 line, and 38 = 1232. C is 1 small space past it: 12 + 1 = 13. C reads 1332 in.
  2. D: the last eighth line before D is also the 38 line, and 38 = 2464. D is 3 small spaces past it: 24 + 3 = 27. D reads 2764 in.
  3. 13 and 27 are odd, so both readings are in lowest terms.
C is 1332 in and D is 2764 in.
Measuring hardware

Bolt, drill and wrench sizes in inches are written as fractions, and they are read the same way as a tape. A drill bit marked 38 cuts a hole 38 in across. A bolt is sized by its diameter, measured across the threads, and its length is measured from under the head to the end. A wrench or socket fits the head across the flats, from one flat face to the opposite flat face, not corner to corner. The bolt in the drawing has these sizes as an example: diameter 12 in, length 214 in, head 34 in across the flats.

In a set marked in sixteenths, sizes step by 116 in. To find the size after 12 in, write it as 816 and add one sixteenth: 916 in. To compare a 58 socket with a 916 socket, write 58 as 1016: the 58 is bigger by 116 in.

Read each mark on the rule below for Try it 4.2. Give each reading to the nearest 116 in, in lowest terms.

Try it 4.2

  2. Mark B
  3. Mark C
  4. Mark D
  5. Mark E
  6. Mark F

Chapter 4 Fractions4.3 Equivalent fractions and lowest terms4.3 Equivalent fractions and lowest terms

Equivalent fractions are written differently but have the same value. In the figure below, 12, 24, 48 and 816 of the bars are shaded. The four shaded parts are the same length.

Making an equivalent fraction

Multiply or divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number. The value of the fraction does not change. To write 34 in sixteenths, multiply the top and bottom by 4: 34 = 1216.

A fraction is in lowest terms when no whole number bigger than 1 divides evenly into both the numerator and the denominator. To put a fraction in lowest terms, divide the top and the bottom by a number that goes into both, and repeat until no number bigger than 1 goes into both. This book writes tape readings in lowest terms: 134 in, not 11216 in.

Example 4.4Reducing a reading
Write 1216 and 2464 in lowest terms.
Solution
  1. 1216: both numbers are even. Divide both by 2 to get 68, then by 2 again to get 34. 3 is odd, so stop.
  2. 2464: divide by 8 in one step. 24 ÷ 8 = 3 and 64 ÷ 8 = 8, so 2464 = 38.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
12a b/c16=
Display 3⌟4
Sharp EL-531XT
12a b/c16=
Display 3┌4
When you press =, the display shows the fraction in lowest terms. The TI-30Xa shows 3⌟4 and the Sharp shows 3┌4. Read either one as 34.
1216 = 34 and 2464 = 38
A quick test for tape fractions

Tape and rule fractions have 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 as the denominator. If the numerator is odd, the fraction is already in lowest terms. If the numerator is even, divide the top and the bottom by 2 and test again.

Comparing fractions

When two fractions have the same denominator, the one with the bigger numerator is bigger: 916 is bigger than 716. When the denominators are different, rewrite the fractions with the same denominator first. A denominator that the fractions share is a common denominator. For tape fractions, 16 works for halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths. Use 32 or 64 when a fraction has 32 or 64 on the bottom.

Example 4.5Putting sizes in order
Three bolts have diameters of 38 in, 516 in and 14 in. List them from smallest to largest.
Solution
  1. Change each to sixteenths: 38 = 616, 516 stays as it is, and 14 = 416.
  2. Put the numerators in order: 4, 5, 6.
  3. The rule shows the same order from left to right.
14, 516, 38

For fractions that are not tape fractions, use the smallest number that both denominators divide into evenly. For 23 and 34 that number is 12: 23 = 812 and 34 = 912, so 34 is bigger.

Try it 4.3

  2. Write 1416 in lowest terms.
  3. Write 2032 in lowest terms.
  4. Write 4864 in lowest terms.
  5. Write 58 in sixteenths.
  6. Write 34 in 32nds.
  7. Which is bigger, 38 or 716?
  8. Which is bigger, 532 or 18?
  9. Put in order from smallest: 34, 58, 1116.
  10. Which is bigger, 23 or 58? Use 24 as the common denominator.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 4 Fractions4.4 Improper fractions and mixed numbers4.4 Improper fractions and mixed numbers

An improper fraction has a numerator equal to or bigger than its denominator, so it is worth one whole or more. A mixed number is a whole number and a proper fraction written together. Tape readings such as 234 in are mixed numbers. Improper fractions make multiplying and dividing easier.

Example 4.6Improper to mixed
Change 4316 to a mixed number.
Solution
  1. Divide the numerator by the denominator: 43 ÷ 16 = 2 with a remainder. 2 × 16 = 32 and 43 − 32 = 11.
  2. The whole number is 2. The remainder 11 goes over the same denominator: 1116.
4316 = 21116
Example 4.7Mixed to improper
Change 358 to an improper fraction.
Solution
  1. Multiply the whole number by the denominator: 3 whole inches hold 3 × 8 = 24 eighths.
  2. Add the numerator: 24 + 5 = 29. Write it over the same denominator.
358 = 298
Try it 4.4

  2. Change 2916 to a mixed number.
  3. Change 218 to a mixed number.
  4. Change 238 to an improper fraction.
  5. Change 512 to an improper fraction.
  6. Change 11516 to an improper fraction.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 4 Fractions4.6 Adding and subtracting fractions4.6 Adding and subtracting fractions

To add or subtract fractions with the same denominator, add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator: 316 + 516 = 816 = 12. When the denominators are different, change to a common denominator first: 78 − 516 = 1416 − 516 = 916. Then put the answer in lowest terms.

Example 4.8Stacking plates
Three plates are stacked. They are 38 in, 14 in and 316 in thick. How thick is the stack?
Solution
  1. Change to sixteenths: 616, 416 and 316.
  2. Add the numerators: 6 + 4 + 3 = 13.
  3. The total is 1316. 13 is odd, so it is in lowest terms.

To add mixed numbers, add the whole numbers and add the fractions. If the fractions come to one whole or more, change that part to a mixed number and carry the whole number.

Example 4.9Total of a cut list
Find the total length of the three pieces: 1234 in, 858 in, 1512 in.
Solution
  1. Add the whole numbers: 12 + 8 + 15 = 35.
  2. Change the fractions to eighths and add them: 68 + 58 + 48 = 158.
  3. 158 = 178. Carry the 1: 35 + 1 = 36. The total is 3678 in.

To subtract mixed numbers, subtract the fractions first and then the whole numbers. When the fraction on top is smaller than the fraction you take away, borrow 1 from the whole number. Write the borrowed 1 as a fraction with the same denominator, such as 88 or 1616, and add it to the fraction. For example, 514 − 2716 = 5416 − 2716 = 42016 − 2716 = 21316.

Example 4.10What is left of the bar?
A piece 2958 in long is cut from a 48 in bar. Ignore the saw cut. How long is the offcut?
Solution
  1. There is no fraction in 48 to take 58 from, so borrow 1: 48 = 47 88.
  2. Fractions: 88 − 58 = 38.
  3. Whole numbers: 47 − 29 = 18.

Chapter 4 Fractions4.7 Multiplying and dividing fractions4.7 Multiplying and dividing fractions

To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators, multiply the denominators and put the answer in lowest terms: 23 × 34 = 612 = 12. A whole number can be written over 1: 6 = 61. Change mixed numbers to improper fractions before you multiply.

In word problems, the word "of" means multiply. 34 of a 24 in bar is 34 × 241 = 724 = 18 in.

Saw cuts in fractions

When a problem gives the kerf as a fraction of an inch, work with it like any other fraction. With a kerf of 18 in, 4 cuts remove 4 × 18 = 48 = 12 in of stock. The problems in this book give the kerf whenever it counts.

Example 4.11Pieces and saw cuts
Four pieces, each 1134 in long, are cut from a 48 in bar. You make 4 cuts and the kerf is 18 in. How long is the offcut?
Solution
  1. Pieces: 4 × 1134 = 4 × 474 = 1884 = 47 in.
  2. Saw cuts: 4 × 18 = 12 in.
  3. Offcut: 48 − 47 − 12 = 12 in.

The reciprocal of a fraction is the fraction turned upside down. The reciprocal of 34 is 43, and the reciprocal of 5 (or 51) is 15. A number times its reciprocal is 1: 34 × 43 = 1212 = 1.

Dividing by a fraction

To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first. Then turn the number you are dividing by upside down and multiply.

For example, a 3012 in bar cut into 4 equal pieces, ignoring the saw cuts, gives 3012 ÷ 4 = 612 × 14 = 618 = 758 in for each piece.

Example 4.12How many pieces?
How many spacers 134 in long can be cut from a 24 in bar? Ignore the saw cuts. How long is the offcut?
Solution
  1. 24 ÷ 134 = 241 × 47 = 967 = 1357.
  2. Only whole spacers count: 13 spacers.
  3. 13 spacers use 13 × 134 = 2234 in. The offcut is 24 − 2234 = 114 in.

Lengths that are not on the tape

Some answers have denominators that are not on a tape, such as thirds. To mark them, multiply the fraction part by 16 and round to the nearest whole number of sixteenths. A 25 in bar cut into 3 equal pieces gives 253 = 813 in. 13 × 16 = 513, which rounds to 5, so mark each piece at 8516 in. Chapter 5 does the same job with decimal inches.

Chapter 4 Fractions4.8 Carpentry: tape, cut lengths and kerf4.8 Carpentry: tape, cut lengths and kerf

Carpenters read the tape on long boards, so the whole number of inches is often large. The method from Section 4.2 does not change: find the last whole inch, then count the sixteenths past it. A cut list then adds and subtracts those readings, and every saw cut takes a kerf.

Example 4.13Reading the tape on a board
Read marks A, B and C in Figure 4.10.
Solution
  1. A: past the 46 line by 7 sixteenths. A reads 46716 in.
  2. B: past the 47 line by 12 sixteenths, and 1216 = 34. B reads 4734 in.
  3. C: past the 48 line by 10 sixteenths, and 1016 = 58. C reads 4858 in.
A = 46716 in, B = 4734 in, C = 4858 in
Example 4.14A cut list from one board
Three pieces, 2238 in, 3112 in, 1858 in, are cut from a 96 in board. You make 3 cuts and the kerf is 18 in. How long is the offcut?
Solution
  1. Add the pieces: 2238 + 3112 + 1858 = 7212 in.
  2. Saw cuts: 3 × 18 = 38 in.
  3. Offcut: 96 − 7212 − 38 = 2318 in.

Blocking pieces 1412 in long are cut from a 96 in board. You make one cut for each block and the kerf is 18 in. How many blocks do you get, and how long is the offcut?

Fractions in the building code

The BC Building Code limits holes and notches in framing as a fraction of the member’s depth. Article 9.23.5.1, Sentence (1) says holes drilled in roof, floor or ceiling framing members shall be not larger than one-quarter the depth of the member and shall be located not less than 50 mm from the edges, unless the depth of the member is increased by the size of the hole (page 9-175). The code works in millimetres, so these answers are in millimetres.

Example 4.16The largest hole in a joist
A floor joist is 38 mm by 235 mm, so its depth is 235 mm. What is the largest hole Article 9.23.5.1 allows in it?
Solution
  1. One-quarter of the depth: 14 × 235 = 2354.
  2. 2354 = 5834 mm, which is 58.75 mm.

Example 4.17Notches and studs
Article 9.23.5.2, Sentence (1) allows a notch on the top of a floor, roof or ceiling member within half the joist depth from the edge of bearing, not deeper than one-third the joist depth (page 9-176). Article 9.23.5.3, Sentence (1) says the undamaged part of a loadbearing stud shall not be less than two-thirds the depth of the stud (page 9-176). Find (a) the deepest notch and the farthest it may sit from the bearing edge in a 286 mm deep joist, and (b) the deepest hole or notch in a loadbearing stud 89 mm deep.
Solution
  1. (a) Depth: 13 × 286 = 2863 = 9513 mm. Distance: 12 × 286 = 143 mm.
  2. (b) Two-thirds must stay: 23 × 89 = 1783 = 5913 mm.
  3. The rest may be removed: 89 − 5913 = 2923 mm, which is 13 of 89.
