Chapter
5

Decimals

A metric drawing might give a size of 76.2 mm, flat bar might cost $3.99 a metre, and a calculator answer might come out as 2.83 in. Each of these is a decimal.

This chapter covers place value after the decimal point, reading a metric rule, rounding, and adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing decimals. It then links decimals to the fractions in Chapter 4, so you can change a decimal inch to the nearest sixteenth and mark it on a tape.

In this chapter you will

  • Read and write decimals using place value
  • Read a metric rule to the nearest 0.5 mm
  • Compare and round decimals
  • Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals
  • Change fractions to decimals and decimals to fractions
  • Change a decimal inch to the nearest 1/16 or 1/32 in
  • Work with money to the nearest cent

Key words

  • decimal
  • decimal point
  • decimal place
  • decimal inch

Chapter 5 Decimals5.1 Decimals and place value5.1 Decimals and place value

A decimal is a number written with a decimal point. The point separates the whole number part from the part that is less than one. Each place after the point is worth one tenth of the place to its left: tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.

NumberTensOnes.TenthsHundredthsThousandths
25.425.4
76.276.2
3.1753.175
0.3750.375
Table 5.1Place value on both sides of the decimal point.

Each digit after the point fills one decimal place. 2.375 has three decimal places. A decimal is a fraction with 10, 100 or 1,000 on the bottom: 0.7 = 710, 0.25 = 25100 and 0.375 = 3751,000. Write a 0 in front of the point when there is no whole number, as in 0.375. It makes the point easy to see.

Example 5.1Reading a decimal size
A drawing gives a hole position as 12.07 mm. Read the number in words and say what the 7 is worth.
Solution
  1. The whole number part is 12.
  2. The 0 is in the tenths place and the 7 is in the hundredths place.
  3. Read it as twelve and seven hundredths. The 7 is worth 7100, or 0.07.
Twelve and seven hundredths millimetres. The 7 is worth 0.07 mm.

Reading a metric rule

On the metric rules in this book, each small line is 1 mm, the longer lines mark every 5 mm, and the numbered lines mark every 10 mm (1 cm). This book reads metric rules to the nearest 0.5 mm. A mark halfway between two millimetre lines reads as .5.

Example 5.2Reading the metric rule
Read marks A, B and C on the rule above.
Solution
  1. A: past the 1 cm line (10 mm) by 7 small spaces: 10 + 7 = 17 mm.
  2. B: past the 20 mm line by 3 spaces and then half a space: 23.5 mm.
  3. C: past the 40 mm line by 1 space and half a space: 41.5 mm.
A = 17 mm, B = 23.5 mm, C = 41.5 mm
Try it 5.1
  1. Write 3.06 in words.
  2. What is the 5 worth in 0.375?
  3. How many decimal places does 9.525 have?
  4. Write 910 as a decimal.
  5. Write 45100 as a decimal.
  6. Write 0.125 as a fraction over 1,000.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.2 Comparing and rounding decimals5.2 Comparing and rounding decimals

To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare the digits from the left. Add zeros on the right so both numbers have the same number of decimal places. Zeros on the right of a decimal do not change its value: 0.38 = 0.380. To compare a 0.375 in plate with a 0.38 in plate, write 0.375 and 0.380. The tenths are the same, and 8 hundredths is more than 7 hundredths, so the 0.38 in plate is thicker, by 0.005 in.

More digits is not bigger

0.375 has more digits than 0.38, but it is the smaller number. Compare place by place from the left, not by counting digits.

Decimals round the same way as whole numbers. Find the place you are rounding to, look at the digit to its right, and round up if that digit is 5 or more. Then drop every digit after the rounding place.

Example 5.3Rounding a size
Round 12.738 mm to one decimal place and to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. One place: the tenths digit is 7. The digit to its right is 3, so the 7 stays: 12.7 mm.
  2. Two places: the hundredths digit is 3. The digit to its right is 8, so the 3 goes up to 4: 12.74 mm.
12.7 mm to one place, 12.74 mm to two places.
Example 5.4Rounding to the nearest 0.5 mm
A calculation gives 23.38 mm. Round it to the nearest 0.5 mm so you can mark it with a metric rule.
Solution
  1. Double the number: 23.38 × 2 = 46.76.
  2. Round to the nearest whole number: 47.
  3. Halve it: 47 ÷ 2 = 23.5.
23.5 mm
Try it 5.2
  1. Which is bigger, 0.6 or 0.58?
  2. Put in order from smallest: 0.5, 0.125, 0.25.
  3. Round 6.35 to one decimal place.
  4. Round 9.525 to two decimal places.
  5. Round 3.175 mm to the nearest 0.5 mm.
  6. Round 18.74 mm to the nearest whole millimetre.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.3 Adding and subtracting decimals5.3 Adding and subtracting decimals

To add or subtract decimals, line up the decimal points, one under the other. Fill empty places with zeros, then add or subtract as with whole numbers. The point in the answer goes straight below the points above it.

Example 5.5Total of a metric cut list
Find the total length of four pieces: 152.4 mm, 76.2 mm, 38.1 mm, 12.7 mm.
Solution
  1. Line up the points: each number has one decimal place.
  2. Tenths: 4 + 2 + 1 + 7 = 14. Write 4, carry 1.
  3. Whole numbers: 152 + 76 + 38 + 12 + 1 (carried) = 279.

Example 5.6Finding a hidden length
A stepped pin is 120.65 mm long overall. Two of its steps are 25.4 mm and 38.1 mm long. How long is the third step?
Solution
  1. Add the known steps: 25.4 + 38.1 = 63.5.
  2. Subtract from the overall length: write 63.5 as 63.50 and line up the points.
  3. 120.65 − 63.50 = 57.15.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.4 Multiplying decimals5.4 Multiplying decimals

To multiply decimals, multiply as if there were no points. Then count the decimal places in the numbers you multiplied and give the answer that many decimal places. For 1.5 × 0.25: 15 × 25 = 375. 1.5 has one place and 0.25 has two, so the answer has three: 0.375.

Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1,000 moves the point 1, 2 or 3 places to the right: 2.375 × 1,000 = 2,375.

Example 5.7Twelve equal pieces
You need 12 pieces, each 152.4 mm long. What total length do they use? Ignore the saw cuts.
Solution
  1. Estimate first: 12 × 150 = 1,800.
  2. Multiply without the point: 12 × 1,524 = 18,288.
  3. 152.4 has one decimal place, so the answer has one: 1,828.8. It is close to the estimate.

  3. To the nearest 0.5 mm: 9.525 × 2 = 19.05, which rounds to 19, and 19 ÷ 2 = 9.5.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.5 Dividing decimals5.5 Dividing decimals

When you divide by a whole number, divide as usual and keep the point in the same place in the answer. When you divide by a decimal, move the point to the right in both numbers until the number you divide by is a whole number. Dividing by 10, 100 or 1,000 moves the point 1, 2 or 3 places to the left: 254 ÷ 100 = 2.54.

When a division does not come out even, keep going past the last digit: write zeros after the point and bring them down. Section 5.8 shows this by hand, and how to round the answer to hundredths or thousandths.

Example 5.9Dividing by a decimal
How many 0.25 m lengths can be cut from a 7.5 m bar? Ignore the saw cuts.
Solution
  1. 0.25 has two decimal places, so move the point two places to the right in both numbers: 7.5 ÷ 0.25 becomes 750 ÷ 25 = 30.
30 lengths
Example 5.10Pieces with saw cuts
How many 152.4 mm pieces can you cut from a 2,438.4 mm bar? You make one cut for each piece and the kerf is 3.2 mm. How long is the offcut?
Solution
  1. Each piece uses its length plus one saw cut: 152.4 + 3.2 = 155.6 mm.
  2. 2,438.4 ÷ 155.6 = 15.67. Only whole pieces count: 15 pieces.
  3. 15 pieces use 15 × 155.6 = 2,334 mm. The offcut is 2,438.4 − 2,334 = 104.4 mm.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.6 Fractions and decimals5.6 Fractions and decimals

The fraction bar means divide, so to change a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator: 38 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. An inch size written this way is a decimal inch: 0.375 in is 38 in. For a mixed number, change only the fraction part and keep the whole number: 258 in = 2.625 in.

To change a decimal with three places or fewer to a fraction, write it over 10, 100 or 1,000 and put it in lowest terms: 0.375 = 3751,000 = 38 (divide both by 125). The fraction key does this for you (2nd F⇄D on the TI-30Xa, a b/c on the Sharp), as Chapter 4 showed.

Some fractions never end as a decimal. 23 = 0.666… and 512 = 0.4166… go on forever. Section 5.8 divides them by hand and rounds them to three decimal places.

Decimal inches to the nearest sixteenth

A tape is marked in sixteenths, but a calculator gives decimal inches such as 2.83 in. To mark the length, change the decimal part to the nearest 116 in. For finer work on a steel rule, use the nearest 132 in. Always say which one you used.

  1. Keep the whole number of inches.
  2. Multiply the decimal part by 16 (or by 32).
  3. Round to the nearest whole number. That is the number of sixteenths (or 32nds).
  4. Write it over 16 (or 32) and put it in lowest terms.
Example 5.11Marking 2.83 in on a tape
A calculation gives 2.83 in. Change it to the nearest 116 in, and to the nearest 132 in.
Solution
  1. Keep the 2 inches. The decimal part is 0.83.
  2. Nearest 116: 0.83 × 16 = 13.28, which rounds to 13. That gives 1316, so 21316 in.
  3. Nearest 132: 0.83 × 32 = 26.56, which rounds to 27. That gives 2732, so 22732 in.

Example 5.12Millimetres to the nearest sixteenth
A metric part is 50 mm long. What is that to the nearest 116 in?
Solution
  1. Change to inches by dividing by 25.4, and multiply by 16 in the same line to count sixteenths: 50 ÷ 25.4 × 16 = 31.496 (to three places).
  2. Round to the nearest whole number: 31.496 is less than 31.5, so 31 sixteenths.
  3. 3116 = 11516.

The fraction key does not round to the tape

The fraction key gives the exact fraction, not the nearest sixteenth. On the TI-30Xa, 0.83 2nd F⇄D shows 83⌟100. On the Sharp, 0.83 = a b/c shows 83┌100. Both mean 83100, not a tape reading. Use the multiply-by-16 method instead.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.7 Money5.7 Money

Money is written with two decimal places: dollars, then cents. $3.99 is 3 dollars and 99 cents. Round money answers to the nearest cent, which is two decimal places. The calculator does not show zeros at the end of a decimal: 4 × 12.85 shows 51.4, which means $51.40. Always write money with two decimal places.

Flat bar at $3.99 per metre: 7.5 m cost 7.5 × 3.99 = $29.925. The third decimal digit is 5, so round up to the nearest cent: $29.93.

Example 5.13Adding up an order
An order has 4 boxes of bolts at $12.85 a box and 2 cans of cutting oil at $8.49 a can. What is the total?
Solution
  1. Bolts: 4 × 12.85 = 51.40.
  2. Oil: 2 × 8.49 = 16.98.
  3. Total: 51.40 + 16.98 = 68.38.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.8 Dividing to thousandths and rounding5.8 Dividing to thousandths and rounding

Many divisions do not come out even. To carry on, divide as usual and write the point in the answer straight above the point in the number you are dividing. When you run out of digits, write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down. Keep going until you have one more decimal place than you need, then round.

  1. Divide the whole number part as usual.
  2. Write the point in the answer above the point in the number.
  3. Write a 0 after the last digit, bring it down and divide again. Repeat.
  4. Stop one place past the place you round to. Then round.
Example 5.14Dividing past the last digit
A 9.25 m length of trim is cut into 4 equal pieces. Ignore the saw cuts. How long is each piece? Round to two and to three decimal places.
Solution
  1. Start with 9. 4 goes into 9 twice: 2 × 4 = 8, and 9 − 8 = 1.
  2. Write the point in the answer. Bring down the 2 to make 12. 4 goes into 12 3 times: 3 × 4 = 12, and 12 − 12 = 0.
  3. Bring down the 5 to make 5. 4 goes into 5 once: 1 × 4 = 4, and 5 − 4 = 1.
  4. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 10. 4 goes into 10 twice: 2 × 4 = 8, and 10 − 8 = 2.
  5. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 20. 4 goes into 20 5 times: 5 × 4 = 20, and 20 − 20 = 0.
  6. The answer is 2.3125 m. It ends here, because the remainder is 0.
  7. To two decimal places: the digit after the hundredths is 2, so 2.3125 rounds to 2.31. To three places: the digit after the thousandths is 5, so it rounds up to 2.313.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
9.25÷4=
Display 2.3125
Sharp EL-531XT
9.25÷4=
Display 2.3125
2.31 m to two decimal places, 2.313 m to three. Three decimal places of a metre is the nearest millimetre: 2,313 mm.
Example 5.15A division that never ends
A 2 kg bag of grout is shared equally among 7 forms. How much goes in each form? Round to three decimal places.
Solution
  1. Start with 2. 7 goes into 2 zero times. Write 0.
  2. Write the point in the answer. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 20. 7 goes into 20 twice: 2 × 7 = 14, and 20 − 14 = 6.
  3. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 60. 7 goes into 60 8 times: 8 × 7 = 56, and 60 − 56 = 4.
  4. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 40. 7 goes into 40 5 times: 5 × 7 = 35, and 40 − 35 = 5.
  5. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 50. 7 goes into 50 7 times: 7 × 7 = 49, and 50 − 49 = 1.
  6. The digits keep coming, so stop at four places: 0.2857.
  7. The fourth digit is 7, which is 5 or more, so the third digit goes up: 0.286.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
2÷7=
Display 0.285714286
Sharp EL-531XT
2÷7=
Display 0.285714285
The display shows 0.285714286. Round it the same way.
0.286 kg in each form, to three decimal places.
Example 5.16A fraction that does not end
Change 512 to a decimal by hand. Round to three decimal places.
Solution
  1. Start with 5. 12 goes into 5 zero times. Write 0.
  2. Write the point in the answer. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 50. 12 goes into 50 4 times: 4 × 12 = 48, and 50 − 48 = 2.
  3. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 20. 12 goes into 20 once: 1 × 12 = 12, and 20 − 12 = 8.
  4. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 80. 12 goes into 80 6 times: 6 × 12 = 72, and 80 − 72 = 8.
  5. Write a 0 at the end of the number and bring it down to make 80. 12 goes into 80 6 times: 6 × 12 = 72, and 80 − 72 = 8.
  6. The 6 repeats forever: 0.4166…
  7. To three places, look at the fourth digit, 6. Round up: 0.417.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
5÷12=
Display 0.416666667
Sharp EL-531XT
5÷12=
Display 0.416666666
512 ≈ 0.417. The ≈ sign means "is about".
Carry one digit past the place

To round to thousandths you need the digit after the thousandths. Divide to four decimal places, round to three, and write only the three.

Chapter 5 Decimals5.9 Carpentry: decimal feet and pricing5.9 Carpentry: decimal feet and pricing

A builder’s plans or a calculator may give lengths in decimal feet, such as 12.75 ft. A tape reads feet, inches and sixteenths. A foot has 12 inches, so to change the decimal part of a foot to inches, multiply it by 12. To go the other way, divide the inches by 12.

Example 5.17Decimal feet to a tape reading
A rafter calculation gives 8.6 ft. What do you mark on the tape, to the nearest 116 in?
Solution
  1. Keep the 8 feet. The decimal part is 0.6 ft.
  2. 0.6 × 12 = 7.2 in. Keep the 7 inches.
  3. Change the 0.2 in to sixteenths: 0.2 × 16 = 3.2, which rounds to 3.

Chapter
6

Percent, Ratio and Proportion

Shop math is full of comparisons. A waste allowance adds 10% to an order. A coating is mixed 4 parts to 1. A pump moves so many litres per minute. A drawing shows a 2,400 mm wall as a 120 mm line.

This chapter shows how percents, ratios, rates and proportions work, how they connect to the fractions and decimals you already know, and how to read a scale drawing. Percent is shown on both calculators, because the Sharp EL-531XT and the TI-30Xa use the % key in different ways.

In this chapter you will

  • Change between percents, decimals and fractions
  • Find a percent of a number, and find what percent one number is of another
  • Add a waste allowance and work out increases and decreases
  • Write and simplify ratios, and share an amount in a ratio
  • Work with rates and solve proportions
  • Read and make scale drawings in metric and imperial

Key words

  • percent
  • ratio
  • rate
  • proportion
  • scale
  • gross pay
  • net pay
  • unit price
  • inverse proportion

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.1 What percent means6.1 What percent means

Percent means “out of 100”. The sign % stands for percent. 25% means 25 out of every 100. If a square is split into 100 equal parts and 25 of them are shaded, 25% of the square is shaded.

A percent is one more way to write a part of a whole. You already know two others: a fraction and a decimal. 25% = 25100 = 0.25. All three describe the same amount.

Moving between percent and decimal

Percent to decimal: divide by 100, which moves the decimal point two places left. 35% = 0.35.

Decimal to percent: multiply by 100, which moves the decimal point two places right. 0.08 = 8%.

Example 6.1Percent to decimal and fraction
Write 35%, 6.5% and 150% as decimals. Write 35% as a fraction in lowest terms.
Solution
  1. 35% = 35 ÷ 100 = 0.35.
  2. 6.5% = 6.5 ÷ 100 = 0.065. The point moves two places left, so a zero fills the empty place.
  3. 150% = 150 ÷ 100 = 1.5. A percent over 100 is more than one whole.
  4. 35% = 35100. Divide the top and bottom by 5: 35100 = 720.
0.35, 0.065 and 1.5. 35% = 720.
Example 6.2Fraction to percent
A crew has finished 38 of a pipe run. What percent is finished?
Solution
  1. Change the fraction to a decimal: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
  2. Multiply by 100 to change the decimal to a percent: 0.375 × 100 = 37.5.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
3÷8×100=
Display 37.5
Sharp EL-531XT

Display 37.5
37.5% is finished.

Table 6.1Percents you will meet often, with their decimals and fractions in lowest terms.
Mixed numbers and percents over 100%

One whole is 100%, so every whole number in a mixed number adds 100%. To change a mixed number to a percent, change it to a decimal first, then multiply by 100. 234 = 2 + 3 ÷ 4 = 2.75, and 2.75 × 100 = 275%. Check: 2 wholes are 200% and 34 is 75%, so the total is 275%.

Going the other way, 275% = 2.75 = 234. A percent over 100% always gives a number bigger than 1.

  2. Write 7.5% as a decimal.
  3. Write 0.06 as a percent.
  4. Write 1.25 as a percent.
  5. Write 40% as a fraction in lowest terms.
  6. Write 58 as a percent.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.2 Finding a percent of a number6.2 Finding a percent of a number

In a percent question, the word “of” means multiply. To find 15% of 240, change 15% to a decimal and multiply: 0.15 × 240.

Both calculators also have a % key. They use it in different ways. On the TI-30Xa the % key is a second function, and you finish with = (TI-30Xa guidebook, p. 4). On the Sharp EL-531XT, 2ndF % works the calculation out by itself, so there is no = at the end (Sharp EL-531XT Calculation Examples [4]).

Example 6.3Brackets for a second job
A pallet holds 240 brackets. 15% of them are set aside for a second job. How many brackets is that?
Solution
  1. Change the percent to a decimal: 15% = 0.15.
  2. Multiply: 0.15 × 240 = 36.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
240×152nd%=
Display 36.
Sharp EL-531XT
240×152ndF%
Display 36.
With the % key, the TI-30Xa keys end with =, and the Sharp keys end with 2ndF %. The decimal method, 0.15 × 240 =, gives 36 on both calculators too.
36 brackets.
The Sharp % key ends the calculation

On the Sharp EL-531XT, do not press = after 2ndF %. The answer is already on the display. On the TI-30Xa, press = after % to finish.

A quick 10% check

10% of a number is the number divided by 10: move the decimal point one place left. 10% of 240 is 24, so 15% must be about one and a half times that, 36. Use this to check your calculator answer.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.3 Finding the percent and the whole6.3 Finding the percent and the whole

Sometimes you know the part and the whole and you want the percent. Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100.

Percent of a whole
Percent = Part ÷ Whole × 100
The part and the whole must be in the same unit.
Example 6.4Welds that failed inspection
An inspector checks 240 welds and 18 of them fail. What percent fail?
Solution
  1. The part is 18 and the whole is 240.
  2. 18 ÷ 240 = 0.075.
  3. 0.075 × 100 = 7.5.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
18÷2402nd%=
Display 7.5
Sharp EL-531XT
18÷2402ndF%
Display 7.5
Here the % key does the × 100. Keying 18 ÷ 240 × 100 = gives the same 7.5.
7.5% of the welds fail.

When you know the part and the percent, you can find the whole. Change the percent to a decimal and divide the part by it. In Example 6.3, 36 brackets were 15% of the pallet. If you did not know the pallet size, you could find it: 36 ÷ 0.15 = 240 brackets.

Three questions, one relationship

Part = decimal × Whole. Find the part by multiplying. Find the decimal by dividing the part by the whole. Find the whole by dividing the part by the decimal.

Try it 6.3

  2. 12 is what percent of 400?

  4. 30 is 25% of what number?
  5. 18 is 6% of what number?
  6. A 750 mm piece is cut from a 3,000 mm bar. What percent of the bar is the piece?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.4 Waste allowance, increase and decrease6.4 Waste allowance, increase and decrease

Some material is always lost to cutting, fitting and mistakes. A waste allowance is extra material added to an order to cover that loss. A 10% waste allowance means you order the amount you need plus 10% of it.

Adding a percent is a percent increase. Taking a percent away is a percent decrease. You can do either in two steps (find the percent, then add or subtract it) or in one step by multiplying. To add 10%, multiply by 1.10, which is 110%. To take off 30%, multiply by 0.70, which is 70%.

Example 6.5Ordering pipe with a waste allowance
A job needs 85 m of pipe. Add a 10% waste allowance. The pipe is sold in 6 m lengths. How many lengths do you order?
Solution
  1. 10% of 85 = 0.1 × 85 = 8.5 m.
  2. Add it on: 85 + 8.5 = 93.5 m.
  3. Lengths: 93.5 ÷ 6 = 15.5833…
  4. A part length still has to be bought, so round up to 16.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
85+102nd%=
Display 93.5
Sharp EL-531XT
85+102ndF%
Display 93.5
Pressing + and then % adds 10% of 85 to 85 on both calculators (TI-30Xa guidebook, p. 4, and Sharp EL-531XT Calculation Examples [4]). In one step without the % key: 85 × 1.1 = 93.5.
93.5 m of pipe, which is 16 lengths.
Example 6.6A sale price
A tool is priced at $400.00. It is on sale at 30% off. What is the sale price?
Solution
  1. 30% of $400.00 = 0.3 × 400 = $120.00.
  2. Subtract: $400.00 − $120.00 = $280.00. In one step: 0.7 × 400 = 280.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
400−302nd%=
Display 280.
Sharp EL-531XT
400−302ndF%
Display 280.
Pressing − and then % takes 30% of 400 away from 400 on both calculators (TI-30Xa guidebook, p. 4, and Sharp EL-531XT Calculation Examples [4]).
The sale price is $280.00.

To find a percent change, find the amount of the change, divide it by the original amount (the amount before the change), and multiply by 100.

Percent change
Percent change = (New − Original) ÷ Original × 100
A positive answer is an increase. A negative answer is a decrease.
Example 6.7A pay raise
An apprentice’s wage goes from $24.00 to $25.20 an hour. What is the percent increase?
Solution
  1. Change: $25.20 − $24.00 = $1.20.
  2. Divide by the original wage: 1.20 ÷ 24.00 = 0.05.
  3. Multiply by 100: 5%.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
(25.2−24)÷24×100=
Display 5.
Sharp EL-531XT
(25.2−24)÷24×100=
Display 5.
The brackets make both calculators find the change before dividing.
A 5% increase.
Up 10% and down 10% is not a round trip

Start with 200. Up 10% gives 200 × 1.1 = 220. Down 10% from there gives 220 × 0.9 = 198, not 200. Each percent is taken of a different starting amount.

  3. A $250.00 price is cut by 20%. New price?
  4. A 1,200 mm piece grows by 5%. New length?

  6. A tank level drops from 1,500 L to 1,200 L. Percent decrease?

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.5 Ratio6.5 Ratio

A ratio compares two amounts. A coating mixed 4 parts base to 1 part hardener has a ratio of base to hardener of 4 to 1. You can write it three ways: 4 : 1, 4 to 1 or 41.

Order matters. The ratio of hardener to base is 1 : 4, not 4 : 1. A ratio is simplified the same way as a fraction: divide both numbers by the same number until they share no common factor. Before you compare two amounts, put them in the same unit.

For example, to compare a 750 mm piece with a 2.5 m piece, first write 2.5 m as 2,500 mm. The ratio 750 : 2,500 simplifies to 3 : 10 when you divide both numbers by 250.

Example 6.8Sharing an amount in a ratio
You need 750 mL of mixed coating. The label gives a mix of 4 parts base to 1 part hardener. How much of each do you measure?
Solution
  1. Add the parts: 4 + 1 = 5 parts.
  2. One part: 750 ÷ 5 = 150 mL.
  3. Base: 4 × 150 = 600 mL. Hardener: 1 × 150 = 150 mL.
  4. Check: 600 + 150 = 750 mL.
Calculator

Sharp EL-531XT

Display 600.
600 mL of base and 150 mL of hardener.

Carpenters write a roof slope as a ratio too, such as 4 in 12. Section 6.11 compares roof slopes with the limits in the BC Building Code.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.6 Rate6.6 Rate

A rate compares two amounts in different units: litres per minute, dollars per metre, millimetres per minute. A unit rate is the amount for one unit, such as 150 L in one minute. Find it by dividing.

Example 6.9Pump rate
A pump moves 1,200 L in 8 minutes. What is its rate? At that rate, how long does it take to fill a 2,700 L tank?
Solution
  1. Rate: 1,200 ÷ 8 = 150 L per minute.
  2. Time: 2,700 ÷ 150 = 18 minutes.

  2. 96 fittings in 8 hours. Fittings per hour?

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.7 Proportion6.7 Proportion

A proportion says that two ratios are equal. 14 = 520 is a proportion, because both ratios simplify to 1 : 4. In a proportion the cross products are equal: 1 × 20 = 4 × 5 = 20.

When one of the four numbers is missing, set up the two ratios with the same units in the same places, then solve for the missing number.

Solving a proportion
a ÷ b = c ÷ x
x = b × c ÷ a
Multiply the two numbers that sit across from each other, then divide by the third.
Example 6.10Welding time for a larger order
A welder finishes 8 brackets in 2.5 hours. At the same rate, how long do 20 brackets take?
Solution
  1. Write the proportion with brackets on top and hours below: 82.5 = 20x.
  2. Cross multiply: 8 × x = 2.5 × 20 = 50.
  3. Divide: x = 50 ÷ 8 = 6.25 hours.
  4. 6.25 hours is 6 hours and 0.25 × 60 = 15 minutes.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
2.5×20÷8=
Display 6.25
Sharp EL-531XT
2.5×20÷8=
Display 6.25
6.25 hours, which is 6 hours 15 minutes.
Keep the units lined up

If brackets are on top in the first ratio, brackets go on top in the second ratio too. Mixing them up gives an answer that is far too big or far too small. Check it with common sense: more brackets must take more time.

In every proportion in this section, both amounts grow together: more brackets take more hours. Some amounts work the other way. More workers on a job take fewer hours. That is an inverse proportion, and Section 6.10 shows how to solve it.

  2. Solve 25 = x45.
  3. Solve 6x = 924.

  5. A crew lays 18 m of pipe in 4 hours. How long for 45 m?
  6. A mix is 3 : 1. You have 1.8 L of the first part. How much of the second part?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.8 Scale drawings6.8 Scale drawings

A drawing of a large part is smaller than the part. The scale is the ratio of a length on the drawing to the real length. A scale of 1 : 20 means 1 mm on the drawing stands for 20 mm on the real part.

Drawing to real: multiply by the second number. Real to drawing: divide by it. A larger second number gives a smaller drawing. A scale such as 2 : 1 makes the drawing larger than the part, which is useful for small details.

The plate above measures 60 mm by 35 mm on the paper, so the real plate is 60 × 20 = 1,200 mm long and 35 × 20 = 700 mm wide.

Example 6.11Measuring a drawing
A line on a drawing at 1 : 50 measures 63 mm with a rule, as shown. How long is the real part?
Solution
  1. Drawing to real, so multiply by 50.
  2. 63 × 50 = 3,150 mm.
Calculator

Display 3150.
Sharp EL-531XT

3,150 mm, which is 3.15 m.

A scale can also be written as two lengths. A drawing that states its scale as 14″ = 1′-0″ uses 14 inch on the drawing for 1 foot on the real job. Since 1 ft = 12 in, that ratio is 14 : 12, which is 1 : 48.

Example 6.12An imperial scale
A drawing is marked 14″ = 1′-0″. A line measures 312 in, as shown. How long is the real length?
Solution
  1. Count how many quarter inches are in the line: 3.5 ÷ 0.25 = 14.
  2. Each quarter inch is 1 ft, so the real length is 14 ft.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.9 Money on the job6.9 Money on the job

Percents, rates and rounding come together when you look at a pay stub or a till receipt. Gross pay is hours worked times the hourly rate. Net pay is what is left after deductions are taken off. Money is rounded to the cent, two decimal places.

Overtime is paid at a higher rate. The rate is set by the job, so it is given in each problem here. A rate of 1.5 times means each overtime hour pays one and a half regular hours.

Example 6.13A week’s pay with overtime
An apprentice earns $25.40 an hour. On this job, hours over 40 in a week are paid at 1.5 times the hourly rate. This week the apprentice works 45 hours. What is the gross pay?
Solution
  1. Regular pay: 40 × $25.40 = $1,016.00.
  2. Overtime rate: 1.5 × $25.40 = $38.10 an hour.
  3. Overtime pay: 5 × $38.10 = $190.50.
  4. Gross pay: $1,016.00 + $190.50 = $1,206.50.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
40×25.4+5×25.4×1.5=
Display 1206.5
Sharp EL-531XT
40×25.4+5×25.4×1.5=
Display 1’206.5
BEDMAS does both multiplications before the addition, on both calculators.
Gross pay is $1,206.50.

Most things you buy in British Columbia carry two sales taxes. The federal goods and services tax (GST) is collected by the Canada Revenue Agency. The provincial sales tax (PST) is collected by the Province of British Columbia. The B.C. government says that, generally, the rate of PST is 7% on the purchase or lease price of goods and services, with some exceptions. Its guide for businesses says PST is charged on the price before the GST is added, so each tax is found on the price before tax.

Example 6.14GST and PST on a purchase

Solution
  1. GST: 5% of $249.00 = 0.05 × 249 = $12.45.
  2. PST: 7% of $249.00 = 0.07 × 249 = $17.43.
  3. Total: $249.00 + $12.45 + $17.43 = $278.88.

Example 6.15Discount first, then tax

  1. Take the discount off first: $189.95 − 20% = 0.8 × 189.95 = $151.96.

The unit price is the cost of one unit: one litre, one metre, one screw. Divide the price by the number of units. It lets you compare packages of different sizes.

Example 6.16Which bag is the better buy?
Cable ties come in a bag of 100 for $6.49 and a bag of 500 for $27.95. Find the cost of one tie in each bag, in cents.
Solution
  1. Bag of 100: $6.49 ÷ 100 = $0.0649, which is 6.49¢ a tie.
  2. Bag of 500: $27.95 ÷ 500 = $0.0559, which is 5.59¢ a tie.
  3. 5.59¢ is less than 6.49¢.

A quick tax check

GST and PST together are 12% of the price before tax. 10% is easy to find in your head, so the total tax is a little more than 10%. On $249.00, 10% is $24.90, and the two taxes together are $29.88.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.10 Inverse proportion6.10 Inverse proportion

In Section 6.7 both amounts grew together. Twice as many brackets took twice as long. In an inverse proportion, one amount goes up as the other goes down. Twice as many workers take half as long. The two amounts multiply to the same number every time.

To solve one, multiply the two numbers you know that belong together. That product is the total job. Then divide it by the new number.

Inverse proportion
a × b = c × x
x = a × b ÷ c
a and b belong together. c is the new amount and x is the one you are finding.
Example 6.17More hands, less time
3 pipefitters can install a run of pipe in 8 hours. Working at the same rate, how long would 4 pipefitters take?
Solution
  1. The whole job is 3 × 8 = 24 worker-hours.
  2. Share it among 4 workers: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.
  3. Check with common sense: more workers, so less time.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
3×8÷4=
Display 6.
Sharp EL-531XT
3×8÷4=
Display 6.
6 hours.
Example 6.18A faster pump
A tank fills in 45 minutes when a pump moves 120 L per minute. How long does it take at 150 L per minute?
Solution
  1. The tank holds 120 × 45 = 5,400 L.
  2. At the new rate: 5,400 ÷ 150 = 36 minutes.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
120×45÷150=
Display 36.
Sharp EL-531XT

Direct or inverse?

Ask what happens when one amount doubles. If the other amount doubles too, it is a direct proportion: set two ratios equal, as in Section 6.7. If the other amount halves, it is an inverse proportion: multiply, then divide.

  6. Direct or inverse? The speed of a pump and the time to fill a tank.

Chapter 6 Percent, Ratio and Proportion6.11 Carpentry: roof slope, waste and scale6.11 Carpentry: roof slope, waste and scale

Carpenters write the slope of a roof as a rise in a run: 4 in 12 means the roof rises 4 in for every 12 in it runs across. That is the ratio 4 : 12, which simplifies to 1 : 3. The BC Building Code writes the same idea as “1 in 3”: 1 unit of rise in 3 units of run.

Table 9.26.3.1, Roofing Types and Slope Limits, forms part of Sentence 9.26.3.1.(1) of the BC Building Code 2024 (Division B, page 9-241). It sets the slopes on which each kind of roofing may be applied. For asphalt shingles it gives a minimum slope of 1 in 3 in normal application and 1 in 6 in low slope application. Sentences (2) and (3) of the Article allow lower slopes for some built-up roofs and metal roof systems.

Type of roofingMinimum slope in the codeAs a rise in 12
Asphalt shingles, low slope application1 in 62 in 12
Asphalt shingles, normal application1 in 34 in 12
Cedar shakes1 in 34 in 12
Wood shingles1 in 43 in 12
Clay tile1 in 26 in 12
Slate shingles1 in 26 in 12
Table 6.3Some minimum slopes from Table 9.26.3.1 (BCBC 2024, Division B, Article 9.26.3.1. (page 9-241)). None of these rows has a maximum slope. The last column is worked out here: 12 ÷ the second number.
Example 6.19Does the roof meet the code?
A garage roof is framed at 5 in 12. Write the slope as “1 in ?”. Is it steep enough for asphalt shingles in normal application?
Solution
  1. 5 in 12 is the ratio 5 : 12. Divide both numbers by 5 to make the rise 1: 1 : 2.4.
  2. So the slope is 1 in 2.4. The code minimum for asphalt shingles in normal application is 1 in 3.
  3. A smaller second number means less run for each unit of rise, so a steeper roof. 2.4 is less than 3, so 1 in 2.4 is steeper than 1 in 3.
Calculator

Sharp EL-531XT

Display 2.4
1 in 2.4. Yes, it is steeper than the 1 in 3 minimum in Table 9.26.3.1.
Example 6.20Sheathing with a waste allowance
A roof takes 38 sheets of sheathing. The estimator adds a 12% waste allowance for cuts. How many whole sheets do you order?
Solution
  1. 12% of 38 = 0.12 × 38 = 4.56 sheets.
  2. Add it on: 38 + 4.56 = 42.56.
  3. A part sheet still has to be bought, so round up to 43.

Chapter
7

Measurement and Unit Conversion

A metric drawing, an inch tape, a pump rated in US gallons and a heater set in °F can all turn up on the same job. Before you can add, compare or cut, every number has to be in the same unit.

This chapter covers the metric system and its prefixes, imperial units and feet-and-inches, and how to convert between them with exact conversion factors. It finishes with units of area and volume, litres and gallons, and temperature. Every factor in this chapter is exact or is taken from a published source, and the source is given with each table.

In this chapter you will

  • Use SI units and the prefixes kilo, centi and milli
  • Work with inches, feet and yards, and with feet and inches
  • Convert between metric and imperial with exact factors
  • Convert units of area and volume
  • Convert between litres, US gallons and imperial gallons
  • Convert temperatures between °C and °F

Key words

  • unit
  • metric system
  • SI
  • prefix
  • imperial system
  • conversion factor

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.1 Units and the metric system7.1 Units and the metric system

A unit is a fixed amount used to measure something: a metre, an inch, a litre. A measurement is always a number and a unit. “2,400” on its own means nothing on the job. 2,400 mm and 2,400 in are very different lengths.

The metric system is built on powers of ten. Its modern form is the SI, the International System of Units. The SI base units include the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass and the second (s) for time (NIST SP 1038, section 4.1.1). The litre (L) is accepted for use with the SI for volume (NIST SP 1038, section 4.1.2 and the note to the volume table in section 5.1.5).

A prefix in front of a unit multiplies it by a power of ten. Kilo means 1,000, so 1 km = 1,000 m. Milli means 11,000, so 1 mm = 11,000 m.

PrefixSymbolMultiplies the unit byExample
kilok1,0001 km = 1,000 m
hectoh1001 hL = 100 L
decada101 dam = 10 m
decid0.11 dm = 0.1 m
centic0.011 cm = 0.01 m
millim0.0011 mm = 0.001 m
microµ0.000 0011 µm = 0.000 001 m
Table 7.1SI prefixes. Source: Weights and Measures Act (Canada), Schedule I, Part V, and NIST SP 1038, Table 2. NIST notes that deci, deka (deca) and hecto are rarely used.

Each step on the ladder in the chapter opener is a power of ten, so a metric conversion only moves the decimal point. Going to a smaller unit, the number gets bigger, so multiply. Going to a bigger unit, the number gets smaller, so divide.

Example 7.1Metric conversions
Convert: (a) 2.45 m to mm, (b) 375 mm to m, (c) 1,250 mL to L, (d) 0.85 t to kg.
Solution
  1. (a) 1 m = 1,000 mm. Smaller unit, so multiply: 2.45 × 1,000 = 2,450 mm. The point moves 3 places right.
  2. (b) Bigger unit, so divide: 375 ÷ 1,000 = 0.375 m. The point moves 3 places left.
  3. (c) 1 L = 1,000 mL. 1,250 ÷ 1,000 = 1.25 L.
  4. (d) 1 t (tonne) = 1,000 kg (Weights and Measures Act, Schedule I, Part IV). 0.85 × 1,000 = 850 kg.
2,450 mm, 0.375 m, 1.25 L and 850 kg.

Very large and very small numbers, such as 1,000,000 mm² in a square metre, can also be written with a power of ten. Section 7.7 shows this scientific notation and the EE key on both calculators.

Try it 7.1
  1. 3.6 m to mm
  2. 850 mm to m
  3. 42 cm to mm
  4. 6,096 mm to m
  5. 2.5 L to mL
  6. 1,800 kg to t
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.2 Imperial units, feet and inches7.2 Imperial units, feet and inches

The imperial system uses the inch, foot, yard, pound and gallon. Canadian law defines the yard as 0.9144 m, the foot as 13 yard and the inch as 136 yard (Weights and Measures Act, Schedule II). The US defines the same inch, foot and yard (NIST SP 1038), so a US tape and a Canadian tape agree. Table 7.2 lists the length units.

Lengths on the job are often written in feet and inches, such as 7′ 912″ (7 feet 912 inches). To work with them on a calculator, change them to inches first. Multiply the feet by 12 and add the inches.

For example, 7′ 912″ is 7 × 12 + 9.5 = 93.5 in.

Example 7.2Inches to feet and inches
A cut list gives a length of 14234 in. Write it in feet and inches.
Solution
  1. Divide by 12: 142.75 ÷ 12 = 11.8958… The whole number part is 11 ft.
  2. Inches left over: 142.75 − 11 × 12 = 10.75 in.
  3. 10.75 in is 1034 in.

11′ 1034″

Example 7.3Adding feet and inches
Two pieces of 6′ 434″ and 2′ 1012″ are laid end to end. Find the total length.
Solution
  1. Add the feet: 6 + 2 = 8 ft. Add the inches: 434 + 1012 = 1514 in.
  2. 1514 in is more than a foot: 1514 − 12 = 314 in, and carry 1 ft.
  3. Total: 8 + 1 = 9 ft and 314 in.
  4. Check in inches: 76.75 + 34.5 = 111.25 in = 9′ 314″.

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.3 Converting with exact factors7.3 Converting with exact factors

A conversion factor is the number you multiply or divide by to change units. The inch is defined as exactly 25.4 mm, so 25.4 is the factor between inches and millimetres. It is exact, not rounded, and it gives the same answer on every job.

Inches and millimetres
mm = in × 25.4
in = mm ÷ 25.4
1 in = 25.4 mm exactly (NIST SP 1038, section 5.1.3). It also follows from the Weights and Measures Act: 0.9144 m ÷ 36 = 0.0254 m.

inch (in)millimetre (mm)25.4exact
inch (in)centimetre (cm)2.54exact
foot (ft)metre (m)0.3048exact
yard (yd)metre (m)0.9144exact
mile (mi)kilometre (km)1.609 344exact
pound (lb)kilogram (kg)0.453 592 37exact
Table 7.3Length and mass factors. Source: NIST SP 1038, sections 5.1.3 and 5.2, which prints exact factors in bold. The yard and the pound are also defined this way in the Weights and Measures Act (Canada), Schedule II. To go the other way, divide. Long decimals are printed in groups of three digits, as in the source. Key them without the spaces.

A drawing calls for 38 in plate. What is that in millimetres?
Solution
  1. Inches to millimetres: multiply by 25.4.
  2. 38 × 25.4 = 0.375 × 25.4 = 9.525 mm.

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.4 Units of area and volume7.4 Units of area and volume

Area is measured in square units and volume in cubic units. A square unit is a square 1 unit on each side. A cubic unit is a cube 1 unit on each side. Because a square has two sides that are measured, the length factor is used twice for area. For volume it is used three times.

AreaVolume
1 m² = 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000 mm²1 m³ = 1,000 L
1 ft² = 12 × 12 = 144 in²1 L = 1,000,000 mm³ = 1,000 cm³
1 in² = 645.16 mm² (exact)1 ft³ = 12 × 12 × 12 = 1,728 in³
1 ft² = 0.092 903 04 m² (exact)1 in³ = 16.387 064 cm³ (exact)
Table 7.4Area and volume factors. Sources: NIST SP 1038, sections 5.1.4 and 5.1.5, for the square inch, square foot and cubic inch. The Weights and Measures Act (Canada), Schedule I, Part IV, for the litre (11,000 m³), and Schedule II for 1 in² = 1144 ft² and 1 in³ = 11,728 ft³.
Example 7.8A plate in square metres
A plate is 2,400 mm by 1,200 mm. Find its area in mm² and in m².
Solution
  1. Area = length × width = 2,400 × 1,200 = 2,880,000 mm².
  2. 1 m² = 1,000,000 mm², so divide: 2,880,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 2.88 m².
  3. Check with metres first: 2.4 m × 1.2 m = 2.88 m².

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.5 Litres and gallons7.5 Litres and gallons

There are two gallons, and they are not the same size. The US gallon is 231 in³ (NIST SP 1038, section 3.2). Since 1 in³ = 16.387 064 cm³ exactly, the US gallon is 231 × 16.387 064 = 3,785.411 784 cm³, which is exactly 3.785 411 784 L. The imperial gallon is defined in the Weights and Measures Act (Canada), Schedule II, as 454 609100 000 000 m³, which is exactly 4.546 09 L.

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.6 Temperature7.6 Temperature

Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (°C) in the metric system and degrees Fahrenheit (°F) in the imperial system. The two scales are linked by an exact formula. NIST SP 1038 (section 5.3, note 33) gives °C = (°F − 32) ÷ 1.8, and turned around it gives °F = 1.8 × °C + 32. Both are exact definitions, so round only the final answer.

Celsius and Fahrenheit
°F = 1.8 × °C + 32
°C = (°F − 32) ÷ 1.8
Exact. Follow BEDMAS: in the first formula multiply before you add, and in the second subtract inside the brackets before you divide.
Example 7.13Celsius to Fahrenheit
A water heater is set to 60 °C. What is that in °F?
Solution
  1. °F = 1.8 × 60 + 32. Multiply first: 1.8 × 60 = 108.
  2. Then add: 108 + 32 = 140.
Calculator

Display 140.
Sharp EL-531XT
1.8×60+32=
Display 140.
140 °F
Example 7.14Fahrenheit to Celsius
An oven for drying electrodes is set to 350 °F. What is that in °C, to one decimal place?
Solution
  1. °C = (350 − 32) ÷ 1.8. Brackets first: 350 − 32 = 318.
  2. Divide: 318 ÷ 1.8 = 176.6667…, which rounds to 176.7.
Calculator

Without the brackets, both calculators divide 32 by 1.8 first and give a wrong answer.
176.7 °C
A change in temperature has no 32

A rise or drop is converted with the 1.8 alone: a change of 1 °C is a change of 1.8 °F (NIST SP 1038, note 33). A part that warms up by 25 °C warms up by 25 × 1.8 = 45 °F.

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.7 Powers of ten and scientific notation7.7 Powers of ten and scientific notation

The metric prefixes in Section 7.1 are powers of ten. 1,000 is 10 × 10 × 10, which is written 103: ten to the power 3. 1,000,000 is 106. A negative power means divide: 10−3 is 1 ÷ 1,000 = 0.001, the milli in millimetre.

Scientific notation writes a number as a number from 1 up to 10, times a power of ten. 6,400,000 is 6.4 × 106. 0.0254 is 2.54 × 10−2. The power tells you how many places the decimal point moves: right for a positive power, left for a negative one.

Example 7.15Writing numbers in scientific notation
Write (a) 2,880,000 mm² and (b) 0.000 35 m in scientific notation. (c) Write 3.6 × 104 as an ordinary number.
Solution
  1. (a) Put the point after the first digit: 2.88. The point moved 6 places left, so the power is 6. 2,880,000 mm² = 2.88 × 106 mm².
  2. (b) The first digit that is not zero is 3. The point moves 4 places right to make 3.5, so the power is −4. 0.000 35 m = 3.5 × 10−4 m.
  3. (c) A power of 4 moves the point 4 places right: 3.6 × 104 = 36,000.
2.88 × 106 mm², 3.5 × 10−4 m and 36,000.

Both calculators take a power of ten with one key. On the TI-30Xa it is EE. On the Sharp EL-531XT it is Exp. Key the number, then EE or Exp, then the power. A calculator also switches to scientific notation by itself when an answer has too many digits for the display.

Example 7.16Scientific notation on the calculator
A tank holds 3.6 × 108 mm³. There are 1 × 106 mm³ in a litre. How many litres does it hold?
Solution
  1. Divide the volume by the size of one litre: 3.6 × 108 ÷ (1 × 106).
  2. Dividing powers of ten takes the powers away: 8 − 6 = 2, so the answer is 3.6 × 102 = 360.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
3.6EE8÷1EE6=
Display 360.
Sharp EL-531XT
3.6Exp8÷1Exp6=
Display 360.
EE (TI-30Xa) and Exp (Sharp EL-531XT) key the power of ten that belongs to the number in front of them, so no brackets are needed.
360 L. This is the tank of Example 7.10: 1,200 × 600 × 500 = 360,000,000 mm³.

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.8 Decimal feet7.8 Decimal feet

Site plans and some layout tools give lengths in decimal feet: feet and hundredths of a foot, such as 12.35 ft. A hundredth of a foot is 0.01 × 12 = 0.12 in, a little less than 18 in. Your tape reads feet, inches and sixteenths, so you need to change between the two.

Changing between the two

To decimal feet: change the inches and sixteenths to inches, divide by 12, and add the whole feet.

From decimal feet: keep the whole feet. Multiply the decimal part by 12 to get inches. Keep the whole inches, and multiply what is left by 16 to count sixteenths.

Example 7.17Feet, inches and sixteenths to decimal feet
Write 10′ 4316″ in decimal feet, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Inches: 4 + 3 ÷ 16 inches. Divide by 12 to change them to feet.
  2. Add the whole feet: 10 + (4 + 3 ÷ 16) ÷ 12 = 10.349… ft.
  3. Round to two decimal places: 10.35 ft.

Sharp EL-531XT
10+(4+3÷16)÷12=
Display 10.34895833
The brackets make both calculators add the inches before dividing by 12.
10.35 ft

A plan gives a length of 12.35 ft. What do you mark on the tape, to the nearest 116 in?
Solution
  1. Whole feet: 12 ft. The decimal part is 0.35 ft.
  2. Inches: 0.35 × 12 = 4.2 in. Keep the 4 whole inches.
  3. Sixteenths: 0.2 × 16 = 3.2, which rounds to 3 sixteenths.
  4. Put it together: 12′ 4316″.

Chapter 7 Measurement and Unit Conversion7.9 Carpentry: code values, board feet and floor area7.9 Carpentry: code values, board feet and floor area

The BC Building Code states its limits in millimetres. On a job laid out in inches you convert them, but the code value itself never changes. The rise limit is 200 mm, not the inch number you worked out. When you round a converted limit to a tape reading, round so that you stay inside the limit: round a maximum down and a minimum up.

Table 9.8.4.1 forms part of Sentence 9.8.4.1.(1) (BCBC 2024, Division B, Article 9.8.4.1. (page 9-30)). For private stairs, which serve single dwelling units, it gives a maximum rise of 200 mm and a minimum rise of 125 mm. Table 9.8.4.2, in Sentence 9.8.4.2.(1) (BCBC 2024, Division B, Article 9.8.4.2. (page 9-31)), gives private stairs a minimum run of 255 mm and a maximum run of 355 mm.

Example 7.19A code maximum in inches
The maximum rise for private stairs is 200 mm (Table 9.8.4.1). Convert it to sixteenths of an inch. What is the largest tape reading that stays within the limit?
Solution
  1. 200 ÷ 25.4 × 16 = 125.98… sixteenths.
  2. The nearest sixteenth is 126 sixteenths, which is 71416 = 778 in. But 126 ÷ 16 × 25.4 = 200.03 mm, a little over 200 mm.
  3. For a maximum, round down: 125 sixteenths = 71316 in, which is 198.44 mm.
  4. The code value is still 200 mm.

Lumber is often counted in board feet. NIST SP 1038 (section 5.1.5) gives 1 board foot = 0.002 359 737 m³. Divided by 1 in³ = 16.387 064 cm³, that is 144 in³: a board 12 in by 12 in by 1 in. For a board with its thickness and width in inches and its length in feet, the formula below follows from 144 in³. Use the sizes the problem or the order gives.

Board feet
Board feet = thickness (in) × width (in) × length (ft) ÷ 12
Thickness × width × (length × 12) ÷ 144 is the same as thickness × width × length ÷ 12.
Example 7.21Board feet in a lumber order
An order has 25 pieces sized 2 in × 8 in × 12 ft. How many board feet is that? What is the volume in m³, to three decimal places?
Solution
  1. One piece: 2 × 8 × 12 ÷ 12 = 16 board feet.
  2. 25 pieces: 25 × 16 = 400 board feet.
  3. In m³: 400 × 0.002 359 737 = 0.943895…, which rounds to 0.944 m³.

Chapter
8

Formulas and Transposing

A formula is a short rule that tells you how to work something out. Shop drawings, code books and manuals are full of them: the area of a plate, the distance around a pipe, the volume of a tank.

This chapter shows you how to read a formula, put your own numbers into it, and turn it around to find a different value. Turning a formula around is called transposing. It lets you start from the answer you need, such as an area, and find the size that gives it. Every result is checked by putting it back into the formula.

In this chapter you will

  • Read a formula and name its subject, variables and constants
  • Substitute values into a formula and work it out with BEDMAS
  • Use inverse operations to keep an equation balanced
  • Transpose one-step and two-step formulas
  • Transpose formulas with squares and square roots, such as A = π × r²
  • Check every answer by substituting it back

Key words

  • formula
  • variable
  • constant
  • subject of a formula
  • substitute
  • inverse operation
  • transpose

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.1 Reading a formula8.1 Reading a formula

A formula is a rule written with letters and symbols. The formula for the area of a rectangle is A = l × w. It says: the area A equals the length l times the width w.

A letter that stands for a quantity that can change is a variable. A value that never changes is a constant. In C = π × D, C and D are variables and π is a constant.

The letter on its own on the left of the equals sign is the subject of the formula. The formula tells you how to work out the subject from the other values.

FormulaWhat it works outWhat the letters mean
A = l × wArea of a rectangleA area, l length, w width
P = 2 × (l + w)Perimeter of a rectangleP perimeter (distance around)
C = π × DDistance around a circleC circumference, D diameter
A = π × r²Area of a circler radius (half the diameter)
V = l × w × hVolume of a box shapeV volume, h height
tF = 1.8 × tC + 32Temperature in °F from °CtF degrees Fahrenheit, tC degrees Celsius
Table 8.1Formulas used in this chapter. Chapters 9, 10 and 11 explain where the shape formulas come from.

Some books leave out the × sign: lw means l × w and 2l means 2 × l. A small raised 2 means squared: r² means r × r. This book writes the × sign every time.

Try it 8.1
  1. What is the subject of V = l × w × h?
  2. Name the constant in A = π × r².
  3. Name the variables in C = π × D.
  4. Rewrite 2lw with × signs.
  5. What does s² mean?
  6. Name the two constants in tF = 1.8 × tC + 32.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.2 Substituting values8.2 Substituting values

To substitute means to put a number in place of a letter. Write the formula, write it again with the numbers in place of the letters, then work it out using BEDMAS from Chapter 3.

  1. Write the formula.
  2. Write it again with each letter replaced by its value. Keep every bracket.
  3. Work it out in BEDMAS order: brackets, exponents, division and multiplication, then addition and subtraction.
  4. Write the answer with its unit.
Example 8.1Area and perimeter of a plate
A plate is 1,200 mm long and 800 mm wide. Use A = l × w to find its area and P = 2 × (l + w) to find the distance around it.
Solution
  1. Area: A = 1,200 × 800 = 960,000.
  2. Perimeter: P = 2 × (1,200 + 800). Brackets first, 1,200 + 800 = 2,000. Then 2 × 2,000 = 4,000.
Calculator

Perimeter

Display 4000.
Sharp EL-531XT
Area

Display 960’000.
Perimeter

Display 4’000.
Key the brackets. Without them the calculator works 2 × 1,200 first and then adds 800.
A = 960,000 mm² (square millimetres) and P = 4,000 mm.
Example 8.2Formulas with π and a square
A disc has a diameter of 150 mm, so its radius is 75 mm. Use C = π × D to find the distance around it and A = π × r² to find its area. Round to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Distance around: C = π × 150 = 471.24. Use the π key. It holds many more digits than 3.14.
  2. Area: A = π × 75². The exponent comes first, so square only the 75: 75² = 5,625. Then π × 5,625 = 17,671.46.

Example 8.3Converting a temperature
The formula tF = 1.8 × tC + 32 changes a Celsius temperature to Fahrenheit. Change 20 °C to °F.
Solution
  1. tF = 1.8 × 20 + 32
  2. Multiply first: 1.8 × 20 = 36. Then add: 36 + 32 = 68.
68 °F

Electrical work uses formulas too. The two below link voltage, current, resistance and power. Substitute into them the same way: write the formula, put the numbers in place of the letters, then work it out.

Electrical formulas
V = I × R
P = V × I
V voltage in volts (V), I current in amperes (A), R resistance in ohms (Ω), P power in watts (W). V = I × R is called Ohm's law. Section 8.9 works both formulas and turns them around.
Use the same units

Every length in a formula must be in the same unit. A plate 1.2 m long and 800 mm wide must be changed to 1,200 mm by 800 mm, or 1.2 m by 0.8 m, before you multiply. Chapter 7 shows how.

Try it 8.2

  2. P = 2 × (l + w) with l = 600 mm and w = 450 mm.
  3. C = π × D with D = 300 mm. Round to two decimal places.
  4. A = π × r² with r = 20 cm. Round to two decimal places.
  5. V = l × w × h with l = 2 m, w = 1.5 m and h = 0.5 m.
  6. tF = 1.8 × tC + 32 with tC = 35 °C.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.3 Keeping an equation balanced8.3 Keeping an equation balanced

An equals sign says that both sides have the same value. Think of a balance scale that is level. If you take something off one pan, you must take the same off the other pan, or the scale tips. The same rule keeps an equation true: whatever you do to one side, do to the other side.

To find an unknown value you undo what has been done to it. Each operation has an inverse operation that undoes it.

If the letter has beenUndo it byExample
added to (+ 250)subtracting (− 250)x + 250 − 250 = x
subtracted from (− 75)adding (+ 75)x − 75 + 75 = x
multiplied (× 4)dividing (÷ 4)4 × x ÷ 4 = x
divided (÷ 3)multiplying (× 3)x ÷ 3 × 3 = x
squared (x²)taking the square root (√)√(x²) = x
Table 8.2Operations and their inverses.
Example 8.4Undoing an operation
A 900 mm bar is cut into a 250 mm piece and a second piece, so x + 250 = 900. Solve it. Then solve 4 × x = 1,000 and x ÷ 3 = 125.
Solution
  1. 250 was added to x. Subtract 250 from both sides: x = 900 − 250 = 650. Check: 650 + 250 = 900.
  2. x was multiplied by 4. Divide both sides by 4: x = 1,000 ÷ 4 = 250. Check: 4 × 250 = 1,000.
  3. x was divided by 3. Multiply both sides by 3: x = 125 × 3 = 375. Check: 375 ÷ 3 = 125.
The second piece is 650 mm. Then x = 250 and x = 375.
Key idea

Do the same thing to both sides. Pick the inverse operation that leaves the letter on its own.

Try it 8.3
  1. Solve x + 38 = 120.
  2. Solve x − 45 = 155.
  3. Solve 6 × x = 1,500.
  4. Solve x ÷ 4 = 35.
  5. Solve x + 1,275 = 6,000.
  6. Solve 12 × x = 3,000.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.4 Transposing one-step formulas8.4 Transposing one-step formulas

To transpose a formula means to rearrange it so that a different letter becomes the subject. You use the balance rule from the last section. The letters stay letters until the end, then you substitute the numbers.

  1. Find the letter you want on its own.
  2. Ask what has been done to it.
  3. Undo that with the inverse operation, on both sides.
  4. Write the new formula with the letter you want on the left.
  5. Substitute the numbers, work it out, then check.

In the Shape Canvas, change one size and the numbers that depend on it update. Transposing lets you work the other way, from a value you need, such as an area, back to the size that gives it.

Example 8.5Given the area, find the width
A rectangular plate must have an area of 960,000 mm². It is 1,200 mm long. Transpose A = l × w to find the width.
Solution
  1. w has been multiplied by l. Divide both sides by l.
  2. A ÷ l = l × w ÷ l, so w = A ÷ l.
  3. w = 960,000 ÷ 1,200 = 800
Calculator
TI-30Xa
960000÷1200=
Display 800.
Sharp EL-531XT
960000÷1200=
Display 800.
w = 800 mm. Check: 1,200 × 800 = 960,000.
Example 8.6Given the distance around, find the diameter
A tape wrapped once around a round tank reads 1,000 mm. Transpose C = π × D and find the diameter to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. D has been multiplied by π. Divide both sides by π, so D = C ÷ π.
  2. D = 1,000 ÷ π = 318.31

Example 8.7Find the height of a tank
A tank with a rectangular base 1.2 m long and 0.8 m wide must hold 0.576 m³. Transpose V = l × w × h to find the height.
Solution
  1. h has been multiplied by l and by w. Divide both sides by l × w, so h = V ÷ (l × w).
  2. h = 0.576 ÷ (1.2 × 0.8) = 0.576 ÷ 0.96 = 0.6

The brackets matter. Keyed as 0.576 ÷ 1.2 × 0.8, both calculators divide by 1.2 and then multiply by 0.8, which gives 0.384.
0.6 m. Check: 1.2 × 0.8 × 0.6 = 0.576.

Ohm's law turns around the same way: I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. Section 8.9 has worked examples.

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.5 Transposing two-step formulas8.5 Transposing two-step formulas

In a two-step formula, two things have been done to the letter you want. Undo them in the reverse order. The last thing done is the first thing you undo, just as you take off your boots before your socks.

Example 8.8Find the length from the perimeter
A rectangular frame uses 5,000 mm of flat bar all the way around. It is 900 mm wide. Transpose P = 2 × (l + w) to find the length.
Solution
  1. Undo the × 2: divide both sides by 2. P ÷ 2 = l + w
  2. Undo the + w: subtract w from both sides. l = P ÷ 2 − w
  3. l = 5,000 ÷ 2 − 900 = 2,500 − 900 = 1,600
Calculator
TI-30Xa
5000÷2−900=
Display 1600.
Sharp EL-531XT
5000÷2−900=
Display 1’600.
1,600 mm. Check: 2 × (1,600 + 900) = 5,000.
Example 8.9Fahrenheit to Celsius
Transpose tF = 1.8 × tC + 32 to make tC the subject. Then change 350 °F to °C, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. tC was multiplied by 1.8 and then 32 was added. Undo the + 32 first: tF − 32 = 1.8 × tC
  2. Then undo the × 1.8: tC = (tF − 32) ÷ 1.8
  3. tC = (350 − 32) ÷ 1.8 = 318 ÷ 1.8 = 176.67
Calculator

Display 176.6666667
Keyed without brackets, 350 − 32 ÷ 1.8 gives 332.22, because the calculator divides first.
176.67 °C. NIST publishes the same conversion: tC = (tF − 32) / 1.8.
Example 8.10Height of a gusset
A triangular gusset has an area given by A = b × h ÷ 2. Its base is 400 mm and its area must be 60,000 mm². Find the height.
Solution
  1. Undo the ÷ 2: 2 × A = b × h
  2. Undo the × b: h = 2 × A ÷ b
  3. h = 2 × 60,000 ÷ 400 = 300

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.6 Formulas with squares and square roots8.6 Formulas with squares and square roots

Squaring and taking the square root undo each other. If a letter has been squared, take the square root of both sides to get it back.

Example 8.11Side of a square plate
A square plate must have an area of 62,500 mm². Transpose A = s² and find the side.
Solution
  1. s has been squared. Take the square root of both sides, so s = √A.
  2. s = √62,500 = 250
Calculator

250 mm. Check: 250² = 250 × 250 = 62,500.

In A = π × r², two things are done to r: it is squared, then multiplied by π. Undo them in reverse order. Divide by π first, then take the square root.

Radius from the area of a circle
r = √(A ÷ π)  D = 2 × r
Divide by π first, then take the square root. Double r to get the diameter.
Example 8.12Given the area, find the radius
A round plate must have an area of 50,000 mm². Find its radius and its diameter, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Undo the × π: A ÷ π = r²
  2. Undo the square: r = √(A ÷ π)
  3. r = √(50,000 ÷ π) = 126.16
  4. D = 2 × r = 2 × 126.1566… = 252.31 (use the unrounded r)

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.7 Checking by substituting back8.7 Checking by substituting back

A transposed formula can look right and still be wrong. The check takes a few seconds: put your answer back into the formula you started with, together with the values you were given. If the formula works out to the value you were given, your answer is right. If you rounded the answer, the check comes out close rather than exact.

Example 8.14Catching a mistake
A learner transposes V = l × w × h and writes h = V × l ÷ w. With V = 0.45 m³, l = 1.5 m and w = 0.6 m this gives h = 1.125 m. Check the answer and correct it.
Solution
  1. Substitute back: 1.5 × 0.6 × 1.125 = 1.0125. That is not 0.45, so the answer is wrong.
  2. The mistake: l multiplies h, so it must divide. h = V ÷ (l × w) = 0.45 ÷ (1.5 × 0.6) = 0.5
  3. Substitute back: 1.5 × 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.45. It checks.

Key idea

Transpose with letters, substitute the numbers, then check by putting the answer back into the original formula.

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.8 From words to formulas and equations8.8 From words to formulas and equations

On the job, math usually arrives as words: "the offcut is 315 mm shorter than the bar", "the bill is a $75 call-out plus $95 an hour". To work with it, turn the words into symbols.

An expression is a group of numbers, letters and operation signs with no equals sign, such as x + 250 or 3 × l. An equation says that two quantities are equal, so it has an equals sign: x + 250 = 900. A formula is an equation that works as a rule for any values you put in.

OperationKey wordsExampleIn symbols
+ addplus, more than, longer than, added to, increased by, total, sum, altogether250 mm longer than the barb + 250
− subtractminus, less than, shorter than, take away, decreased by, difference, left over315 mm shorter than the barb − 315
× multiplytimes, product, double, twice, tripletwice the width2 × w
÷ dividedivided by, shared equally, cut into equal pieces, half, quartera bar cut into 4 equal piecesb ÷ 4
= equalsis, equals, gives, comes to, totals, makesthe total is 900 mm… = 900
Table 8.3Key words and the operations they usually mean. Read the whole sentence: a key word is a clue, not a rule.
Less than turns the order around

"75 less than x" is x − 75, not 75 − x. Start from the amount that something is taken from. In the same way, "315 mm shorter than the bar" is b − 315.

To turn a story into an equation and solve it, work through these steps. Example 8.15 starts with the first part: writing expressions.

  1. Read the story to the end. Find what you are asked for.
  2. Choose a letter for the unknown and say what it stands for, with its unit.
  3. Turn the key words into symbols and write the equation. The equals sign goes where the story says is, totals or comes to.
  4. Solve with inverse operations, as in Sections 8.3 to 8.5.
  5. Check the answer in the story, not only in the equation.
  6. Write the answer as a sentence with its unit.
Example 8.15Writing expressions
Let L be the length of a bar in millimetres. Write an expression for each: (a) 150 mm longer than the bar, (b) the bar less a 3 mm saw cut, (c) twice the bar, (d) the bar cut into 5 equal pieces, (e) 4 bars and a 600 mm offcut.
Solution
  1. (a) "longer than" adds: L + 150.
  2. (b) "less" takes 3 away from the bar: L − 3.
  3. (c) "twice" multiplies by 2: 2 × L.
  4. (d) "cut into equal pieces" divides: L ÷ 5.
  5. (e) 4 bars is 4 × L. Then add the offcut: 4 × L + 600.
L + 150, L − 3, 2 × L, L ÷ 5 and 4 × L + 600.
Example 8.16One-step equations from a story
(a) A piece is cut from a 2,440 mm board. The piece left over measures 1,685 mm. Ignore the saw cut. How long is the piece that was cut off? (b) Four equal shelves use 3,360 mm of board. How long is each shelf?
Solution
  1. (a) Let x be the piece cut off, in mm. The two pieces make the board: x + 1,685 = 2,440. Subtract 1,685 from both sides: x = 2,440 − 1,685 = 755. Check in the story: 755 + 1,685 = 2,440 mm.
  2. (b) Let s be one shelf, in mm. Four shelves: 4 × s = 3,360. Divide both sides by 4: s = 3,360 ÷ 4 = 840. Check: 4 × 840 = 3,360 mm.

Example 8.17A two-step equation from a story
A fence has a 1,200 mm gate and n boards, each 140 mm wide, set edge to edge. The whole fence is 3,580 mm long. How many boards are there?
Solution
  1. Let n be the number of boards. The boards give 140 × n, and the gate adds 1,200: 140 × n + 1,200 = 3,580.
  2. Undo in reverse order. Undo the + 1,200 first: 140 × n = 3,580 − 1,200 = 2,380.
  3. Then undo the × 140: n = 2,380 ÷ 140 = 17.
  4. Check in the story: 140 × 17 + 1,200 = 2,380 + 1,200 = 3,580 mm.

Example 8.18A bill written as an equation
A mobile welder charges a $75 call-out fee plus $95 an hour. The bill comes to $502.50. How many hours did the job take?
Solution
  1. Let h be the hours. "$95 an hour" means $95 for each hour, so the hours cost 95 × h. Add the call-out fee: 75 + 95 × h = 502.50.
  2. Undo the + 75: 95 × h = 502.50 − 75 = 427.50.
  3. Undo the × 95: h = 427.50 ÷ 95 = 4.5.
  4. Check: 75 + 95 × 4.5 = 75 + 427.50 = $502.50.

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.9 Electrical formulas8.9 Electrical formulas

Section 8.2 gave two electrical formulas: Ohm's law, V = I × R, and the power formula, P = V × I. Here they are used as math only: substitute, transpose and check, the same skills as the rest of this chapter.

The formulas follow from how the units are defined. NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) gives 1 Ω = 1 V/A, one ohm is one volt per ampere, and 1 V = 1 W/A, one volt is one watt per ampere.

Example 8.19Ohm's law and power
A heating coil on a test bench has a resistance of 12 Ω and carries a current of 1.5 A. Use V = I × R to find the voltage across it. Then use P = V × I to find the power.
Solution
  1. V = I × R = 1.5 × 12 = 18 V.
  2. P = V × I = 18 × 1.5 = 27 W. Use the voltage you just found.

Example 8.20Ohm's law turned around
Make I the subject of V = I × R and find the current when V = 24 V and R = 16 Ω. Then make I the subject of P = V × I and find the current when P = 60 W and V = 12 V.
Solution
  1. In V = I × R, I has been multiplied by R. Divide both sides by R: I = V ÷ R.
  2. I = 24 ÷ 16 = 1.5 A.
  3. In P = V × I, I has been multiplied by V. Divide both sides by V: I = P ÷ V = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 A.

Chapter 8 Formulas and Transposing8.10 Stair formulas and the BC Building Code8.10 Stair formulas and the BC Building Code

A carpenter laying out a stair starts from one measurement, the total rise: the height from the finished floor at the bottom to the finished floor at the top. Each step up is a riser. The height of one step is the unit rise. The run of one step is the unit run, and the horizontal length of the whole flight is the total run.

The BC Building Code (BCBC 2024) sets the limits. It says the rise is "measured as the vertical nosing-to-nosing distance" (Division B, Sentence 9.8.4.1.(1), page 9-30), and it defines run as "the horizontal distance between two adjacent tread nosings on a stair" (Division A, Sentence 1.4.1.2.(1), page 1-23). A flight is "a series of steps between landings" (Division A, page 1-18).

Stair formulas
number of risers = total rise ÷ maximum rise, rounded up to a whole number
unit rise = total rise ÷ number of risers
number of treads = number of risers − 1
total run = number of treads × unit run
Work in millimetres. Round the number of risers up, never down: rounding down makes each riser taller than the maximum.
Stair typeRise, max.Rise, min.Run, max.Run, min.
Private200 mm125 mm355 mm255 mm
Public180 mm125 mmNo limit280 mm
Table 8.4Rise and run for rectangular treads. BCBC 2024, Division B, Table 9.8.4.1 (Sentence 9.8.4.1.(1), page 9-30) and Table 9.8.4.2 (Sentence 9.8.4.2.(1), page 9-31).

The notes to both tables say that private stairs "are exterior and interior stairs that serve" single dwelling units, houses with a secondary suite including their common spaces, and garages that serve those houses. Public stairs "are all stairs not described as service stairs or private stairs." Article 9.8.3.3 adds that "the vertical height of any flight of stairs shall not exceed 3.7 m" (page 9-30).

Example 8.21Risers for a house stair
A private stair in a house has a total rise of 2,690 mm. Find the number of risers and the unit rise, to two decimal places. Check the unit rise against Table 9.8.4.1.
Solution
  1. Number of risers: 2,690 ÷ 200 = 13.45. Round up to 14.
  2. Unit rise: 2,690 ÷ 14 = 192.14 mm.
  3. Check: 192.14 mm is not more than 200 mm and not less than 125 mm, so it meets the table.
  4. Why not 13 risers? 2,690 ÷ 13 = 206.92 mm, taller than the 200 mm maximum.

Example 8.22Total run
The stair in Example 8.21 has 14 risers. The drawing gives a unit run of 260 mm. Check the unit run against Table 9.8.4.2, then find the total run.
Solution
  1. 260 mm is not less than 255 mm and not more than 355 mm, so it meets the table for a private stair.
  2. Number of treads: 14 − 1 = 13.
  3. Total run: 13 × 260 = 3,380 mm.

Example 8.23A public stair
A public stair has a total rise of 3,150 mm. Check the height of the flight against Article 9.8.3.3. Find the number of risers and the unit rise. The drawing gives a unit run of 300 mm. Find the total run.
Solution
  1. 3,150 mm is less than 3.7 m = 3,700 mm, so one flight is allowed.
  2. Risers: 3,150 ÷ 180 = 17.5. Round up to 18.
  3. Unit rise: 3,150 ÷ 18 = 175 mm, between 125 mm and 180 mm.
  4. The run of 300 mm is not less than 280 mm. Treads: 18 − 1 = 17. Total run: 17 × 300 = 5,100 mm.

Every riser in a flight must be the same height, within a small tolerance. Sentence 9.8.4.4.(1) allows a maximum tolerance of "5 mm between adjacent treads or landings" and "10 mm between the tallest and shortest risers in a flight". Sentence 9.8.4.4.(3) sets the same 5 mm and 10 mm for the run of rectangular treads (page 9-32).

Example 8.24Checking a built flight
The risers of a built flight measure, from the bottom: 188, 191, 190, 196, 189 and 191 mm. Do they meet Sentence 9.8.4.4.(1)?
Solution
  1. Adjacent risers: 191 − 188 = 3, 191 − 190 = 1, 196 − 190 = 6, 196 − 189 = 7, 191 − 189 = 2.
  2. Two differences, 6 mm and 7 mm, are more than 5 mm.
  3. Tallest and shortest: 196 − 188 = 8 mm, which is within 10 mm.
No. The flight meets the 10 mm rule but fails the 5 mm rule between adjacent risers, at the fourth riser.

The stair formulas transpose like any other formula. From unit rise = total rise ÷ number of risers you get total rise = number of risers × unit rise, and from total run = number of treads × unit run you get unit run = total run ÷ number of treads.

Try it 8.10

  3. A public stair has a total rise of 2,880 mm. Find the number of risers and the unit rise.
  4. A stair has 15 risers of 186 mm. Find the total rise.
  5. A private stair has 12 treads and a total run of 3,060 mm. Find the unit run. Does it meet Table 9.8.4.2?
  6. Two adjacent risers measure 184 mm and 191 mm. Do they meet Sentence 9.8.4.4.(1)?

9

Perimeter and Circumference

How much flat bar goes around a guard? How long is the band that wraps a tank? How big a sheet rolls into a round duct? Each question asks for a distance around the outside of a shape.

This chapter works out the distance around rectangles, triangles and other straight-sided shapes, and then around circles. The distance around a circle is always π × D, the number π times the diameter. The same formula gives the stretch-out, the length of flat sheet that rolls into a pipe or a round duct.

In this chapter you will

  • Find the perimeter of straight-sided shapes
  • Find a missing side from a perimeter
  • Name the parts of a circle
  • Use C = π × D, and find D from C
  • Find the stretch-out of a pipe or duct
  • Find arcs and composite perimeters

Key words

  • perimeter
  • radius
  • diameter
  • circumference
  • pi (π)
  • stretch-out
  • arc

Chapter 9 Perimeter and Circumference9.1 Perimeter of straight-sided shapes9.1 Perimeter of straight-sided shapes

The perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a flat shape. Picture walking along every edge until you are back where you started. Add up every edge you walked.

Perimeter
Rectangle: P = 2 × (l + w)  Square: P = 4 × s
Triangle: P = a + b + c  Regular polygon: P = n × s
l length, w width, s side, a, b and c the three sides, n the number of equal sides
Example 9.1A rectangular guard frame
A guard frame is 1,500 mm long and 750 mm wide. How much flat bar goes around it?
Solution
  1. Two lengths and two widths: P = 2 × (l + w).
  2. P = 2 × (1,500 + 750) = 2 × 2,250 = 4,500

Example 9.3Feet and inches

  2. P = 2 × (150 + 105) = 510 in.
  3. 510 ÷ 12 = 42.5 ft, which is 42 ft and 0.5 × 12 = 6 in.

Chapter 9 Perimeter and Circumference9.2 The parts of a circle and π9.2 The parts of a circle and π

The radius (r) is the distance from the centre of a circle to its edge. The diameter (D) is the distance across the circle through the centre, so it is two radii: D = 2 × r and r = D ÷ 2. The circumference (C) is the distance around the circle. It is the perimeter of a circle.

Wrap a string once around any circle and lay it along the diameter. It fits a little more than 3 times, every time, for a washer or a tank. That number is pi, written π. It is about 3.14159, and its digits never end.

CalculatorThe π key

Both calculators show π to 10 digits. Use the key every time instead of typing 3.14.
3.14 is not π

π × 600 = 1,884.96, but 3.14 × 600 = 1,884. The short value is almost 1 mm short on a 600 mm circle, and the error grows with the size of the job.

Circumference

If you know the radius, double it first to get D.
Example 9.4From a diameter and from a radius
Find the circumference of a disc 450 mm in diameter, and of a ring with a radius of 125 mm. Round to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Disc: C = π × 450 = 1,413.72.
  2. Ring: double the radius first, D = 2 × 125 = 250. Then C = π × 250 = 785.40.

Example 9.6Turns of a wheel
A wheel 600 mm in diameter rolls along a floor. In one turn it rolls one circumference. How far does it roll in 25 turns? How many turns does it make in 50 m?
Solution
  1. One turn: π × 600 mm. 25 turns: 25 × π × 600 = 47,123.89 mm, about 47.12 m.
  2. Turns in 50 m = 50,000 mm: 50,000 ÷ (π × 600) = 26.53.

Key idea

Double the diameter and the circumference doubles. Halve it and the circumference halves. C and D always keep the same ratio, π.

Chapter 9 Perimeter and Circumference9.4 Stretch-out of a pipe or duct9.4 Stretch-out of a pipe or duct

Open out the side of a cylinder and it lies flat as a rectangle. One side of the rectangle is the length of the cylinder. The other side wrapped once around the cylinder, so it is the circumference. This length is the stretch-out. To make a round duct, you cut a sheet as long as the stretch-out and roll it.

Measure around when you can

A tape wrapped once around a part reads the stretch-out directly. You need π only when you start from the diameter.

Example 9.7Sheet for a round duct
A round duct is 300 mm in diameter and 1,200 mm long. The drawing adds 25 mm to the stretch-out for a lap seam. What size sheet is cut? Give the sheet length to the nearest millimetre.
Solution
  1. Stretch-out: π × 300 = 942.48 mm.
  2. Add the seam allowance from the drawing: 942.48 + 25 = 967.48 mm.

Example 9.8A jacket around a pipe
A sheet-metal jacket wraps around the outside of a pipe. The outside diameter is 658 in. Find the stretch-out to the nearest 1/16 in.
Solution
  1. The jacket wraps the outside surface, so use the outside diameter.
  2. π × 6.625 = 20.813 in.
  3. Sixteenths: 0.813 × 16 = 13.01, which rounds to 13.

Chapter 9 Perimeter and Circumference9.5 Arcs9.5 Arcs

An arc is a part of the circumference. A 90° arc is a quarter of the circle, because a full turn is 360°. Find the fraction of the circle, then take that fraction of π × D.

Arc length
arc = angle ÷ 360 × π × D
Half circle: π × D ÷ 2. Quarter circle: π × D ÷ 4.
Example 9.9A curved handrail
A curved handrail follows a 120° arc of a circle 2,400 mm in diameter. How long is the rail? Round to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. 120° is 120 ÷ 360 = one third of the circle.
  2. arc = 120 ÷ 360 × π × 2,400 = 2,513.27

Chapter 9 Perimeter and Circumference9.6 Composite perimeters9.6 Composite perimeters

A composite shape is made of simple parts. Break it down: split it into straight edges and arcs, find any missing lengths, then add only the edges on the outside. The dashed lines used to split a shape are not edges.

Example 9.10A slot
A slot has straight sides 60 mm long and round ends 30 mm across. Find the distance around the slot.
Solution
  1. Two straight sides: 2 × 60 = 120 mm.
  2. Two half circles make one whole circle with D = 30 mm: π × 30 = 94.25 mm.
  3. Add: 120 + 94.25 = 214.25.
Calculator
TI-30Xa

Display 214.2477796
Sharp EL-531XT

Display 214.2477796
214.25 mm
Example 9.11A plate with a round end
A plate is a 400 mm by 200 mm rectangle with a half circle on one end. Find its perimeter.
Solution
  1. Part A gives three outside edges: 400 + 400 + 200 = 1,000 mm. Its right side is the dashed line, inside the plate.
  2. Part B is a half circle with D = 200 mm: π × 200 ÷ 2 = 314.16 mm.
  3. Add: 1,000 + 314.16 = 1,314.16.
1,314.16 mm
Example 9.12A belt around two pulleys
A belt runs around two pulleys, each 200 mm in diameter. The centres are 800 mm apart. How long is the belt?
Solution
  1. The two straight runs are each as long as the centre distance: 2 × 800 = 1,600 mm.
  2. The belt wraps half of each pulley. Two halves make one circle: π × 200 = 628.32 mm.
  3. Add: 1,600 + 628.32 = 2,228.32.
2,228.32 mm
Try it 9.6
