  2. A 600 mm by 400 mm plate has a 50 mm radius on each corner. Find the perimeter.
  3. Two pulleys 150 mm in diameter have centres 600 mm apart. Find the belt length.
  4. A quarter circle has r = 300 mm. Find the perimeter, both straight edges and the arc.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 9 Perimeter and Circumference9.7 Carpentry: plates, rim joists, fascia and trim9.7 Carpentry: plates, rim joists, fascia and trim

A carpenter measures around the outside of a building again and again: for the wall plates, for the rim joists of a floor, for the fascia along the roof edge, and for baseboard and trim inside. Each one is a perimeter.

In a wood-frame wall the studs stand on a bottom plate and carry top plates. The BC Building Code says "a bottom wall plate shall be provided in all cases" (BCBC 2024, Division B, Sentence 9.23.11.2.(1), page 9-184), and "at least 2 top plates shall be provided in loadbearing walls", except where Sentences (2) to (4) allow one or none (Sentence 9.23.11.3.(1), page 9-185). A loadbearing wall with a double top plate therefore needs three plates along its length.

Example 9.13Wall plates for a house
The outside walls of a house are 12,200 mm by 8,500 mm. All four walls are loadbearing, with one bottom plate and two top plates. The estimate uses the outside perimeter and ignores openings. How much plate is needed? The plate comes in 4,880 mm lengths. How many lengths are ordered?
Solution
  1. Perimeter: P = 2 × (12,200 + 8,500) = 41,400 mm.
  2. Three plates all the way around: 3 × 41,400 = 124,200 mm.
  3. Lengths: 124,200 ÷ 4,880 = 25.45. Round up to 26, because 25 lengths are too short.

The code defines a rim joist as "the outermost member in floor framing, other than blocking, be it parallel, perpendicular or on an angle to the floor joists" (Division A, Sentence 1.4.1.2.(1), page 1-23). The rim joists run all the way around the floor, so their total length is the perimeter of the floor framing.

Example 9.14Rim joists
A floor frame is 9,760 mm by 7,320 mm. Find the total length of rim joist. The rim board comes in 4,880 mm lengths. How many lengths are needed, ignoring joints?
Solution
  1. P = 2 × (9,760 + 7,320) = 2 × 17,080 = 34,160 mm.
  2. 34,160 ÷ 4,880 = 7 lengths exactly.

Example 9.15Fascia around a roof
A building has walls 10,000 mm by 7,200 mm. Its hip roof overhangs 600 mm on every side, and fascia runs along all four roof edges. How long is the fascia?

  1. The overhang adds 600 mm at each end: length 10,000 + 2 × 600 = 11,200 mm, width 7,200 + 2 × 600 = 8,400 mm.
  2. P = 2 × (11,200 + 8,400) = 39,200 mm.

Example 9.16Baseboard in feet and inches
A room is 14 ft 6 in by 11 ft 9 in. Baseboard runs around the walls except across one door opening 32 in wide. How much baseboard is needed? Give feet and inches.

Chapter
10

Area

Area tells you how much flat surface a part covers. You use it to order plate and sheet, to work out how much coating a floor needs, and to lay out the sheet metal for a duct or a tank. This chapter builds the area formulas one shape at a time, then breaks composite parts into pieces and unfolds solids into flat nets.

In this chapter you will

  • Explain what area is and use square units
  • Find the area of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms and trapezoids
  • Find the area of circles and rings with π × r²
  • Change mm² to m² and in² to ft²
  • Break a composite shape into basic shapes
  • Unfold a solid into a net and find its surface area

Key words

  • area
  • square unit
  • base and height
  • composite shape
  • surface area
  • net

Chapter 10 Area10.1 Area and square units10.1 Area and square units

Area is the amount of flat surface inside a shape. A length is measured in one direction. Area covers two directions at once, so it is measured with squares.

A square unit is a square that is 1 unit long on each side. A square 1 cm on each side has an area of 1 square centimetre, written 1 cm². The small 2 shows that two lengths were multiplied: centimetres times centimetres.

The square units used in this book are mm², cm² and m² (square millimetres, square centimetres and square metres), and in² and ft² (square inches and square feet). A length in mm and an area in mm² measure different things, so always write the small 2 on an area.

Try it 10.1
  1. A plate on a 1 cm grid covers 4 rows of 7 squares. What is its area?
  2. How do you say 35 m² out loud?
  3. Which is an area: 12 ft, 12 ft² or 12 ft³?
  4. A floor is covered by 30 tiles. Each tile is exactly 1 ft². What is the area of the floor?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 10 Area10.2 Rectangles and squares10.2 Rectangles and squares

A rectangle that is 6 squares long and 3 squares wide holds 3 rows of 6 squares. Multiplying the length by the width counts them all at once, so you do not need a grid.

Area of a rectangle and a square
A = l × w
A = s × s = s²
A = area, l = length, w = width, s = side of a square. Both lengths must be in the same unit.

Square millimetres make big numbers, and a large area is easier to read in square metres. One metre is 1,000 mm, so a square metre is 1,000 mm by 1,000 mm. In the same way, a square foot is 12 in by 12 in.

Example 10.1Area of a base plate
A machine base plate is 600 mm long and 450 mm wide. Find its area in mm² and in m².
Solution
  1. A = l × w = 600 × 450 = 270,000 mm².
  2. To change mm² to m², divide by 1,000,000: 270,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.27 m².
  3. Check: in metres the plate is 0.6 m by 0.45 m, and 0.6 × 0.45 = 0.27 m².
Calculator
TI-30Xa
Area in mm²
600×450=
Display 270000.
mm² to m²
270000÷1000000=
Display 0.27
Sharp EL-531XT
Area in mm²
600×450=
Display 270’000.
mm² to m²
270000÷1000000=
Display 0.27
270,000 mm² = 0.27 m²
Divide by 1,000,000, not by 1,000

Changing mm to m divides a length by 1,000. An area has two lengths multiplied, so the factor is used twice: 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000. Dividing 270,000 mm² by 1,000 gives 270, far too big for this plate in m².

The same idea works in imperial units. A sheet 4 ft by 8 ft has an area of 4 × 8 = 32 ft². In inches it is 48 in by 96 in, and 48 × 96 = 4,608 in². The check 32 × 144 = 4,608 shows the two answers agree.

Example 10.2Coating a shop floor
A shop floor is 6 m by 4.5 m. The coating label says one litre covers 5 m². The coating is sold in 1 L tins. How many tins do you buy?
Solution
  1. Area: 6 × 4.5 = 27 m².
  2. Litres: 27 ÷ 5 = 5.4 L.
  3. A part tin still has to be bought, so round up.

Chapter 10 Area10.3 Triangles10.3 Triangles

Every triangle is half of a rectangle or of a parallelogram. To use that idea you need two measurements, the base and the height.

The base is the side you measure from, usually the bottom side. The height is the distance from the base to the opposite corner, measured at right angles to the base. The height is not a sloping side.

Area of a triangle
A = b × h ÷ 2
b = base, h = height at right angles to the base.
Example 10.3A triangular end panel
The end panel of a trough is a triangle with a base of 600 mm and a height of 400 mm. Its two sloping sides are each 500 mm long. Find the area in mm² and in m².
Solution
  1. Use the base and the height. The 500 mm sloping sides are not needed.
  2. A = 600 × 400 ÷ 2 = 120,000 mm².
  3. In m²: 120,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.12 m².
Calculator
TI-30Xa
600×400÷2=
Display 120000.
Sharp EL-531XT
600×400÷2=
Display 120’000.
120,000 mm² = 0.12 m²
The sloping side is not the height

Using the 500 mm side in the example above would give 600 × 500 ÷ 2 = 150,000 mm², which is too big. The height always meets the base at a right angle. A drawing often shows it as a dashed line with a small square at its foot.

Try it 10.3
  1. A right-angled gusset: base 300 mm, height 200 mm. Area?
  2. Base 18 in, height 10.5 in. Area?
  3. Base 1.2 m, height 0.9 m. Area?
  4. Base 300 mm, sloping sides 250 mm, height 200 mm. Area?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 10 Area10.4 Parallelograms and trapezoids10.4 Parallelograms and trapezoids

A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Cut the triangle off one end and move it to the other end: the parallelogram becomes a rectangle with the same base and the same height. So its area is base times height: A = b × h, where h is the height at right angles to the base, not the slanted side.

A trapezoid has one pair of parallel sides, called a and b. Two copies of the same trapezoid, one turned around, fit together to make a parallelogram with base a + b. One trapezoid is half of it.

Area of a trapezoid
A = (a + b) ÷ 2 × h
a and b = the two parallel sides, h = the height between them. (a + b) ÷ 2 is the average width.
Example 10.4A hopper side panel
A hopper side panel is a trapezoid. The parallel sides are 400 mm and 1,200 mm, and the height between them is 700 mm. Find the area in mm² and m².
Solution
  1. A = (a + b) ÷ 2 × h.
  2. Brackets first: 400 + 1,200 = 1,600.
  3. Average width: 1,600 ÷ 2 = 800.
  4. Times the height: 800 × 700 = 560,000 mm² = 0.56 m².
Calculator
TI-30Xa
(400+1200)÷2×700=
Display 560000.
Sharp EL-531XT
(400+1200)÷2×700=
Display 560’000.
The brackets make both calculators add the parallel sides before dividing.
560,000 mm² = 0.56 m²

The quadrilateral family

A quadrilateral is any flat shape with four straight sides. The shapes in this chapter belong to one family. A square is a rectangle with four equal sides, and it is also a rhombus with four right angles. Rectangles and rhombuses are special parallelograms. The table lists what each member has, and the area formula to use.

ShapeSidesAnglesDiagonalsArea
Square4 equal sides, opposite sides parallel4 right anglesEqual length, cross at right angles, cut each other in halfA = s × s
RectangleOpposite sides equal and parallel4 right anglesEqual length, cut each other in halfA = l × w
ParallelogramOpposite sides equal and parallelOpposite angles equalCut each other in halfA = b × h
Rhombus4 equal sides, opposite sides parallelOpposite angles equalCross at right angles, cut each other in halfA = b × h or A = d₁ × d₂ ÷ 2
TrapezoidOne pair of parallel sides, a and bNo fixed ruleNo fixed ruleA = (a + b) ÷ 2 × h
KiteTwo pairs of equal sides that meet at a cornerOne pair of opposite angles equalCross at right angles, one cuts the other in halfA = d₁ × d₂ ÷ 2
The quadrilateral family. Tick marks show sides of equal length. h is always measured at right angles to the base, and d₁ and d₂ are the diagonals.

A rhombus and a kite can also be found from their two diagonals, the lines joining opposite corners. The diagonals cross at right angles, so the shape is exactly half of the rectangle that is d₁ long and d₂ wide: A = d₁ × d₂ ÷ 2. A kite-shaped gusset with diagonals of 600 mm and 400 mm has an area of 600 × 400 ÷ 2 = 120,000 mm².

Try it 10.4
  1. Parallelogram: base 500 mm, slanted side 340 mm, height 300 mm. Area?
  2. Parallelogram: base 30 in, slanted side 15 in, height 12 in. Area?
  3. Trapezoid: parallel sides 300 mm and 500 mm, height 200 mm. Area?
  4. Trapezoid: parallel sides 14 in and 22 in, height 9 in. Area?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 10 Area10.5 Circles and rings10.5 Circles and rings

The area of a circle uses the radius, the distance from the centre to the edge. The radius is half the diameter.

Picture the circle inside a square. The square is 2 r on each side, so it holds 4 small squares that are r by r. The circle covers a bit more than 3 of those small squares: exactly π of them, and π is about 3.14.

Area of a circle
A = π × r²
r = radius. Square the radius first (exponents come before multiplying in BEDMAS), then multiply by π. Use the π key for the full value.
Example 10.5A round blank
A round blank is cut with a radius of 150 mm. Find its area to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. A = π × r².
  2. Square the radius: 150² = 150 × 150 = 22,500.
  3. Multiply by π: π × 22,500 = 70,685.83.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
π×150x²=
Display 70685.83471
Sharp EL-531XT
π×150x²=
Display 70’685.83471
Both calculators square 150 before multiplying by π, because they follow BEDMAS.
70,685.83 mm²
Halve the diameter first

A round cover for an opening 18 in across has r = 9 in, so its area is π × 9² = 254.47 in². Putting the diameter into the formula gives π × 18² = 1,017.88 in², four times too big. When a drawing gives Ø (diameter), divide by 2 before you square.

A half circle has half the area of the full circle, and a quarter circle has a quarter. A ring, such as a washer, a flange or the end of a pipe, is a big circle with a small circle taken out. Find the area of the outside circle (radius R) and subtract the area of the hole (radius r).

Area of a ring
A = π × R² − π × r² = π × (R² − r²)
R = outside radius, r = inside radius. Square each radius before subtracting.
Example 10.6A flange ring
A flat flange ring has an outside diameter of 300 mm and an inside diameter of 200 mm. Find its area to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Halve the diameters: R = 150 mm and r = 100 mm.
  2. Square each one: 150² = 22,500 and 100² = 10,000.
  3. Subtract: 22,500 − 10,000 = 12,500.
  4. Multiply by π: π × 12,500 = 39,269.91.

Square each radius, then subtract

Subtracting the radii first, 150 − 100 = 50, and then squaring gives π × 50² = 7,853.98 mm². That is the area of a small circle, not the ring.

Try it 10.5

  2. Half circle, radius 200 mm. Area to two decimal places?

  4. Tube end: outside diameter 60 mm, wall 5 mm thick. Area of metal to two decimal places?

Chapter 10 Area10.6 Composite shapes10.6 Composite shapes

A composite shape is made of two or more basic shapes: an L-shaped bracket, a plate with a hole, a lug with a round end. The Shape Canvas calls the method break it down.

  1. Split the shape with dashed lines into basic shapes. Label them A, B, C.
  2. Find any missing dimensions from the overall dimensions.
  3. Find the area of each piece.
  4. Add the pieces. Subtract any hole or cut-out.
Example 10.7An L-shaped plate
Find the area of the L-shaped plate.
Solution
  1. Split on the dashed line into A (the upright) and B (the foot).
  2. A: 250 × 600 = 150,000 mm².
  3. B is 800 − 250 = 550 mm long: 550 × 200 = 110,000 mm².
  4. Add: 150,000 + 110,000 = 260,000 mm².
Calculator
TI-30Xa
250×600+550×200=
Display 260000.
Sharp EL-531XT
250×600+550×200=
Display 260’000.
260,000 mm²
Two ways, one answer

The L is also an 800 × 600 rectangle with a 550 × 400 corner missing. 800 × 600 − 550 × 400 = 260,000 mm², the same answer. When two methods agree, you can trust the answer.

Example 10.8A lifting lug
A lifting lug is a 120 mm by 150 mm rectangle with a half circle on top. A 30 mm diameter hole is centred where the half circle meets the rectangle. Find the area of the lug to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. A: 120 × 150 = 18,000 mm².
  2. B: the half circle is 120 mm across, so r = 60 mm. π × 60² ÷ 2 = 5,654.87 mm².
  3. C: r = 15 mm. π × 15² = 706.86 mm².
  4. A + B − C = 22,948.01 mm².

22,948.01 mm²

  3. A 300 mm by 200 mm plate with four 20 mm diameter holes. Area to two decimal places?
  4. A 700 mm by 400 mm plate with a 200 mm by 150 mm notch cut out of one edge. Area?

Chapter 10 Area10.7 Surface area and nets10.7 Surface area and nets

A solid, such as a box or a tank, is covered by faces. Its surface area is the total area of all its outside faces. Surface area tells you how much sheet a tank needs, or how much area there is to paint.

A net is a flat pattern that folds or rolls up to make the solid. The Shape Canvas calls this unfold it. Unfold the solid, find the area of each piece of the net, and add them.

Example 10.9Surface area of a closed box
A closed box is 600 mm long, 400 mm wide and 300 mm high. Find its surface area in mm² and m².
Solution
  1. Top and bottom: 2 × 600 × 400 = 480,000 mm².
  2. Front and back: 2 × 600 × 300 = 360,000 mm².
  3. Two ends: 2 × 400 × 300 = 240,000 mm².
  4. Add the three pairs: 480,000 + 360,000 + 240,000 = 1,080,000 mm².
  5. In m²: 1,080,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 1.08 m².
Calculator
TI-30Xa
2×(600×400+600×300+400×300)=
Display 1080000.
Sharp EL-531XT
2×(600×400+600×300+400×300)=
Display 1’080’000.
1,080,000 mm² = 1.08 m²

A cylinder unrolls into two circles and one rectangle. The rectangle wraps around the circle, so its length is the distance around the circle, π × D. This length is the stretch-out. The width of the rectangle is the height of the cylinder.

Surface area of a closed cylinder
Two ends: 2 × (π × r²)
Side: π × D × h
SA = two ends + side
r = radius, D = diameter, h = height. The side is the stretch-out π × D times the height.
Example 10.10Sheet for a cylinder tank
A closed cylindrical tank has a radius of 300 mm and a height of 1,000 mm. Find its surface area to two decimal places in mm², then in m².
Solution
  1. Two ends: π × 300² = 282,743.34 mm² each, so 565,486.68 mm² for both.
  2. Side: D = 2 × 300 = 600 mm, and π × 600 × 1,000 = 1,884,955.59 mm².
  3. Total: 565,486.68 + 1,884,955.59 = 2,450,442.27 mm².
  4. In m²: 2,450,442.27 ÷ 1,000,000 = 2.45 m² to two decimal places.

A rectangular duct is 12 in by 8 in and 60 in long, open at both ends. Its net is one long rectangle: the four sides side by side. Ignore seams. Find the area of sheet in in² and in ft² to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. The width of the net is the perimeter of the duct: 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 in.
  2. Area: 40 × 60 = 2,400 in².
  3. In ft²: 2,400 ÷ 144 = 16.67 ft².

Chapter 10 Area10.8 Materials takeoff10.8 Materials takeoff

A takeoff is the list of materials a job needs, worked out from the drawings. Area is the first step for drywall, sheathing, flooring, tile, paint and roofing. Sheets, boxes and cans are sold in whole units, so the count is always rounded up. A result of 3.1 sheets means you buy 4.

Sheet sizes, the area a box or can covers, the waste allowance and the price come from the job: the drawings, the product label and the supplier. In this section they are given in each problem.

  1. Find the whole area of the wall, floor, ceiling or roof.
  2. Subtract the openings (doors and windows) that the material does not cover.
  3. If a waste allowance is given, add it: area × (1 + waste % ÷ 100).
  4. Divide by the area that one unit covers.
  5. Round up to the next whole unit, then multiply by the price for the cost.
Materials takeoff
Units = area ÷ coverage of one unit, rounded up
Area with waste = area × (1 + waste % ÷ 100)
Cost = units × price of one unit
Coverage is the area one sheet, box or can covers. A 10% waste allowance multiplies the area by 1.10. Two coats of paint double the area.
Example 10.12Drywall for a wall with openings
A wall is 6 m long and 2.4 m high. It has a door 0.9 m by 2.1 m and a window 1.5 m by 1.2 m. Drywall comes in 1.2 m by 2.4 m sheets at $18.50 each. How many sheets do you buy, and what do they cost?
Solution
  1. Wall: 6 × 2.4 = 14.4 m².
  2. Openings: 0.9 × 2.1 = 1.89 m² and 1.5 × 1.2 = 1.8 m².
  3. Net area: 14.4 − 1.89 − 1.8 = 10.71 m².
  4. One sheet covers 1.2 × 2.4 = 2.88 m². 10.71 ÷ 2.88 = 3.72, so buy 4 sheets.
  5. Cost: 4 × $18.50 = $74.00.

The thickness of the board is a code question, not a math question. BCBC 2024 Sentence 9.29.5.3.(1) says the spacing of supports for single-layer gypsum board must conform to Table 9.29.5.3. (page 9-275). For walls, the table allows 12.7 mm board on studs up to 600 mm o.c., whether the board runs parallel or perpendicular to the studs. 9.5 mm board on walls is listed only perpendicular to the framing, with supports up to 400 mm o.c.

Example 10.13Wall sheathing in feet
An exterior wall is 36 ft long and 8 ft high. The plan subtracts two windows, each 4 ft by 3 ft, and a door 3 ft by 6 ft 8 in. Sheathing comes in 4 ft by 8 ft sheets at $24.95. How many sheets, and what is the cost?
Solution
  1. Wall: 36 × 8 = 288 ft².
  2. Windows: 2 × 4 × 3 = 24 ft². Door: 6 ft 8 in = 80 in, and 80 ÷ 12 = 6⅔ ft, so 3 × 6⅔ = 20 ft².
  3. Net area: 288 − 24 − 20 = 244 ft².
  4. One sheet covers 4 × 8 = 32 ft². 244 ÷ 32 = 7.625, so buy 8 sheets.
  5. Cost: 8 × $24.95 = $199.60.

Example 10.14Floor tile with a waste allowance

Example 10.15Paint for a room, two coats
A room is 4.2 m by 3.6 m and the walls are 2.4 m high. Leave out a door 0.9 m by 2.1 m and a window 1.2 m by 1 m. The walls get two coats. The label says one 3.78 L can covers 35 m². Cans are $54.99. How many cans, and what is the cost?
Solution
  1. The walls unfold into one long rectangle. Its length is the perimeter of the room: 2 × (4.2 + 3.6) = 15.6 m.
  2. Wall area: 15.6 × 2.4 = 37.44 m².
  3. Less the openings: 37.44 − 1.89 − 1.2 = 34.35 m².
  4. Two coats: 34.35 × 2 = 68.7 m². 68.7 ÷ 35 = 1.96, so buy 2 cans.
  5. Cost: 2 × $54.99 = $109.98.

Example 10.16Sheathing a gable roof
A gable roof has two equal sides. Each side measures 12.6 m along the ridge and 4.2 m down the slope from the ridge to the eave. Roof sheathing comes in 1.22 m by 2.44 m sheets at $32.75. Allow 5% waste. How many sheets, and what is the cost?
Solution

  2. Two sides: 2 × 12.6 × 4.2 = 105.84 m².

  5. Cost: 38 × $32.75 = $1,244.50.
  6. The thickness comes from the code. For roofs not used as a walking deck, Sentence 9.23.16.7.(2) points to Table 9.23.16.7.-A (page 9-226). With rafters at 600 mm o.c., plywood needs at least 9.5 mm with the edges supported, or 12.5 mm with the edges unsupported.

Chapter
11

Volume and Capacity

Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up or holds. You need it to size a tank, to know how much water fills a pipe run before a pressure test, and to work out what a hopper holds. This chapter counts cubic units, builds the volume formulas for prisms, cylinders, cones, pyramids and spheres, and changes volumes into litres and US gallons.

In this chapter you will

  • Explain volume and use cubic units
  • Find the volume of prisms with V = end area × length
  • Find the volume of cylinders, tanks and pipes
  • Find the volume of cones, pyramids and spheres
  • Change volumes into litres and US gallons
  • Break a composite solid into basic solids

Key words

  • volume
  • cubic unit
  • prism
  • cylinder
  • cone and pyramid
  • sphere
  • capacity

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.1 Volume and cubic units11.1 Volume and cubic units

Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up or holds. Length uses one direction and area uses two. Volume uses three: length, width and height.

Volume is counted in cubes. A cubic unit is a cube 1 unit long on each edge. A cube 1 cm on each edge is 1 cubic centimetre, written 1 cm³. The small 3 shows that three lengths were multiplied. The cubic units in this book are mm³, cm³ and m³, and in³ and ft³.

Changing between cubic units uses the length factor three times. A cubic centimetre is 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm = 1,000 mm³. A cubic metre is 1,000 mm × 1,000 mm × 1,000 mm = 1,000,000,000 mm³. A cubic foot is 12 in × 12 in × 12 in = 1,728 in³.

Three factors, not one

To change mm³ to m³, divide by 1,000,000,000 (1,000 three times). Dividing by 1,000 only changes a length. Many people find it easier to change each length to metres first and then multiply.

Try it 11.1
  1. A block of 1 cm cubes is 5 long, 2 wide and 3 high. How many cm³?
  2. How many mm³ are in 1 cm³?
  3. How many in³ are in 2 ft³?
  4. Which is a volume: 8 m, 8 m² or 8 m³?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.2 Prisms11.2 Prisms

A prism is a solid with two identical, parallel ends joined by flat sides. Cut a slice anywhere along it and the slice is the same shape as the end. A box, a triangular trough and a length of angle bar are all prisms.

Think of the end as one layer. The volume is the area of that layer times how many layers there are, which is the length.

Volume of a prism
V = end area × length
Box: V = l × w × h
Find the end area with the formulas from Chapter 10. All lengths in the same unit.
Example 11.1A rectangular tank
A tank is 1,200 mm long, 600 mm wide and 500 mm high inside. Find its volume in mm³ and in m³.
Solution
  1. V = l × w × h = 1,200 × 600 × 500 = 360,000,000 mm³.
  2. In metres the tank is 1.2 m by 0.6 m by 0.5 m.
  3. V = 1.2 × 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.36 m³.

Example 11.2A triangular trough
A trough is a triangular prism. Its end is a triangle with a base of 400 mm and a height of 300 mm. The trough is 1,000 mm long. Find the volume in m³.
Solution
  1. End area: 400 × 300 ÷ 2 = 60,000 mm².
  2. Volume: 60,000 × 1,000 = 60,000,000 mm³.
  3. In m³: 60,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000,000 = 0.06 m³.

Example 11.3Break down the end of an angle bar
An angle bar has legs of 100 mm and 75 mm, is 10 mm thick and 300 mm long. Find the volume of steel in cm³.
Solution
  1. Break the L-shaped end into two rectangles. Upright: 100 × 10 = 1,000 mm². Flat leg without the corner: (75 − 10) × 10 = 650 mm².
  2. End area: 1,650 mm². Volume: 1,650 × 300 = 495,000 mm³.
  3. In cm³ (1 cm³ = 1,000 mm³): 495,000 ÷ 1,000 = 495 cm³.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.3 Capacity: litres and US gallons11.3 Capacity: litres and US gallons

Capacity is how much a container holds. Liquids are measured in litres (L) or in gallons. The litre is tied to the cubic units: a cube 10 cm (100 mm) on each edge holds exactly 1 L.

1 m³1,000 LexactSI definition of the litre

Example 11.4Litres in a tank
How many litres does the 1,200 mm by 600 mm by 500 mm tank from Example 11.1 hold?
Solution
  1. Its volume is 360,000,000 mm³, which is 0.36 m³.
  2. Method 1: 1 L = 1,000,000 mm³, so 360,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 360 L.
  3. Method 2: 1 m³ = 1,000 L, so 0.36 × 1,000 = 360 L.

Example 11.5A tank in US gallons and litres
A US-made tank is 24 in by 18 in by 12 in inside. Find its capacity in US gallons and in litres, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Volume: 24 × 18 × 12 = 5,184 in³.
  2. US gallons: 1 US gal = 231 in³, so 5,184 ÷ 231 = 22.44 US gal.
  3. Litres: multiply the full gallon value by 3.785411784: 84.95 L.

Two different gallons

The US gallon is defined as 231 in³, which is 3.785411784 L (NIST SP 1038). The imperial gallon is defined as 4.54609 L (Weights and Measures Act). Check which gallon a label means. This book uses US gallons.

Section 11.10 works out tank capacities in litres, US gallons and imperial gallons side by side.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.4 Cylinders: tanks and pipes11.4 Cylinders: tanks and pipes

A cylinder has two equal circular ends joined by a curved side. It works like a prism: every slice is the same circle. So its volume is the circle area times the height (or length).

Volume of a cylinder
V = π × r² × h
r = radius of the end, h = height or length. For a pipe, h is the length of the run.
Example 11.6A vertical tank
A vertical tank is 800 mm across inside and 1,200 mm high. How many litres does it hold, to two decimal places?
Solution
  1. Radius: 800 ÷ 2 = 400 mm.
  2. V = π × 400² × 1,200 = 603,185,789.49 mm³.
  3. Litres: ÷ 1,000,000 gives 603.19 L.
Calculator

603.19 L
Example 11.7Filling a pipe run
A pipe run is 30 m long and the pipe has an inside diameter of 102 mm. How many litres of water fill it, to two decimal places?
Solution
  1. Work in metres. Inside radius: 102 ÷ 2 = 51 mm = 0.051 m.
  2. V = π × 0.051² × 30 = 0.24514 m³.
  3. Litres: × 1,000 = 245.14 L.

Capacity uses the inside diameter, because the water fills the inside. The outside diameter tells you how much space the pipe or tank takes up.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.5 Cones and pyramids11.5 Cones and pyramids

A cone has a circular base that narrows to a point. A pyramid has a flat base, often a square, and triangular sides that meet at a point. A cone holds one third of a cylinder with the same base and height, and a pyramid holds one third of a prism with the same base and height.

Volume of a cone and a pyramid
V = base area × h ÷ 3
Cone: V = π × r² × h ÷ 3
Square pyramid: V = b² × h ÷ 3
h = height at right angles to the base, not the sloping side.
Example 11.8A cone-shaped hopper
A cone-shaped hopper has a radius of 400 mm and a height of 600 mm. How many litres does it hold, to two decimal places?
Solution
  1. Base area: π × 400² = 502,654.82 mm².
  2. V = 502,654.82 × 600 ÷ 3 = 100,530,964.91 mm³.
  3. Litres: ÷ 1,000,000 = 100.53 L.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.6 Spheres11.6 Spheres

A sphere is a perfectly round ball. Every point on its surface is the same distance, the radius, from the centre. Half a sphere is a hemisphere.

Volume of a sphere
V = 4 ÷ 3 × π × r³
Hemisphere: half of that
r = radius. r³ means r × r × r. Use the x³ key, or yˣ 3.
Example 11.9A spherical float
A spherical float has a radius of 150 mm. Find its volume in litres, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. r³ = 150 × 150 × 150 = 3,375,000.
  2. V = 4 ÷ 3 × π × 3,375,000 = 14,137,166.94 mm³.
  3. Litres: ÷ 1,000,000 = 14.14 L.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.7 Composite solids11.7 Composite solids

Many tanks and hoppers are composite solids. Break the solid into basic solids, find each volume, and add. Take away the volume of any hollow part.

Example 11.10A tank with round ends
A tank is a cylinder 1,200 mm long with a hemisphere on each end. The radius is 300 mm. How many litres does it hold, to two decimal places?
Solution
  1. The two hemispheres make one sphere. Cylinder: π × 300² × 1,200 = 339,292,006.59 mm³.
  2. Sphere: 4 ÷ 3 × π × 300³ = 113,097,335.53 mm³.
  3. Total: 452,389,342.12 mm³ = 452.39 L.

Example 11.11A hopper
A hopper is a cylinder 1,000 mm across and 800 mm high, on top of a cone 600 mm high. Find the capacity in litres, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Radius: 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 mm.
  2. A, cylinder: π × 500² × 800 = 628,318,530.72 mm³.
  3. B, cone: π × 500² × 600 ÷ 3 = 157,079,632.68 mm³.
  4. A + B = 785,398,163.40 mm³ = 785.40 L.

Change one value

Double the radius of a cylinder and its volume becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times bigger, because r is squared. Double every length of a solid, and the volume becomes 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times bigger.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.8 Concrete and steel11.8 Concrete and steel

Concrete is ordered by volume. In Canada it is ordered in cubic metres, and some plans and suppliers still use cubic yards. Slabs, footings and walls are prisms, and round piers are cylinders, so the formulas in this chapter give the volume. Change every size to metres first.

A cubic yard is a cube 1 yard on each edge. A yard is exactly 0.9144 m (Weights and Measures Act), so 1 yd³ = 0.9144 × 0.9144 × 0.9144 = 0.764554857984 m³. A yard is also 3 ft, so 1 yd³ = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 ft³.

Concrete volumes
m³ = length × width × thickness, all in metres
yd³ = m³ ÷ 0.9144³
yd³ = ft³ ÷ 27
On the calculator, key ÷ 0.9144 x³ to change m³ into cubic yards.
Example 11.12A garage slab
A garage slab is 7.2 m by 6 m and 100 mm thick. How much concrete is that in m³ and in cubic yards, to two decimal places?
Solution
  1. Thickness in metres: 100 mm = 0.1 m.
  2. V = 7.2 × 6 × 0.1 = 4.32 m³.
  3. Cubic yards: 4.32 ÷ 0.9144³ = 5.65 yd³.

The BC Building Code sets the smallest footing a house may have. Sentence 9.15.3.4.(1) says the minimum footing width or area must comply with Table 9.15.3.4. (page 9-120). For strip footings under exterior walls the table gives 250 mm for 1 floor supported, 350 mm for 2 floors and 450 mm for 3 floors. Under interior walls it gives 200 mm, 350 mm and 500 mm. Column footings, for columns spaced 3 m o.c., need 0.4 m², 0.75 m² and 1.0 m². The table applies unless Sentence (2) (supported joist spans over 4.9 m), Sentence (3) (gravel, sand or silt with a high water table) or Articles 9.15.3.5. to 9.15.3.7. change it.

Sentence 9.15.3.8.(1) (page 9-121) sets the thickness: not less than the greater of 100 mm or the width of the projection of the footing beyond the wall it supports. For a footing centred under a wall, the projection is (footing width − wall thickness) ÷ 2.

Example 11.13Footings at the code minimum
A one-storey house with wood-frame floors has 200 mm concrete foundation walls. The strip footings under the exterior walls are centred under the walls, at the minimum width and thickness the code allows. They run 38 m in all. Find the footing size and the concrete in m³ and yd³.
Solution
  1. Width: 1 floor supported, exterior walls, Table 9.15.3.4.: 250 mm.
  2. Projection: (250 − 200) ÷ 2 = 25 mm.
  3. Thickness, Sentence 9.15.3.8.(1): the greater of 100 mm and 25 mm, so 100 mm.
  4. Volume: 0.25 × 0.1 × 38 = 0.95 m³.
  5. Cubic yards: 0.95 ÷ 0.9144³ = 1.24 yd³.

Minimum is not the design

The code sizes are the smallest a footing may be. The drawings for a job may call for larger footings. Take the sizes from the drawings, and use the code to check that they are not below the minimum.

Example 11.14Footing and foundation wall
A two-storey house has exterior footings at the Table 9.15.3.4. minimum width, centred under 200 mm walls. The walls are 2.4 m high and the footing and the wall each run 40 m. Find the footing thickness, then the total concrete in m³ and yd³.
Solution
  1. Width: 2 floors supported, exterior walls: 350 mm. Projection: (350 − 200) ÷ 2 = 75 mm, so the thickness is the greater of 100 mm and 75 mm: 100 mm.
  2. Footing: 0.35 × 0.1 × 40 = 1.40 m³.
  3. Wall: 0.2 × 2.4 × 40 = 19.20 m³.
  4. Total: 1.40 + 19.20 = 20.60 m³ = 26.94 yd³.
  5. Sentence 9.15.4.6.(1) (page 9-127) also says exterior foundation walls must extend not less than 150 mm above finished ground level. Check on the drawings that the top of the wall is at least that high.

A concrete floor on the ground sits on a layer of crushed stone or gravel. Sentence 9.16.4.3.(1) (page 9-130) says concrete slabs shall not be less than 75 mm thick, not counting any topping. Sentence 9.16.2.1.(1) (page 9-129) says not less than 100 mm of coarse clean granular material, with not more than 10% passing a 4 mm sieve, shall be placed beneath floors-on-ground. Sentence (2) lists the exceptions, such as slabs in garages, carports and accessory buildings.

  2. Granular layer: 100 mm = 0.1 m. 9.6 × 7.2 × 0.1 = 6.912 m³.

Example 11.17Backfill around a footing
A trench 40 m long, 0.6 m wide and 0.5 m deep is dug for a footing. The footing is 350 mm wide and 100 mm thick, and the 200 mm wall on it rises from the top of the footing to the top of the trench and beyond. How much backfill is needed to fill the trench back to the top?
Solution
  1. Trench: 40 × 0.6 × 0.5 = 12 m³.
  2. Footing: 0.35 × 0.1 × 40 = 1.4 m³.
  3. Wall inside the trench: 0.2 × (0.5 − 0.1) × 40 = 3.2 m³.
  4. Backfill: 12 − 1.4 − 3.2 = 7.4 m³.

Concrete and steel are heavy. A load on a truck, a lift with a crane or a load on a beam starts from the mass, and the mass is the volume times the density. Density is the mass of one cubic metre of the material, in kg/m³.

Mass from volume
mass (kg) = volume (m³) × density (kg/m³)
1 t (tonne) = 1,000 kg
Use the density the supplier or the drawings give. The values in Table 11.3 are for practice.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.9 Board feet11.9 Board feet

Softwood and hardwood lumber is often priced by the board foot. One board foot is a piece 1 in thick, 12 in wide and 1 ft long, which is 144 in³, or 1/12 of a cubic foot. Prices are often given per thousand board feet, written MBF.

Lumber is named by its nominal size, such as 2 × 4. The Canadian Wood Council lists the actual surfaced dry (S-Dry) size of a 2 × 4 as 38 mm × 89 mm, or 1½ in × 3½ in. Board feet are tallied on the nominal size: a 1 × 12 that is 16 ft long is sold as 16 board feet, even though the dressed piece is smaller (Briggs, Forest Products Measurements and Conversion Factors, University of Washington).

Board feet
BF = thickness (in) × width (in) × length (ft) ÷ 12
Thickness and width are the nominal sizes in inches. Length is in feet. MBF = 1,000 board feet.
Nominal size, inS-Dry size, mmS-Dry size, in
2 × 438 × 891½ × 3½
2 × 638 × 1401½ × 5½
2 × 838 × 1841½ × 7¼
2 × 1038 × 2351½ × 9¼
2 × 1238 × 2861½ × 11¼
4 × 489 × 893½ × 3½
Table 11.4Nominal and actual surfaced dry lumber sizes, from the Canadian Wood Council table of dimension lumber sizes (cwc.ca/articles/lumber), read Oct 20 2026.
Example 11.20A lumber order
An order is for 24 pieces of 2 × 6, each 12 ft long. The yard charges $1,150.00 per MBF. How many board feet, and what is the cost?
Solution
  1. One piece: 2 × 6 × 12 ÷ 12 = 12 BF.
  2. 24 pieces: 12 × 24 = 288 BF.
  3. Cost: 288 ÷ 1,000 × $1,150.00 = $331.20.

Chapter 11 Volume and Capacity11.10 Tank capacity in litres and gallons11.10 Tank capacity in litres and gallons

A tank may be rated in litres, in US gallons or in imperial gallons. Find the inside volume, change it to litres, and then divide by the size of the gallon you need. The US gallon is 3.785411784 L (231 in³, NIST SP 1038). The imperial gallon is 4.54609 L (Weights and Measures Act). Both factors are exact.

Capacity in three units
L = mm³ ÷ 1,000,000 = m³ × 1,000
US gal = L ÷ 3.785411784
imperial gal = L ÷ 4.54609
Use the inside sizes of the tank. Keep the full litre value in the calculator before dividing.
Example 11.22A rectangular tank
A tank is 1,500 mm by 1,000 mm by 800 mm inside. Find its capacity in litres, US gallons and imperial gallons, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Volume: 1,500 × 1,000 × 800 = 1,200,000,000 mm³ = 1,200 L.
  2. US gallons: 1,200 ÷ 3.785411784 = 317.01 US gal.
  3. Imperial gallons: 1,200 ÷ 4.54609 = 263.96 imperial gal.

Example 11.23A round tank
A vertical tank is 1,200 mm across and 2,500 mm high inside. Find its capacity in litres, US gallons and imperial gallons, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Radius: 1,200 ÷ 2 = 600 mm = 0.6 m. Height 2.5 m.
  2. Volume: π × 0.6² × 2.5 = 2.82743 m³ = 2,827.43 L.
  3. US gallons: ÷ 3.785411784 = 746.93 US gal.
  4. Imperial gallons: ÷ 4.54609 = 621.95 imperial gal.

Chapter
12

Angles and Right Triangles

Square corners hold a shop together. A frame that is out of square will not sit flat, a brace cut to the wrong length will not fit, and a bolt circle laid out at the wrong angle will not line up with its flange.

This chapter starts with angles: how they are measured in degrees and how they are named. Then it moves to the right triangle and the Pythagorean theorem, the rule that lets you find a missing side, check a corner for square with the 3-4-5 method and work out the diagonal of a frame.

In this chapter you will

  • Measure and name angles in degrees
  • Tell acute, right, obtuse and straight angles apart
  • Find a missing angle on a line, around a point and in a triangle
  • Name the legs and the hypotenuse of a right triangle
  • Use the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side
  • Check a corner for square with the 3-4-5 method and with diagonals

Key words

  • angle
  • degree
  • right angle
  • acute angle
  • obtuse angle
  • leg
  • hypotenuse
  • Pythagorean theorem

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.1 Angles and degrees12.1 Angles and degrees

An angle is the amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point. The point is called the vertex, and the two lines are the arms of the angle.

Angles are measured in degrees. One full turn is 360 degrees, written 360°. Half a turn is 180°, and a quarter turn is 90°.

Long arms do not make a bigger angle

The size of an angle is the amount of turn, not the length of the arms. A 50° angle drawn with 20 mm arms is the same angle as one drawn with 2 m arms.

Equal parts of a turn come up in layout work all the time. Holes spaced evenly around a circle, such as the bolt holes in a flange, split the full 360° turn into equal angles.

Example 12.1Angle between bolt holes
Six bolt holes are spaced evenly around a circle. What is the angle between two holes that are next to each other, measured at the centre?
Solution
  1. A full turn is 360°.
  2. Six equal spaces share the turn: 360° ÷ 6 = 60°.
60° between holes.
Try it 12.1
  1. How many degrees are in half a turn?
  2. How many degrees are in one eighth of a turn?
  3. Eight bolt holes are evenly spaced on a circle. Angle between neighbours?
  4. Five holes are evenly spaced on a circle. Angle between neighbours?
  5. Twelve holes are evenly spaced on a circle. Angle between neighbours?
  6. What fraction of a full turn is 270°?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.2 Types of angles12.2 Types of angles

Angles are named by their size. The most important one in the shop is the right angle, exactly 90°. A right angle is a square corner, and drawings mark it with a small square instead of an arc.

An acute angle is less than 90°. An obtuse angle is more than 90° and less than 180°. A straight angle is exactly 180°: the two arms make a straight line.

Two facts let you find a missing angle without a protractor. Angles that sit side by side on a straight line add to 180°. Angles that go all the way around a point add to 360°. For example, if three lines meet at a point and two of the angles are 110° and 95°, the third angle is 360° − 110° − 95° = 155°.

Example 12.2A bent strap
A flat strap is bent so that one side of the bend makes an angle of 125° with the straight part, as shown. Find the angle on the other side of the bend.
Solution
  1. The two angles sit on a straight line, so they add to 180°.
  2. Missing angle = 180° − 125° = 55°.
55°, an acute angle.

Angles that add to 90° or to 180°, the equal angles across from each other where two lines cross, and the angles made where a line crosses two parallel lines are in Section 12.7, Angle pairs and parallel lines.

Try it 12.2
  1. Name each angle: 35°, 90°, 150°, 89°, 180°.
  2. Two angles on a straight line. One is 72°. Find the other.
  3. Two angles on a straight line. One is 135°. Find the other.
  4. Three angles around a point: 120°, 135° and ?. Find the ?
  5. Four equal angles go around a point. How big is each?
  6. Is 91° acute, right or obtuse?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.3 Angles in a triangle12.3 Angles in a triangle

The three angles inside any triangle add to 180°. You can see why by tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and laying them side by side. They fit together into a straight line.

Angles in a triangle
∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°
In a right triangle: the two acute angles add to 90°
∠ means "angle". A right triangle already uses 90° of the 180°, so the other two angles share the other 90°.
Example 12.3The third angle of a gusset
A triangular gusset has angles of 48° and 67°. Find the third angle.
Solution
  1. The three angles add to 180°.
  2. Third angle = 180° − 48° − 67° = 65°.
65°

A triangle with two equal sides also has two equal angles. They are the angles at the ends of the third side. If the angle between the equal sides is 40°, the other two angles share 180° − 40° = 140°, so each one is 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.

Try it 12.3
  1. A triangle has angles of 35° and 85°. Find the third angle.
  2. A triangle has angles of 90° and 27°. Find the third angle.
  3. One acute angle of a right triangle is 45°. Find the other.
  4. Can a triangle have two right angles? Why?
  5. A gusset has two equal sides with 50° between them. Find the other two angles.
  6. All three angles of a triangle are equal. How big is each?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.4 Right triangles and the Pythagorean theorem12.4 Right triangles and the Pythagorean theorem

A right triangle has one right angle. Its sides have special names. The two sides that make the right angle are the legs. The side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse.

The Pythagorean theorem links the three sides of every right triangle. Square each leg and add the results. The total is the square of the hypotenuse.

Figure 12.5 shows it with real squares. A right triangle with legs of 3 and 4 units has a hypotenuse of 5 units. The squares on the legs hold 9 and 16 small squares. The square on the hypotenuse holds 25, and 9 + 16 = 25.

Pythagorean theorem
a² + b² = c²
Find the hypotenuse: c = √(a² + b²)
Find a leg: a = √(c² − b²)
a and b are the legs, c is the hypotenuse. The second and third lines are the theorem transposed (Chapter 8) to make c or a the subject.
  1. Sketch the triangle and mark the right angle.
  2. Label the hypotenuse c and the legs a and b.
  3. To find the hypotenuse, square both legs, add, then take the square root.
  4. To find a leg, square the hypotenuse and the known leg, subtract, then take the square root.
  5. Check: the hypotenuse must be the longest side.
Example 12.4Length of a gusset edge
A triangular gusset has legs of 400 mm and 250 mm. Find the length of the sloped edge (the hypotenuse) to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. c² = 400² + 250² = 160,000 + 62,500 = 222,500.
  2. c = √222,500.
Calculator

471.70 mm
Example 12.5Finding a leg
A brace 2,000 mm long runs from the floor to a column. Its top end is 1,350 mm above the floor. How far from the column is its bottom end? Give the answer to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. The brace is the hypotenuse: c = 2,000. The known leg is a = 1,350.
  2. b² = 2,000² − 1,350² = 4,000,000 − 1,822,500 = 2,177,500.
  3. b = √2,177,500.
Calculator

Sharp EL-531XT

1,475.64 mm. Check: it is shorter than the 2,000 mm brace.
Add to find the hypotenuse, subtract to find a leg

If you add the squares when you are looking for a leg, your answer will be longer than the hypotenuse. That cannot happen. A leg is always shorter than the hypotenuse.

Example 12.6Feet and inches
A right triangle has legs of 2′ 8″ and 1′ 8″. Find the hypotenuse to the nearest 1/16″, in feet and inches.
Solution
  1. Change the legs to inches: 2′ 8″ = 2 × 12 + 8 = 32″ and 1′ 8″ = 1 × 12 + 8 = 20″.
  2. c² = 32² + 20² = 1,024 + 400 = 1,424.
  3. c = √1,424 = 37.73592″ (the display shows more digits).
  4. Change the decimal part to sixteenths: 0.73592 × 16 = 11.77, which rounds to 12 sixteenths.
  5. 12/16 = 34 in lowest terms.
Calculator
TI-30Xa

Sharp EL-531XT

Display 37.73592453
3734″, which is 3′ 134″.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.5 The 3-4-5 check for square12.5 The 3-4-5 check for square

The theorem also works backwards. If the sides of a triangle fit a² + b² = c², the corner between a and b is a right angle. The smallest whole numbers that fit are 3, 4 and 5: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².

Any multiple of 3, 4 and 5 works too, in any unit. Pick the largest set that fits on the work. A reading error of 1 mm matters less on a 1,000 mm diagonal than on a 500 mm one.

  1. From the corner, measure and mark 3 units along one edge.
  2. From the same corner, measure and mark 4 units along the other edge.
  3. Measure the straight distance between the two marks.
  4. If it is exactly 5 units, the corner is square. If it is longer, the corner is open past 90°. If it is shorter, the corner is closed to less than 90°.
Example 12.7Is the frame square?
You mark 600 mm along one side of a frame corner and 800 mm along the other. The tape reads 1,006 mm between the marks. Is the corner square?
Solution
  1. For a square corner: 600² + 800² = 360,000 + 640,000 = 1,000,000, and √1,000,000 = 1,000 mm.
  2. The tape reads 1,006 mm, which is 6 mm too long.
  3. A diagonal that is too long means the corner is opened past 90°.
No. Close the corner until the marks are 1,000 mm apart.
Leg aLeg bDiagonal cCheck: a² + b² = c²
300 mm400 mm500 mm90,000 + 160,000 = 250,000 = 500²
600 mm800 mm1,000 mm360,000 + 640,000 = 1,000,000 = 1,000²
3 ft4 ft5 ft9 + 16 = 25 = 5²
6 ft8 ft10 ft36 + 64 = 100 = 10²
Table 12.1Multiples of 3-4-5 in metric and imperial units.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.6 Diagonals of rectangles12.6 Diagonals of rectangles

A diagonal joins opposite corners of a rectangle. It cuts the rectangle into two right triangles, so its length comes from the Pythagorean theorem: d = √(l² + w²).

Diagonals are the fastest check for a whole frame. Measure both diagonals corner to corner. If the opposite sides are equal and the two diagonals are equal, every corner is 90°.

Example 12.8Diagonal of a base frame
A base frame is 2,400 mm long and 1,200 mm wide. What should each diagonal measure, to the nearest millimetre?
Solution
  1. d² = 2,400² + 1,200² = 5,760,000 + 1,440,000 = 7,200,000.
  2. d = √7,200,000 = 2,683.28 mm.
Calculator

Display 2683.281573
Sharp EL-531XT

Display 2’683.281573
2,683 mm
Squaring a frame

When the two diagonals of a frame are different, the two corners at the ends of the long diagonal are less than 90°. Push those two corners toward each other and measure again until both diagonals match.

  2. A frame is 1,800 mm by 750 mm. Find the diagonal.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.7 Angle pairs and parallel lines12.7 Angle pairs and parallel lines

Some pairs of angles come up so often that they have names. Two angles that add to 90° are complementary angles. The two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary. Two angles that add to 180° are supplementary angles. The two angles at the bend of the strap in Example 12.2 are supplementary: 125° + 55° = 180°.

When two straight lines cross, they make four angles. The angles across from each other are vertically opposite angles, and they are always equal. Each angle and the angle beside it sit on a straight line, so they are supplementary.

Two lines are parallel when they run in the same direction and stay the same distance apart, like the two rails of a gate or the top and bottom plates of a wall. A line that crosses two or more lines is a transversal. Where a transversal crosses two parallel lines, it makes the same four angles at each crossing.

Angle pairWhere the angles areRuleIn Figure 12.7
Complementaryany two anglesadd to 90°the two acute angles of a right triangle
Supplementaryany two anglesadd to 180°a and b, a and d
Vertically oppositeacross from each other at a crossingequala and c, b and d
Correspondingin the same position at each crossingequala and e, d and h
Alternatebetween the parallel lines, on opposite sides of the transversalequalc and e, d and f
Co-interiorbetween the parallel lines, on the same side of the transversaladd to 180°d and e, c and f
Table 12.2Angle pairs and their rules.
Example 12.9Angles on a gate brace
A brace crosses the two parallel rails of a gate. At the top rail, angle a is 52°. Find angles b to h.
Solution
  1. b sits beside a on the straight rail: b = 180° − 52° = 128°.
  2. c is opposite a, so c = 52°. d is opposite b, so d = 128°.
  3. Corresponding angles are equal, so the bottom crossing repeats the top one: e = 52°, f = 128°, g = 52°, h = 128°.
  4. Check with a co-interior pair: d + e = 128° + 52° = 180°.
a, c, e and g are 52°. b, d, f and h are 128°.
Example 12.10Crossed braces
Two braces cross like an X. One of the four angles where they cross is 68°. Find the other three.
Solution
  1. The angle beside 68° makes a straight line with it: 180° − 68° = 112°.
  2. Vertically opposite angles are equal: 68° across from 68°, and 112° across from 112°.
  3. Check: 68° + 112° + 68° + 112° = 360°, a full turn.
112°, 68° and 112°.
Try it 12.7
  1. Find the complement of 28°.
  2. Find the supplement of 28°.
  3. Two lines cross. One angle is 104°. Find the other three.
  4. A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One of the eight angles is 41°. What sizes are the other seven?
  5. Two alternate angles lie between two parallel lines. One is 73°. Find the other.
  6. Two co-interior angles lie between two parallel lines. One is 115°. Find the other.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.8 Degrees, minutes and seconds12.8 Degrees, minutes and seconds

A degree can be split into smaller parts. One degree is 60 minutes, and one minute is 60 seconds. An angle written this way is in degrees, minutes and seconds, D°M′S for short. 36°52′12″ is read "36 degrees, 52 minutes, 12 seconds".

The marks ′ and ″ are the same marks used for feet and inches. After a degree sign they mean minutes and seconds. An angle can also be written in decimal degrees, such as 36.87°. The SIN, COS and TAN keys work in decimal degrees, so you need to change from one form to the other.

Degrees, minutes and seconds
1° = 60′ and 1′ = 60″, so 1° = 3,600″
decimal degrees = D + M ÷ 60 + S ÷ 3,600
minutes = decimal part of the degrees × 60
seconds = decimal part of the minutes × 60
D, M and S are the degrees, minutes and seconds.
Example 12.11D°M′S to decimal degrees
A drawing gives an angle of 36°52′12″. Change it to decimal degrees.
Solution
  1. Minutes: 52 ÷ 60 = 0.866667.
  2. Seconds: 12 ÷ 3,600 = 0.003333.
  3. Add: 36 + 0.866667 + 0.003333 = 36.87°.

  3. Seconds: 0.2 × 60 = 12″.

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.9 Stair geometry12.9 Stair geometry

A straight stair is a row of small right triangles that make one large right triangle. Each step has a unit rise, the height of one riser, and a unit run, the depth of one tread measured from nosing to nosing. The whole flight has a total rise from floor to floor and a total run along the floor. The stringer, the board that carries the treads, slopes along the long side.

Chapter 8 shows the stair formulas: how many risers a stair needs, the unit rise and the total run. This section puts those numbers on a drawing, checks them against the BC Building Code and finds the stringer line with the Pythagorean theorem.

Stair geometry
treads = risers − 1 (a flight from floor to floor)
total rise = risers × unit rise
total run = treads × unit run
stringer line = √(total rise² + total run²)
The stringer line is the hypotenuse of the right triangle that has the total rise and the total run as its legs. The board for a stringer is longer than the line, to leave room for the cuts at each end.

What the BC Building Code says

The BC Building Code 2024 (BCBC), Division B, Part 9, limits the rise and run of stairs. The limits depend on the stair type. In the code, private stairs are "exterior and interior stairs that serve a. single dwelling units, b. houses with a secondary suite including their common spaces, or c. garages that serve houses described in Clause a) or b)". Public stairs are "all stairs not described as service stairs or private stairs" (Notes to Tables 9.8.4.1. and 9.8.4.2., page 9-31). The rise and run tables do not apply to "stairs serving areas only used as service rooms or service spaces".

What is limitedPrivate stairPublic stairWhere in the BCBC 2024, Division B
Rise, maximum200 mm180 mmArticle 9.8.4.1, Sentence (1), Table 9.8.4.1, page 9-31
Rise, minimum125 mm125 mmArticle 9.8.4.1, Sentence (1), Table 9.8.4.1, page 9-31
Run, maximum355 mmNo limitArticle 9.8.4.2, Sentence (1), Table 9.8.4.2, page 9-31
Run, minimum255 mm280 mmArticle 9.8.4.2, Sentence (1), Table 9.8.4.2, page 9-31
Depth of a rectangular treadnot less than its run and not more than its run plus 25 mmthe sameArticle 9.8.4.2, Sentence (2), page 9-31
Risers in one flight5 mm between adjacent treads or landings, 10 mm between the tallest and shortestthe sameArticle 9.8.4.4, Sentence (1), page 9-32
Runs of rectangular treads in one flight5 mm between adjacent treads, 10 mm between the deepest and shallowestthe sameArticle 9.8.4.4, Sentence (3), page 9-32
Table 12.3Stair limits quoted from the BCBC 2024. The rise "is measured as the vertical nosing-to-nosing distance" (Sentence 9.8.4.1.(1)).

Clear height over a stair is measured "vertically, over the clear width of the stair, from a straight line tangent to the tread and landing nosings to the lowest point above". It "shall not be less than 2 050 mm", and over stairs "serving a single dwelling unit or a house with a secondary suite including their common spaces" it "shall not be less than 1 950 mm" (Article 9.8.2.2, Sentences (1) to (3), page 9-30).

Example 12.15Laying out a stair
A stair in a house runs from one floor to the next. The total rise is 2,720 mm. Use the private stair maximum rise of 200 mm to find the number of risers and the unit rise. The treads have a unit run of 265 mm. Check both against Table 12.3, then find the total run and the stringer line, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Risers (Chapter 8): 2,720 ÷ 200 = 13.6. Round up to 14 risers, so no riser is taller than 200 mm.
  2. Unit rise = 2,720 ÷ 14 = 194.29 mm. It is between 125 mm and 200 mm.
  3. Treads = 14 − 1 = 13. The unit run of 265 mm is between 255 mm and 355 mm.
  4. Total run = 13 × 265 = 3,445 mm.
  5. Stringer line = √(2,720² + 3,445²).

Example 12.16A deck stair in inches
A deck stair has 6 risers of 714″ and 5 treads with a unit run of 1012″. Find the total rise, the total run and the stringer line to the nearest 1/16″. Then change the unit rise and run to millimetres (1 in = 25.4 mm, Chapter 7) and check them against the private stair limits.
Solution
  1. Total rise = 6 × 7.25 = 43.5″. Total run = 5 × 10.5 = 52.5″.
  2. Stringer line = √(43.5² + 52.5²) = 68.180″, which is 68316″ or 5′ 8316″.
  3. Unit rise: 7.25 × 25.4 = 184.15 mm, between 125 mm and 200 mm. Unit run: 10.5 × 25.4 = 266.70 mm, between 255 mm and 355 mm.

Example 12.17Checking the risers of a flight
The risers in one flight measure 191, 194, 189, 195, 192, 190 mm, from the bottom up. Does the flight meet Article 9.8.4.4, Sentence (1)?
Solution
  1. Differences between neighbours: 3, 5, 6, 3, 2 mm. The largest is 6 mm, more than the 5 mm allowed between adjacent treads or landings.
  2. Tallest minus shortest: 195 − 189 = 6 mm. That is inside the 10 mm allowed in a flight.
No. The flight passes the 10 mm check but fails the 5 mm check between the 189 mm and 195 mm risers.

  3. A public stair has a unit run of 275 mm. Does it meet Table 9.8.4.2?

Chapter 12 Angles and Right Triangles12.10 Rafters and squaring a layout12.10 Rafters and squaring a layout

A gable roof is two right triangles back to back. In this section the run of a rafter is the level distance it covers, from the wall line to the centre line of the ridge, and the rise is how far it climbs over that run. The rafter line length is the hypotenuse. When the ridge is in the middle, the run is half the span.

Roof slope is often written as rise in 12: the number of units the roof rises for every 12 units of run. A 5 in 12 roof rises 5 mm for every 12 mm of run, or 5″ for every foot. Chapter 13 finds the angle of the roof from the same two numbers.

Rafter line length
rise = run × (rise in 12) ÷ 12
rafter line length = √(run² + rise²)
length per foot of run = √(12² + (rise in 12)²), in inches
Multiply the length per foot of run by the run in feet to get the rafter line length in inches.
Example 12.18Rafter line length in millimetres
A building is 7,200 mm wide with the ridge in the middle. The roof slope is 5 in 12. Find the run, the rise and the rafter line length.
Solution
  1. Run = 7,200 ÷ 2 = 3,600 mm.
  2. Rise = 3,600 × 5 ÷ 12 = 1,500 mm.
  3. Rafter line length = √(3,600² + 1,500²).

Example 12.19Rafter line length in feet and inches
A 6 in 12 roof has a rafter run of 11′ 6″. Find the rafter line length to the nearest 1/16″, two ways.
Solution
  1. Run = 11 × 12 + 6 = 138″. Rise = 138 × 6 ÷ 12 = 69″.
  2. Way 1: √(138² + 69²) = 154.289″.
  3. Way 2: length per foot of run = √(12² + 6²) = 13.416″. The run is 11.5 ft, and 11.5 × 13.416 = 154.284″. The rounded constant makes the last digit differ a little.

Squaring a layout

The outline of a building, a deck or a wall is laid out square with the methods of Sections 12.5 and 12.6. Use the largest multiple of 3, 4 and 5 that fits at a corner, then check that both diagonals match.

Example 12.20Squaring a foundation layout
A foundation layout is 9,600 mm by 6,000 mm. (a) What 3-4-5 marks would you use at a corner, with 1,200 mm as the unit? (b) What should each diagonal measure, to the nearest millimetre? (c) The diagonals measure 11,332 mm and 11,309 mm. Is the layout square?
Solution
  1. (a) 3 × 1,200 = 3,600 mm along one side and 4 × 1,200 = 4,800 mm along the other. The marks should be 5 × 1,200 = 6,000 mm apart.
  2. (b) d = √(9,600² + 6,000²) = 11,320.78 mm.
  3. (c) The diagonals differ by 11,332 − 11,309 = 23 mm, so the layout is not square.

13

Trigonometry

The Pythagorean theorem finds a side when you know two sides. On the job you often know one side and an angle instead: a brace set at 35°, a ramp that must not be steeper than a given slope, a pipe offset made with 45° fittings.

Trigonometry links the angles of a right triangle to its sides. With three ratios, sine, cosine and tangent, and the SIN, COS and TAN keys on your calculator, you can find any side or any angle of a right triangle.

In this chapter you will

  • Name the opposite side, adjacent side and hypotenuse from a given angle
  • Write the sine, cosine and tangent ratios
  • Use SIN, COS and TAN in DEG mode on both calculators
  • Find a missing side from one side and one angle
  • Find a missing angle with the inverse keys
  • Solve slopes, ramps, pipe offsets, bevels and mitres

Key words

  • trigonometry
  • opposite side
  • adjacent side
  • sine
  • cosine
  • tangent
  • inverse trig function
  • offset

Chapter 13 Trigonometry13.1 Naming the sides13.1 Naming the sides

Trigonometry is the math that links the angles of a right triangle to the lengths of its sides. It always starts from one of the two acute angles. From that angle, each side gets a name.

  • The hypotenuse is across from the right angle. It is the longest side.
  • The opposite side is across from the angle you are working with. It does not touch that angle.
  • The adjacent side is next to the angle. It is the side that touches the angle and is not the hypotenuse.
Mark the angle first

Put your finger on the angle you are working with. The side your finger cannot touch is the opposite side. Of the two sides that touch it, the longer one is the hypotenuse and the other one is the adjacent side.

Try it 13.1
  1. In Figure 13.2, which side is opposite angle X?
  2. Which side is adjacent to angle X?
  3. Which side is the hypotenuse?
  4. Which side is opposite angle Y?
  5. Which side is adjacent to angle Y?
  6. Angle X is 31°. How big is angle Y?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 13 Trigonometry13.2 Sine, cosine and tangent13.2 Sine, cosine and tangent

Draw any right triangle with a 30° angle, large or small. Divide the opposite side by the hypotenuse and you always get 0.5. The ratio of two sides depends only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle. That is why one angle and one side are enough to find the rest.

Each pair of sides gives a ratio with its own name. The sine (sin) of an angle is opposite ÷ hypotenuse. The cosine (cos) is adjacent ÷ hypotenuse. The tangent (tan) is opposite ÷ adjacent.

The three trig ratios
sin A = opposite ÷ hypotenuse
cos A = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse
tan A = opposite ÷ adjacent
A memory aid: SOH CAH TOA. S = O ÷ H, C = A ÷ H, T = O ÷ A.
Example 13.1The ratios of a 3-4-5 triangle
A right triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. Angle A is opposite the side of 3. Write sin A, cos A and tan A as fractions and as decimals.
Solution
  1. From A: opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = 5.
  2. sin A = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6.
  3. cos A = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.
  4. tan A = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75.
sin A = 3/5 = 0.6, cos A = 4/5 = 0.8, tan A = 3/4 = 0.75.

The trig keys and DEG mode

Angles in this book are in degrees, so both calculators must be in degree mode. On the TI-30Xa, check that DEG shows in the display. If it does not, press DRG until it does. On the Sharp EL-531XT, DEG shows at the top of the display, and the DRG key steps through DEG, RAD and GRAD. Chapter 2 shows the keys.

The keys go in a different order. On the TI-30Xa, key the angle first, then SIN, COS or TAN. On the Sharp, press sin, cos or tan first, then the angle, then =.

CalculatorCheck your mode: sin 30°

Sharp EL-531XT

Display 0.5
If sin 30° does not give 0.5, the calculator is not in degree mode. In radian mode the same keys give −0.988. Press DRG until DEG shows, then try again.

Chapter 13 Trigonometry13.3 Finding a side13.3 Finding a side

  1. Mark the angle you know.
  2. Name the side you know and the side you want: opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse.
  3. Pick the ratio that uses those two sides: SOH, CAH or TOA.
  4. Write the ratio with the numbers in it and transpose it for the side you want.
  5. Check: the hypotenuse must be the longest side.
When the side you want is on the bottom, divide

If the unknown side is the hypotenuse in SOH or CAH, or the adjacent side in TOA, it sits under the fraction bar. Then you divide the known side by sin, cos or tan instead of multiplying.

Example 13.2Height of a brace (sine)
A brace 2,400 mm long is set at 35° to the floor. How high up the wall does it reach? Give the answer to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. From the 35° angle: the brace is the hypotenuse, the height is the opposite side.
  2. Opposite and hypotenuse: SOH. sin 35° = opposite ÷ 2,400.
  3. Multiply both sides by 2,400: opposite = 2,400 × sin 35°.

The top chord of a truss rises at 22° over a half span of 4,200 mm. How high is the peak above the bottom chord? Give the answer to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. The half span is the adjacent side. The height is the opposite side.
  2. Opposite and adjacent: TOA. opposite = 4,200 × tan 22°.

A brace must reach 1,800 mm up a column and meet the floor at 50°. How long is the brace? Give the answer to two decimal places.

  2. SOH: sin 50° = 1,800 ÷ hypotenuse.
  3. Transpose: hypotenuse = 1,800 ÷ sin 50°.

Chapter 13 Trigonometry13.4 Finding an angle13.4 Finding an angle

When you know two sides, work out their ratio and then turn the ratio back into an angle. That is the job of an inverse trig function: SIN⁻¹, COS⁻¹ and TAN⁻¹. They are the second functions of the SIN, COS and TAN keys.

On the TI-30Xa, key the ratio, then 2nd and SIN, COS or TAN. Put a division in brackets so it is worked out first. On the Sharp, press 2ndF and sin, cos or tan first, then the ratio, then =.

Example 13.6The angles of a 3-4-5 triangle
Find both acute angles of a 3-4-5 triangle to two decimal places. Angle A is opposite the side of 3.
Solution
  1. From A, the opposite side is 3 and the adjacent side is 4: TOA.
  2. tan A = 3 ÷ 4, so A = tan⁻¹(3 ÷ 4) = 36.87°.
  3. The two acute angles add to 90°: B = 90° − 36.87° = 53.13°.

Display 36.86989765
Any ratio that uses two known sides gives the same angle. Here SOH, sin A = 3 ÷ 5, checks the answer.
A = 36.87°, B = 53.13°
Ratio key or angle key?

SIN, COS and TAN turn an angle into a ratio. SIN⁻¹, COS⁻¹ and TAN⁻¹ turn a ratio into an angle. A sine or cosine ratio is always less than 1, because the hypotenuse is the longest side. If yours is more than 1, the sides are mixed up.

  2. Opposite 700, hypotenuse 1,000. Find the angle to two decimal places.
  3. Adjacent 1,100, hypotenuse 1,400. Find the angle to two decimal places.
  4. Opposite 9″, adjacent 12″. Find both acute angles to two decimal places.
  5. sin A = 0.5. Find A.
  6. tan A = 1. Find A.
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 13 Trigonometry13.5 Slopes and ramps13.5 Slopes and ramps

A slope is a right triangle lying on its side. The rise is the opposite side, the run is the adjacent side and the length along the slope is the hypotenuse. The angle of the slope comes from the tangent: angle = tan⁻¹(rise ÷ run).

Slopes are also given as a percent grade: rise ÷ run × 100. A slope written as 1 in 12 rises 1 unit for every 12 units of run.

Example 13.7Angle and grade of a ramp
A ramp rises 450 mm over a run of 5,400 mm. Find its angle and its percent grade to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Rise and run are opposite and adjacent: TOA.
  2. Angle = tan⁻¹(450 ÷ 5,400).
  3. Grade = 450 ÷ 5,400 × 100 = 8.33%.
Calculator
TI-30Xa
(450÷5400)2ndTAN⁻¹
Display 4.763641691
Sharp EL-531XT
2ndFtan⁻¹(450÷5400)=
Display 4.763641691
Angle 4.76°, grade 8.33%. The drawing is to scale: a slope this gentle looks almost flat.
1 in 12

450 ÷ 5,400 is the same ratio as 1 ÷ 12. So a slope of 1 in 12 has the same angle, 4.76°.

Example 13.8Fall of a drain line
A drain line runs 12,000 mm at a grade of 2%. How far does it fall, and what is its angle to two decimal places?
Solution
  1. Grade = fall ÷ run × 100, so fall = run × grade ÷ 100 = 12,000 × 2 ÷ 100 = 240 mm.
  2. Angle = tan⁻¹(2 ÷ 100) = tan⁻¹(0.02) = 1.15°. Key it the same way as the ramp angle.
Fall 240 mm, angle 1.15°.

Inches per foot

A slope can also be given as the rise in inches for every foot (12″) of run, such as 14″ per foot. Divide the inches by 12 to get the ratio rise ÷ run. 14″ per foot is 0.25 ÷ 12, the same as 1 in 48, which is also written 1:48. As a grade it is 0.25 ÷ 12 × 100 = 2.08%, and its angle is tan⁻¹(0.25 ÷ 12) = 1.19°.

A roof that rises 5″ per foot is a 5 in 12 roof. Its ratio is 5 ÷ 12, which is 1 in 2.4, and its angle is tan⁻¹(5 ÷ 12) = 22.62°. Section 13.8 works with roof slopes in this form.

One slope, five ways
14″ per foot = 1 in 48 = 1:48 = 2.08% grade = 1.19°. The first three are ratios of rise to run, the grade is the ratio × 100 and the angle comes from TAN⁻¹ of the ratio.
Try it 13.5
  1. Rise 300 mm, run 4,000 mm. Find the angle and the grade to two decimal places.
  2. A slope of 1 in 20. Find the angle to two decimal places.
  3. A 1% grade over a 15,000 mm run. How far does it fall?
  4. A ramp is 3,000 mm long, measured along the slope. It slopes at 4°. Find the rise to two decimal places.
  5. A roof rises 6″ for every 12″ of run. Find its angle to two decimal places.
  6. A ramp must rise 600 mm at an angle of 3°. How long is the run, to the nearest millimetre?
Answers are in the Answer Key.

Chapter 13 Trigonometry13.6 Pipe offsets13.6 Pipe offsets

An offset moves a pipe over to a new line that is parallel to the first one. In this book an offset has two fittings of the same angle, and the three measurements of an offset are the sides of a right triangle. In this book, set, run and travel are measured along the centreline of the pipe.

  • Set: how far the pipe moves over, square to the two parallel lines. It is the side opposite the fitting angle.
  • Run: the distance along the line of the pipe that the offset takes up. It is the side adjacent to the fitting angle.
  • Travel: the length along the centreline of the angled part, from one fitting to the other. It is the hypotenuse.
Offsets
travel = set ÷ sin θ
run = set ÷ tan θ
set = travel × sin θ
θ (theta) is the fitting angle. These are SOH and TOA with the set as the opposite side.
Example 13.9A 45° offset
A line must move over 450 mm using 45° fittings. Find the travel and the run, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Travel = 450 ÷ sin 45°.
  2. Run = 450 ÷ tan 45°. Since tan 45° = 1, the run equals the set: 450.00 mm.

A line must move over 14″ using 60° fittings. Find the travel and the run to the nearest 1/16″.
Solution
  1. Travel = 14 ÷ sin 60° = 16.166″.
  2. Run = 14 ÷ tan 60° = 8.083″.
  3. Change each decimal part to sixteenths and round.

Where offset constants come from

Travel = set ÷ sin θ is the same as set × (1 ÷ sin θ). The number 1 ÷ sin θ depends only on the fitting angle, so it can be worked out once and kept in a table. The same goes for 1 ÷ tan θ for the run. Every one of these numbers comes from the calculator:

Chapter 13 Trigonometry13.7 Bevel and mitre angles13.7 Bevel and mitre angles

A mitre joint joins two pieces at a corner. Each piece is cut at an angle so that the joint line splits the corner angle in half. For a square corner (90°), each piece is cut at 45° to its edge.

A frame with equal sides and equal corners turns 360° in all, so each corner turns 360° ÷ n, where n is the number of sides. The corner angle inside the frame is 180° − 360° ÷ n, and each piece is cut at half of that to its edge.

Sides nCorner angle 180° − 360° ÷ nCut angle to the edge (half the corner)Angle away from a square cut
490°45°45°
6120°60°30°
8135°67.5°22.5°
12150°75°15°
Table 13.2Mitre angles for frames with equal sides.

A bevel is an angled face cut along the edge of a plate. In this book the bevel angle is measured from the square edge. Through the full thickness t, the bevel is t × tan(angle) wide at the top. Two plates bevelled at the same angle and butted together open a groove of twice the bevel angle.

Example 13.11Width of a bevel
A 12 mm plate is bevelled at 30° through its full thickness. How wide is the bevel at the top, to two decimal places?
Solution
  1. The thickness is the side adjacent to the bevel angle. The width is the opposite side: TOA.
  2. Width = 12 × tan 30°.

Carpentry slopes are right triangles too. A roof slope written as rise in 12, a stair step with its unit rise and unit run, and a ramp written as 1 in 10 all give a rise and a run. The angle is tan⁻¹(rise ÷ run), the same as for the ramps in Section 13.5. Section 12.10 finds rafter lengths from the same numbers.

Example 13.13A slope in inches per foot
A drain line slopes 14″ per foot. Write the slope as 1 in …, as a percent grade and as an angle to two decimal places. How far does it fall over a 30 ft run?
Solution
  1. Ratio: 0.25 ÷ 12. Turn it over: 12 ÷ 0.25 = 48, so the slope is 1 in 48.
  2. Grade = 0.25 ÷ 12 × 100 = 2.08%.
  3. Angle = tan⁻¹(0.25 ÷ 12) = 1.19°.
  4. Fall = 30 ft × 0.25″ per foot = 7.5″.

The BC Building Code 2024 (BCBC), Division B, sets the slopes that roof coverings may be put on. Sentence 9.26.3.1.(1) says the slopes "shall conform to Table 9.26.3.1." In that table (page 9-242), asphalt shingles have a minimum slope of "1 in 3" for normal application and "1 in 6" for low slope application, with "no limit" as the maximum. Wood shingles have a minimum of "1 in 4" and cedar shakes "1 in 3".

Example 13.14Shingles on a 3 in 12 roof
Can asphalt shingles go on a 3 in 12 roof in normal application? In low slope application? Compare the angles.
Solution
  1. 3 in 12 is 3 ÷ 12 = 1 in 4. Its angle is tan⁻¹(3 ÷ 12) = 14.04°.
  2. Normal application needs at least 1 in 3 = 4 in 12, an angle of tan⁻¹(1 ÷ 3) = 18.43°. The roof is flatter than that.
  3. Low slope application needs at least 1 in 6 = 2 in 12, an angle of tan⁻¹(1 ÷ 6) = 9.46°. The roof is steeper than that.
Not in normal application. Yes in low slope application.

Roof slope also changes how much venting a roof space needs. Sentence 9.19.1.2.(1) says "the unobstructed vent area shall be not less than 1/300 of the insulated ceiling area." Sentence 9.19.1.2.(2) says "Where the roof slope is less than 1 in 6 or in roofs that are constructed with roof joists, the unobstructed vent area shall be not less than 1/150 of the insulated ceiling area" (page 9-136).

Example 13.15Vent area for a low roof
A roof framed with trusses has a slope of 1.5 in 12. The insulated ceiling below it is 96 m². Which Sentence of Article 9.19.1.2 applies, and what is the least vent area?
Solution
  1. 1.5 in 12 is 1.5 ÷ 12 = 1 in 8. 1 in 6 is 2 in 12. The roof is flatter, so its slope is less than 1 in 6.
  2. Sentence (2) applies: vent area = 96 ÷ 150 = 0.64 m².
  3. For comparison, a roof of 1 in 6 or steeper over the same ceiling needs 96 ÷ 300 = 0.32 m² (Sentence (1)).
Sentence (2). At least 0.64 m² of unobstructed vent area.

Stair angle

Each step of a stair is a small right triangle. The stair angle is tan⁻¹(unit rise ÷ unit run). The largest rise with the smallest run allowed by Tables 9.8.4.1 and 9.8.4.2 (Section 12.9) gives the steepest stair those two limits allow: tan⁻¹(200 ÷ 255) = 38.11° for a private stair and tan⁻¹(180 ÷ 280) = 32.74° for a public stair.

Example 13.16Angle of a stair
The stair in Example 12.15 has a unit rise of 194.29 mm (2,720 ÷ 14) and a unit run of 265 mm. Find the stair angle to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Angle = tan⁻¹(unit rise ÷ unit run) = tan⁻¹(194.29 ÷ 265).
  2. Key 2,720 ÷ 14 in the brackets so the calculator keeps every digit of the unit rise.

Rafter cuts

A rafter sits at the roof angle θ. Two of its cuts are plumb or level when the rafter is in place. The plumb cut at the ridge is vertical. The birdsmouth over the wall has a level seat cut and a plumb heel cut. Because the rafter edge slopes at θ, the seat cut meets the rafter edge at θ, and a plumb cut meets the rafter edge at 90° − θ. A square cut across the rafter is 90° to the edge, so a plumb cut is θ away from square.

Example 13.18Cut angles for a 6 in 12 rafter
Find the roof angle of a 6 in 12 roof, the angle between the seat cut and the rafter edge, and the angle between the plumb cut and the rafter edge, to two decimal places.
Solution
  1. Roof angle θ = tan⁻¹(6 ÷ 12) = 26.57°.
  2. The seat cut is level, so it meets the rafter edge at θ = 26.57°.
  3. The plumb cut meets the rafter edge at 90° − 26.57° = 63.43°. It is 26.57° away from a square cut.

Appendix
A

Kitchen Math

A cook uses the same math as the rest of the shop. A recipe that feeds 12 has to feed 45. A recipe written in cups has to be measured in millilitres. A case of carrots loses weight when it is peeled, so the cook has to buy more than the plate needs.

This appendix covers three kitchen skills: scaling a recipe with a scaling factor, changing between cooking measures, and food yield percent. They use the fractions, decimals and percents from Chapters 4, 5 and 6.

In this appendix you will

  • Find a scaling factor and use it to make a recipe larger or smaller
  • Change cups and spoons to millilitres, and pounds and ounces to kilograms and grams
  • Find a yield percent from a yield test
  • Find the edible portion, the amount to buy and the cost per kilogram after trimming

Key words

  • yield
  • scaling factor
  • as purchased (AP)
  • edible portion (EP)
  • yield percent

Appendix A Kitchen MathA.1 Scaling a recipeA.1 Scaling a recipe

The yield of a recipe is the amount it makes, such as 12 portions or 3 kg. To make a different amount, every ingredient is multiplied by the same number, the scaling factor.

The scaling factor is the new yield divided by the old yield. A factor greater than 1 makes the recipe larger. A factor less than 1 makes it smaller. The yields must be in the same unit: portions with portions, grams with grams.

Scaling a recipe
Scaling factor = new yield ÷ old yield
New amount = old amount × scaling factor
New yield over old yield. Never the other way around.
Example A.1Soup for a bigger crew
A soup recipe makes 12 portions. The kitchen needs 45 portions. Scale the recipe.
Solution
  1. Scaling factor = new yield ÷ old yield = 45 ÷ 12 = 3.75.
  2. Multiply every ingredient by 3.75. For the stock: 2.4 L × 3.75 = 9 L.
IngredientFor 12 portions× 3.75For 45 portions
Chicken stock2.4 L9 L
Diced onion600 g2,250 g
Vegetable oil30 mL112.5 mL
Salt10 mL37.5 mL
Calculator

Display 3.75
Sharp EL-531XT
45÷12=
Display 3.75
The scaling factor is 3.75.
9 L of stock, 2,250 g of onion, 112.5 mL of oil and 37.5 mL of salt.

Sometimes the portion size changes too. Then work out each yield as a total amount first: number of portions × portion size.

Example A.2More portions, bigger portions
A rice recipe makes 20 portions of 150 g and uses 1.2 kg of dry rice. The kitchen needs 64 portions of 200 g. How much dry rice is needed?
Solution
  1. Old yield: 20 × 150 g = 3,000 g.
  2. New yield: 64 × 200 g = 12,800 g.
  3. Scaling factor = 12,800 ÷ 3,000 = 4.2667 (rounded here, kept in full on the calculator).
  4. Rice: 1.2 kg × the factor = 5.12 kg.
Calculator

Display 5.12
Sharp EL-531XT
12800÷3000×1.2=
Display 5.12
Divide and multiply in one run, so the full factor is used: 5.12 kg.
5.12 kg of dry rice.
Example A.3Scaling down
A biscuit recipe makes 40 biscuits with 1,600 g of flour and 1.2 L of milk. Make 15 biscuits.
Solution
  1. Scaling factor = 15 ÷ 40 = 0.375. It is less than 1, so the recipe gets smaller.
  2. Flour: 1,600 g × 0.375 = 600 g.
  3. Milk: 1.2 L × 0.375 = 0.45 L = 450 mL.

New over old

The factor is new yield ÷ old yield. If you divide the other way, a recipe you meant to make larger comes out smaller. Check: more portions needs a factor greater than 1.

Round only what you measure

Keep the full scaling factor on the calculator and round only the amount you will weigh or measure. Measure dry goods by mass when you can. It is more exact than cups.
